items: House and Senate roll calls for the 119th Congress, with each member's yes or no, a phone, an office, and a portrait. Bills and resolutions introduced in this Congress are listed with the person who introduced each one. The floor list is the latest week the House has published. When a measure names taxpayer money, the amount is marked beside the title, and those measures are listed together. Read the full bill or the full resolution. Green is a yes. Rose is a no. Gold is on the floor list. Brass is taxpayer money.
Amounts named in a title or short account
Taxpayer money. The largest amount named in the title or the short account. A paler brass mark is a smaller amount. A deeper bronze mark is a larger amount.
Bills and resolutions introduced in this Congress
Bills and resolutions introduced in the 119th Congress, with a portrait of the person who introduced each one. Read the full bill or the full resolution.
The latest week the House has published
The House floor list for the latest published week. Gold means the item is scheduled.
Yes and no on each House vote
House roll calls for 2025 and 2026. Green is a yes. Rose is a no.
Yes and no on each Senate vote
Senate roll calls copied from Voteview. A unanimous consent vote has no senator-by-senator yes or no.

epa drinking water violation Water These are active community water systems in EPA's Drinking Water System Search. A community system serves homes. The number is EPA's count of quarters with a Safe Drinking Water Act violation over the past three years. That count includes monitoring and reporting violations. It is not a measurement from one tap, and it is not a score this page calculated. A health-based flag means EPA currently marks a violation of a maximum contaminant level, a maximum residual disinfectant level, or a treatment technique. Neighborhoods use the same OpenStreetMap names as the restaurant list. A neighborhood is matched to the community system that serves the most people among systems whose served city matches that neighborhood's city and state. EPA does not publish a separate result for the neighborhood. Cyan is the number of quarters with a violation. A lighter cyan is fewer quarters. A darker cyan is more. Each dot is a neighborhood. The color is the community system that serves the most people in that city and state. A neighborhood with no matching served city is not drawn. The dot is not a sample from a tap. Roads and cities: OpenFreeMap, OpenMapTiles, OpenStreetMap. Each block is one quarter in this count, up to 12. Cyan fills one block for each quarter with a violation. The cyan darkens as that count rises. A chemical appears here when EPA names it on a current health-based violation. Current means the violation is unaddressed or addressed in the 2026Q3 snapshot. Resolved and archived violations are not listed. Above a limit means a maximum contaminant level: EPA recorded that contaminant above the allowed amount. That is not a sample from one tap, and a missed test is not included. A treatment technique is a required process, not a chemical measured in the water. EPA does not publish a ranking of which contaminant is most harmful, and this page does not calculate one. Health goal of zero means EPA's public-health goal is no amount of that contaminant. The sentence is EPA's description of exposure above the limit, from the National Primary Drinking Water Regulations.

Nevada's attorney general, running for governor. Aaron Ford's campaign says he grew up in a working-class family, taught public-school math, earned five degrees, and serves as attorney general. It says he and his wife, Berna, moved to Nevada. He says he would speed housing permits, limit corporate buying of single-family homes, and ban software used to set rents. He says pharmacy benefit managers should pass drug-discount savings to patients, and that he would set up relief for medical debt. He says data centers should bring their own power, grid equipment, and water before they receive tax breaks.

Democratic candidate for New York's 23rd District. His campaign says he was raised in a working family, with a father who ran a small contracting business and a mother who was a school secretary. He says he has been a teacher, a nonprofit leader, and a person of faith, and has also waited tables and kept books for a Main Street business. He says medical debt is a leading cause of bankruptcy and he supports universal health care while opposing cuts to Medicare, Medicaid, VA benefits, and rural hospitals. Republican candidate for governor Aaron Guckian's campaign describes him as a lifelong Rhode Islander with roots in East Greenwich and experience in government, banking, nonprofits, education, and health care. He says the campaign would invest in public schools, teacher support, and vocational and technical programs tied to local employers. He says he would expand training and incentives so the state has more primary-care doctors and dentists, and he calls for targeted tax relief and less wasteful spending.

Candidate for U.S. Senate from Michigan. He says he lives in Ann Arbor with his wife and two daughters. He says he is running so the Senate works for residents rather than for billionaires. He says his local health work included free glasses for children, removing lead from Detroit elementary schools, and making naloxone widely available. He says he led a program to cancel medical debt and wrote a citizen's guide to Medicare for All.

Army Reserve veteran and U.S. representative for Arizona's 8th District. His campaign says he is a former Army Reserve captain and intelligence officer and a former Maricopa County prosecutor, and the son of immigrants whose family fled places including Syria and Venezuela. He says he grew up in the 8th District and is seeking a second term. He says border security is national security and that he will keep voting to stop illegal crossings and defend private property. He says the government should pass a budget and live within its means, and that fentanyl should carry harsher sentences. He says he would fund police, preserve Social Security, and defend the Second Amendment.
District 2 · U.S. House · West Virginia · Democratic

Father and community leader running for Congress. His campaign says he fled an authoritarian regime, arrived without English, and that his family lived in severe poverty. He says he got ahead through public schools, government assistance, faith communities, and neighbors, and that he is running as a father to protect liberty and justice. He says the campaign is values-driven and is trying to reclaim affordability, care, and empowerment. Border Patrol veteran running for Congress. He says El Paso property taxes are too high because of school budgets and bonds, and that he would work with local leaders to make them more affordable. It says he now serves on Agriculture and Natural Resources and is whip of the Blue Dog Coalition. He says he is working to lower the cost of food, housing, health care, and utilities, including by limiting tariffs he argues raise prices for families and farmers. He says water is the issue he hears about most, and he has pushed storage projects, faster environmental review, and funding for local water systems. He says he would cut red tape that stalls infrastructure, support agriculture, and strengthen public safety so families are not choosing between health care and rent.

Surgeon and Army veteran running for Congress in New Jersey's 12th District. He says he built a Princeton practice, has volunteered in disaster zones, and takes no corporate PAC money. Working-class candidate for the U.S. Senate. Adam Withrow says he is not a politician. He says fossil fuels are finite and that the country should start moving off them instead of building the future on older technology. He says medicine has been organized around corporate profit, and that health care for everyone would cost less than half the defense budget. He says he opposes war, and that trade and treating people as equals will do more than bombs.

Her campaign says she is an Afro-Latina mother from New Jersey, the daughter of Colombian and Dominican immigrants, who watched her mother work as a seamstress until a union job changed the family's finances. She says she led New Jersey Working Families, directed politics for Bernie Sanders's 2020 campaign, and served in the Labor Department. She says she has spent 25 years fighting for working families, including New Jersey's $15 minimum wage and paid sick days. She says she is taking that fight to Washington and will take on bosses and bullies in both parties.

Attorney general of Massachusetts, running for re-election. Andrea Campbell's site says she was born and raised in Roxbury and the South End, went from foster care to Princeton and into public service, and is the first Black woman to serve as the state's attorney general. She says she is trying to make life more affordable by putting money back into people's pockets. She says she is defending freedoms against rollbacks from the Trump era. She says she is fighting for the next generation and for wider opportunity for every child, including reproductive rights, civil rights, and cases against powerful corporations.

Independent candidate for governor. Andrea James's site says her family has lived in Massachusetts for seven generations and that she is running to put the government's agenda on the needs of people. She says a governor's priorities should be housing, health care, child care, education, and quality of life, and she calls housing a human right. She says people should be able to see a doctor without going into debt and that families should have child care they trust. She says Massachusetts should not have contracts with ICE, and she wants data centers banned in favor of lower utility costs and green energy.

U.S. representative for Oregon's 6th District, seeking another term. Her campaign says her father immigrated from Mexico, served in the military, and spent three decades as a police officer, and that she was the first in her family to finish college. It says she worked in the Oregon Legislature on health care, the minimum wage, and paid family leave before her election to Congress. She says she will fight rising costs for working families, seek more living-wage jobs, and keep backing worker protections and investments in rural health care, education, and infrastructure. She says she led efforts to cap prescription prices in Oregon and is pushing Congress to let Medicare negotiate drug prices and to strengthen hospital and insurance price transparency. She also treats mental health and substance use as part of health care that is too often overlooked.

Health-care and business candidate running for Congress in Wisconsin's 5th District. His campaign says he is the son of Wisconsin's union movement, a product of public schools, and not a career politician. It says he built a career in health care and business beside workers and manufacturers. He says he would bring practical leadership aimed at lower costs, good-paying jobs, and better health care. He says protecting fair elections and democratic institutions is the issue that makes progress on jobs, health care, and education possible. He says women must be able to make their own reproductive-health decisions and that Congress should secure that right.

U.S. representative, Navy veteran, and firearms-business owner. He says he was commissioned from Notre Dame, served 28 years in the Navy including three combat deployments to Kuwait and Iraq, then earned a master's from the University of Georgia and built Clyde Armory from a garage hobby into a company with two Georgia stores. Elected in 2020, he says he serves on the Appropriations and Budget committees. He says that on April 12, 2013, the IRS confiscated $940,000 from his business through civil asset forfeiture, and that the agency later offered to return part of it if he forfeited the rest. He says most small-business owners hit by that process lacked the money to fight, and he presents the case as a fight against overreaching government. On guns, he argues that taxes on firearms and ammunition, from the National Firearms Act to local per-gun taxes, treat a constitutional right as a privilege and could tax it out of reach.
District 2 · U.S. House · New York · Republican

U.S. representative for New York's 2nd District. His campaign says he has represented the district since 2021 and chairs the House Homeland Security Committee. It also says he is vice chair of a Financial Services subcommittee on capital markets. He says he led the push for permanent funding of the World Trade Center Health Program. He says a tax law he supported raised the state-and-local tax deduction cap from $10,000 to $40,000 and ended federal tax on tips. He also points to an expanded child tax credit, a new deduction for seniors, and a policing bill he says passed the House.

Independent candidate for the U.S. Senate. He says he is a working-class candidate whose jobs have included military service, security, commercial trucking, information technology, food service, maintenance, and scientific research. He says he is running without political connections because he is tired of the status quo. He says government should keep life safe, affordable, peaceful, healthy, and fair, with personal liberty as the minimum. He says tax money should not go mainly to regime-change wars or to tax breaks for corporations that have not shown loyalty to the public. He says candidates, including himself, have a duty to serve the public rather than foreign governments or corporations.

Small-business owner and plumber running for Congress The campaign says Andrew Sneed was born and raised in Huntsville, graduated from Lee High, and later left restaurant work to start over as a plumber's helper. He founded Whole Home Solutions in 2019 and says the company now has several trucks and employees. He says he is running because the district needs a representative who is not a career politician. On health care, he says he wants to expand Medicaid, negotiate drug prices, regulate for-profit insurers, and keep rural hospitals open. On affordability, he says he wants to address housing, lower utility bills, and restore federal investment in energy efficiency. He also calls for congressional term limits, overturning Citizens United, a lobbying waiting period, and a ban on stock trading by members of Congress.

U.S. representative for Indianapolis and a former law enforcement officer. Born and raised in Indianapolis, he says he has focused on the economy, national security, and the middle class, and he serves on Intelligence, Transportation and Infrastructure, and a select committee on the Chinese Communist Party. He says he hosts an annual job fair and a youth opportunities fair. He says he would invest in early childhood and K-12 schools, raise teacher pay, and expand Pell Grants and workforce training as alternatives to a four-year degree. He says tariffs are raising household costs, and he wants tax cuts for working families, small businesses, and entrepreneurs rather than policy aimed at the ultra-wealthy. He says he opposes cuts to SNAP, introduced a Food Deserts Act to finance grocery stores in underserved areas, and supports military and humanitarian aid to Ukraine.

U.S. representative from Kentucky running for the Senate. Andy Barr's campaign calls him an eighth-generation Kentuckian and says he was the first member of the state's House delegation to endorse Donald Trump and chaired Trump's 2024 Kentucky primary campaign. He says he would deport people he calls criminal illegal immigrants, restart border-wall construction, hire more border agents, restore Remain in Mexico, and end catch-and-release. He says he voted for tax cuts that end taxes on Social Security for seniors, on overtime, and on tips, and he wants to expand Kentucky coal and block climate rules he says were imposed through financial regulators. He says he will defend girls' sports and private spaces, veterans' disability and health benefits, the Second Amendment, police funding, sanctions on fentanyl tied to China, and Kentucky farmers, including a federal framework for hemp products.

U.S. representative Andy Biggs is an Arizona native who has represented the state's 5th Congressional District since 2016. He is running for governor with Sine Kerr for lieutenant governor. He says he will eliminate the state income tax, work with local governments to ease property taxes, and cut permitting barriers for new homes. He says he will end state incentives for data centers and set standards to protect Arizona's water and energy. He says he will reconvene a Border Strike Force aimed at human trafficking and drug trafficking and equip police to fight drug trafficking.

Green Party candidate for governor of Maryland. Andy Ellis says he has lived in Baltimore since 2005, coached debate, and spent nearly 15 years in corporate technology. He says he has spent more than a decade organizing the Green Party in Baltimore and across Maryland. He says the state should stop data-center projects that he argues threaten communities, water, and public health. He says unaffiliated and third-party voters are shut out of meaningful elections and that he has a plan aimed at two-party political corruption. He says the state should spread wealth, power, and opportunity so more residents have a say in incentives, public funds, and budgets.

Physician and U.S. representative who chairs the House Freedom Caucus. The son of immigrants who fled communist Eastern Europe after World War II, he says he has been a Johns Hopkins physician, a Naval Reserve veteran, a state senator, and, since 2025, an eighth-term congressman. He chairs the Agriculture appropriations subcommittee. He says he is fighting to restore fiscal responsibility in Washington and protect taxpayer dollars. The campaign describes him as a common-sense conservative with the courage to change Washington. He says he is unafraid to speak for the priorities of Maryland's 1st District.

Community advocate running for Congress in Los Angeles. Angela Gonzales-Torres's campaign says she is a democratic socialist and a lifelong Angeleno from Highland Park, the daughter of a deportee who was raised by a single mother. It says she helps people leaving prison enter college and works on affordable housing that brings younger and older residents together. She says she would abolish ICE, make Los Angeles more affordable, and increase access to critical services. She says housing, health care, and education should be affordable, and she wants higher taxes on the wealthy to pay for them. She says she would abolish super PACs so elections answer to voters rather than donors.

Entrepreneur running for Congress. Angela Rodriguez Prilliman's campaign says she is a Fort Worth mother and entrepreneur who grew up in Stephenville, graduated from Texas A&M, and spent more than a decade in technology. It says she is the Democratic candidate in the 12th District. She says she would seek universal health care and universal child care, paid for by taxes on billionaires. She also lists voting rights, full funding for public schools, and getting billionaire money out of politics. She says Congress should protect AI whistleblowers, set liability and testing rules, and restrict AI companions for children.

Florida state representative and union organizer She says she is a state representative, union organizer, and mother who was born and raised in Jacksonville. She says she started as an organizer in Duval County and ran for office because she wanted more working people in government. She says she is running to lower costs, raise wages, and put working families ahead of billionaires. She says she supports Medicare for All and a national rent freeze with a moratorium on evictions. She says she supports free child care and pre-K, and a Working Families Guarantee for workers.

Neighborhood-council leader running for Congress. Angélica Dueñas's campaign says she was born in Sun Valley to parents who immigrated from Mexico, raised five children, and was the first in her family to finish college. It says she earned degrees from Cal State Los Angeles and Woodbury and served as president of the Sun Valley Area Neighborhood Council. She says she takes no corporate PAC, AIPAC, oil, or drug-company money, and she supports Medicare for All and housing as a right. She says she would abolish ICE, create a path to legal status, and pass the DREAM Act. She says she would raise the minimum wage, protect the right to unionize, and cancel student debt by making public college and trade school tuition-free.

U.S. representative for Missouri's 2nd District. She grew up working at her parents' carpet store in Manchester, studied business at the University of Missouri, and later held management jobs at Hallmark and Ralston Purina before coming to Congress. She says she has worked to cut taxes and regulation so local businesses can hire, and she voted for a tax bill that removes taxes on tips, overtime, and Social Security. She highlights the Fight Online Sex Trafficking Act and funding for rape-kit testing through the Debbie Smith Act. She says she will keep defending a right to life, and she introduced a bill to require medical care for infants born alive after an abortion.

Faith leader and small-business owner running for Congress in Tennessee's 3rd District. Her campaign says she is a progressive faith leader who owns Biased Apparel and is chief executive of Work of Place, a firm that helps congregations use their buildings for neighbors' economic stability. She and her husband Mike live in Chattanooga's Park Central neighborhood. She says workers deserve wages that cover the bills and the freedom to organize, and that rural counties need funded hospitals, schools, and infrastructure. She says she takes no corporate PAC money and wants fair elections and fair maps. She says she would protect reproductive freedom and LGBTQ+ people, treat health care as a human right, and fund Oak Ridge's science without sacrificing the land.

U.S. representative running for another term. Anna Paulina Luna's campaign says she is a mother, Air Force veteran, and one of the younger members of Congress who did not grow up with wealth or a political family. It says her father struggled with substance abuse and her mother raised her on her own. She says big government is often the problem, not the solution, and that her politics come from growing up in hard circumstances and serving in the military. She says she wants reforms aimed at problems people actually face rather than an elitist approach to Congress.
Comptroller on the Kane County list and the Will County list. The lists do not state a party. A vote counts only where this declaration was filed.

Former Wayland selectwoman and business executive running for secretary of state. Anne Brensley's site says she is a former Wayland selectwoman, chief executive of DevCo North America, and was born in Honduras. She says she wants to encourage business growth. She says she will engage directly with disenfranchised voters. She says she will protect the integrity of the ballot and campaign on transparency and local control.

Pediatrician running for U.S. Senate Annie Andrews's campaign says she is a pediatrician and mother who has cared for South Carolina children for nearly twenty years, from newborns to teenagers. She says she is not a career politician. She says families are struggling with grocery prices, child care, and the cost of health care, and her platform treats health care as a right. Her listed plans include tackling debt and congressional perks, cutting taxes, lowering premiums, protecting rural hospitals, and reversing Medicaid cuts. The platform also lists strong schools and affordable child care, reproductive freedom, political corruption, and an end to gun violence.

Maryland attorney general, running for reelection. Anthony Brown's campaign says he is the state's attorney general, an Army veteran, and a lawyer raised by immigrant parents. It says that before this office he served in the legislature, as lieutenant governor, and in Congress. He says he created a civil-rights division and widened the Independent Investigations Division so it can prosecute police-involved deaths. He says he has defended gun-safety laws in court and pursued wage theft and corporate conduct that harms workers and consumers. He says he has sued when federal policy threatened environmental rules, voting rights, and protections for women and immigrants.
District 21 · U.S. House · New York · Republican

Printing-company executive running for Congress in New York's 21st District. His campaign says he is the chief executive of Sticker Mule, an online printing company with plants in New York, South Carolina, and Italy. It says he is paying for the race himself so donors, lobbyists, and special interests will not have a claim on him. He says he would cut waste, bring reliable internet and cell service to the North Country, and oppose regulations he argues are driving up food and utility prices. He says he would work to secure the northern border, treat farmers more fairly, and restore First and Second Amendment rights he says have been restricted in New York.

Libertarian candidate for lieutenant governor. He says he is a high school English and debate teacher in Cibolo and a military veteran. He says he is running so Texans have a choice built on liberty, a balanced budget, and straight talk. He says real tax relief requires cutting spending, and that property-tax plans without spending cuts only move the bill somewhere else. He says he opposes taxpayer-funded welfare and supports immigrants who come to Texas to work. He says Texas should legalize marijuana and end what he calls the lieutenant governor's war on drugs.
District 1 · U.S. House · New Hampshire · Republican

Republican candidate for New Hampshire's 1st District. His campaign says his great-grandparents came through Ellis Island and that he came to the University of New Hampshire in 1983. He says he started a business with a small amount of cash and credit and now oversees more than 20 car dealerships and 11 collision centers employing about a thousand people. His plan leads with lower costs, higher wages, and a balanced-budget amendment. He says he will protect the 2017 tax cuts and the elimination of taxes on tips, overtime, and Social Security, and fully support Social Security and Medicare. He calls for securing the southern and northern borders, a common-sense immigration reform, and defense of every law-abiding citizen's right to own a firearm.

Former Macomb County clerk, running for Michigan secretary of state. Anthony Forlini's campaign says he is a lifelong Michigan resident, a husband, father, and grandfather, and the son of an Italian immigrant. It says he has served as a township supervisor, a state representative, and Macomb County clerk. He says he would protect election integrity by removing ineligible and deceased voters from the rolls and by requiring watermarked ballots statewide. He says he would stop sending voter information to outside groups and audit county clerks so election practices match across the state. He says he would cut secretary of state wait times and make routine services easier to finish online or in person.

Candidate for governor of Michigan. Anthony Hudson's campaign says he was born and raised in Texas and moved to Michigan in 2012 to be in his children's lives. He describes himself as a blue-collar candidate running against what he calls corruption in Lansing. He says he would eliminate property taxes and the state income tax. He says he would stop data-center and solar-panel development and protect farmland. He says he wants lower taxes, smaller government, and decisions returned to local communities.

U.S. representative for Maryland's 6th District, seeking another term. Her campaign says she was raised in Buhl, Idaho, the daughter of a potato farmer, and is the mother of four. It says she led Common Sense Media's Washington office and served as a deputy assistant secretary for communications at the Department of Commerce. She says she will work on rising costs, health care, and equal access to a good education, and that she wants more job training, small-business support, and better-paying work in the district. She points to her work expanding broadband and says technology should drive development across the 6th District. She says she will put progress ahead of partisanship and defend democratic institutions.

Attorney and former mayor running for Congress. April Verlato's campaign says she was born and raised in Arcadia, studied political science at UCLA, and earned a law degree at Southwestern. It says she took over her father's law practice in 2000 and later won a city council seat, serving as mayor. She says the economy should reward innovation and hard work rather than regulations she argues hold back workers and small businesses. She points to her role founding the Downtown Arcadia Improvement Association and says she focused on opportunities for minority-owned businesses. She says she would go to Congress to bring back good-paying jobs and economic growth.
District 8 · U.S. House · New Jersey · Other

Teacher and union representative running for Congress in New Jersey's 8th District. His campaign says he is the son of immigrants, raised in Jersey City by parents who owned a small business, and that he is a teacher, union representative, husband, and father. He says working-class families need a voice that is not a career politician. He says families are dealing with underfunded classrooms, rising costs, and barriers for children with special needs. He says Washington needs practical solutions from people who understand those everyday struggles.

Retired Navy captain running for Congress. Armen Kurdian's campaign says he is a retired Navy captain who served 25 years and is a husband, father, and neighbor in Southern California. He says he is running to put working families ahead of party politics. He says housing, groceries, and gas are squeezing families, and he would lower those costs and stop wasteful spending. He says California's utility bills are among the nation's highest and he would fight to make power cheaper and more reliable. He says he would bring back good-paying jobs, support small business, and cut regulations he argues are pushing employers out.

Libertarian candidate for railroad commissioner. He says he lives in Austin and has been a Libertarian activist for many years. His campaign slogan is to vote Libertarian and downsize government across the board. He says the market, not the state, should choose the energy mix, with no subsidies or mandates that pick winners among oil, gas, wind, solar, or nuclear. He says mineral and surface owners should be protected from eminent-domain abuse, and that disputes with energy developers should be settled by voluntary agreements. He says operators should plug wells and clean sites through bonding and insurance priced to their risk, rather than through taxpayer bailouts.

Retired programmer and president of the Fairfax County Taxpayers Alliance. His campaign says he grew up in Washington, D.C., earned degrees from the University of Pennsylvania, and moved to Vienna in 1976. He says he worked 40 years as a computer programmer and has been taxpayers-alliance president for 29 years. He says inflation is the tax people pay for government spending, and that chronic disease from ultra-processed food drives trillions in medical spending that could be cut without cutting programs. He says abortion takes a life, that it should stay legal in rare cases to save the mother, and that marriage should be encouraged. He says public schools should compete through vouchers, teach phonics and arithmetic, and post the Ten Commandments, and that immigrants should be vetted before they enter.
District 10 · U.S. House · North Carolina · Democratic

Clinician running for Congress in North Carolina's 10th District. Her campaign says she treats patients who cannot afford to be sick and is running because the 10th District needs someone who sees that directly. Her campaign lists universal health care, rules for artificial intelligence and data centers, anti-corruption, and affordability as its top issues.

U.S. representative from northeast Iowa running for the Senate. She is a mother and a former journalist who previously represented Iowa's 67th House district, including Hiawatha, Robins, Cedar Rapids, and Marion, where she says she lives. In Congress she serves on Appropriations, the Select Committee on Communist China, and the Ethics Committee. She says she is working with President Trump to secure the border, cut wasteful spending, and pursue pro-growth policies. She says she has introduced bipartisan bills to improve child care for working families and to ban federal lobbying as a check on corruption. She says that on Appropriations she works to account for every taxpayer dollar, and that on the China committee she works to hold the Chinese Communist Party accountable.

U.S. senator and former Florida attorney general She says she is a fifth-generation Floridian raised in Plant City who earned degrees from the University of Florida and a master of laws from Stetson. She says she was a federal prosecutor and a circuit judge before her election as attorney general, and that she was sworn into the Senate on January 21, 2025, after an appointment by Governor Ron DeSantis. She says she supports America First policies on law and order, economic prosperity, and American sovereignty. She says that as attorney general she championed public safety, support for law enforcement, and efforts against violent crime. She says that as a senator she is working to uphold conservative values and strengthen national security.
No 2026 issue list was found for this candidate.

U.S. representative running for another term. August Pfluger's campaign says he is a seventh-generation Texan who grew up on a family ranch, graduated from San Angelo Central and the Air Force Academy, and spent 20 years as a combat pilot and a national-security adviser to Donald Trump. It says he still works in the family ranching business and founded an energy investment company in the Permian Basin. He says Republicans delivered border-wall money, support for immigration enforcement, and tax cuts that include no tax on tips, overtime, and Social Security. He says he helped secure billions in border reimbursements for states such as Texas and will keep defending conservative Texas values and national security.

Business owner running for Congress in Pennsylvania's 4th District. Aurora Stuski says she has lived in West Norriton for 35 years, owns a business, and is the mother of three. She describes herself as a conservative running to lower costs and support law enforcement. She says she will work to lower costs for families and make it easier for small businesses to operate. She also says she will back law enforcement, secure the border, and push for more transparent government.

Attorney and Republican nominee for Florida's 2nd District The campaign says he is a Panama City native, a conservative attorney, and former general counsel to U.S. Senator Rick Scott. He graduated from Mosley High School, played college soccer, earned a law degree from Duke, and lives in Panama City with his wife, Hala, and their three children. He says he is running to secure the border, defend Florida values, back law enforcement and the military, and put American families first. He says he is fully pro-life from conception and will defend parental rights against policies he says undermine families. He says he will defend the First and Second Amendments and work so veterans can get care and everyday essentials stay affordable.

U.S. representative for Georgia's 8th District. He lives in Tifton and says his experience runs from the cattle farm to the boardroom. A University of Georgia graduate, he says he spent 20 years running his own small business and serves on the Intelligence, Armed Services, and Agriculture committees. He says he represents Georgia values and free-market principles, and that the goal is to protect personal freedoms, individual liberties, and economic opportunity for the next generation. He says his agenda is to strengthen local businesses and benefit Georgia families. He supports limited government, small-business job growth, a strong national defense, and a healthy agricultural economy.

U.S. representative and the first woman of color elected to Congress from Massachusetts. She says she is an advocate, policy-maker, activist, and survivor, elected in 2018 to the 7th District. She says the people closest to the pain should be closest to the power. She says the campaign has worked on abortion access, student-loan cancellation, and housing justice. She says more than $35 million has come home for community health centers, transit, workforce training, and climate justice. Her site lists a just economy, the climate crisis, housing as a human right, and changes to the criminal legal system among the issues she is organizing around.

Navy captain and Democratic nominee for Florida's 7th District His campaign says he grew up in a Central Florida family, attended the U.S. Naval Academy, and served 24 years in the Navy and Navy Reserve, including medevac flights and combat missions. He later worked at the State Department and for Senator Bill Nelson, then served as NASA chief of staff. He says his first priority is making Florida affordable again by reversing health-care premium hikes and tariffs he calls illegal. He says he would push competition among power companies and property insurers, raise the federal minimum wage, and pass the PRO Act. He says he would restore Medicaid funding, negotiate drug prices, and protect Social Security and Medicare.

Porter County commissioner running for Congress. A Purdue graduate in mathematics and German, she worked as a software engineer and project manager at United Airlines and later as a financial advisor and certified financial planner. Elected to the Porter County Board of Commissioners in 2022, she says she knocked on more than 11,000 doors and has volunteered with Rotary and SCORE. She says safe cities, secure borders, and smarter spending are her vision, including arresting and prosecuting criminals and ending catch-and-release. She says she would curb inflation and waste so families keep more purchasing power, and reduce the national debt by putting American families and businesses ahead of foreign interests. She says schools should teach students how to think, that girls' sports and facilities should be reserved for biological females, and that law-abiding people should keep the right to bear arms.

Veterinarian running for Congress in Oregon's 1st District. Her campaign says Barbara Kahl is an Oregon native who spent about 20 years in business, including finance work at Intel, and earned her veterinary degree in 2006. It says she later served as chief veterinarian for American Samoa, where she built an animal-control unit, and that she has testified before the Oregon Legislature. She says economic growth comes first, through small-business relief, infrastructure, and jobs, and she wants housing built faster by cutting permitting delays. On schools, she supports public schools, school choice, vocational pathways, and funding that follows the student, and she says parents rather than federal officials should control curriculum. She also calls for lower health-care costs and stronger veterans' care, more accountable federal spending, forest stewardship that keeps timber communities working, and support for ports and local police.

Oakland mayor running for re-election. Barbara Lee says that in her year as mayor she has worked to root out corruption at City Hall, reopen fire stations, and stabilize the budget. She is asking voters for another four years. She says streets are getting cleaner and that she wants more good-paying local jobs. She says she will keep a broad approach to homelessness and add affordable housing across the city. She says she is using prevention programs against crime and wants Oakland to be a model of accountable city government.

U.S. representative and small-business owner Barry Moore is a member of Congress and the owner of a waste-removal and demolition company he and his wife started after he earned an agricultural science degree at Auburn and served in the Alabama National Guard. He previously served in the Alabama House, where he says he judged votes by faith, family, finance, and freedom. He says illegal immigration should face zero tolerance, and he wants people in the country illegally deported, beginning with those he calls the most violent. He points to tax cuts on tips, overtime, and Social Security, and says he is working to cut regulations and shrink the federal government. He says violent criminals should be prosecuted fully and that federal law enforcement should be funded to focus on crime rather than political opponents.

Marine infantry officer and attorney running for Indiana secretary of state. Beau Bayh's campaign describes him as a seventh-generation Hoosier who served as a Marine infantry officer and rose to captain, including the Scout Sniper Unit Leader's Course. He says his first priority is to stop waste and insider dealing in the secretary of state's office, including unnecessary travel, luxury vehicles, no-bid contracts, and high-paying jobs for family and friends. He says illegal votes should not count and that every eligible Hoosier should be able to vote. He supports statewide ballot referendums, including on redistricting, and says he will advocate for new small businesses and for working families.

U.S. representative for Vermont The campaign says Becca Balint is the first woman and openly LGBTQ+ person to represent Vermont in Congress. It says she is a teacher and parent, served in the state Senate, and now sits on the House Judiciary Committee and in the Progressive Caucus. Her campaign says housing is a human right and points to the Community Housing Act, which she introduced to fund affordable housing, renter protections, and down-payment help. The site says she has introduced bills to expand mental health care after disasters and for young people. It says she cosponsored the Freedom to Vote Act and the John Lewis Voting Rights Act and wants Supreme Court term limits and tighter ethics rules.

Democrat running for Congress in Nebraska's 3rd District. Her campaign says she is a lifelong resident of the 3rd District running against Adrian Smith, and that her neighbors include farmers, factory workers, and small-business owners facing the same pressures her family does. She says a nearby farm going to auction is part of why she is running. She says she would protect Social Security, Medicare, and SNAP, bring back funding Congress already approved, and invest in public schools without banning books. She supports unions, a woman's private medical decisions, veterans, and equipping police, and she says a secure border should come with a fair immigration system. She also says she would respect the Second Amendment while working to prevent violence, expand senior care, and improve access to health care.

Marine veteran running for Congress in Michigan's 2nd District. His campaign says he grew up on a farm in Hesperia, enlisted at 18, and served nearly 20 years in the Marine Corps as an infantryman, including combat tours. He says he is running to keep serving rural Michigan. He says he would bring down grocery and gas prices, back small businesses, strengthen collective bargaining, and bring manufacturing jobs back with Buy American policies. He supports more funding for public schools, larger Pell Grants, and vocational training, and he says he backs Medicare for All. He also lists veterans, the natural environment, and community safety among his priorities.

U.S. representative for Virginia's 6th District. Ben Cline's office says he serves on Judiciary, Appropriations, Intelligence, and Budget. He represented the 24th District in the Virginia House of Delegates from 2002 to 2018, chaired its Militia, Police, and Public Safety committee, and worked as an assistant commonwealth's attorney and as chief of staff to Congressman Bob Goodlatte. He grew up in Rockbridge County and lives in Botetourt County with his wife Elizabeth and their two daughters. His office lists the economy, energy, veterans, health care, and reforming Congress among the issues he works on.

Candidate for Congress who says Utah, not a party, will set his votes. He describes a childhood in which his mother worked as hard as anyone he knew, the lights sometimes went out, and he took his first job at 11. He says his work in Congress would focus on lowering housing costs, getting people medical care, and making daily life easier for Utah families. He says he will work with anyone for results and will also stand alone when he thinks democracy, protest, or due process is being trampled. His priorities page also lists protecting the environment and defending human rights and opportunity.

U.S. senator running for another term. Ben Ray Luján's campaign says he filed for another Senate term and has focused on costs, health care, and internet access for New Mexico. He says he has worked to lower prescription prices and to protect Medicare, Medicaid, and Social Security. He says he has defended nutrition assistance for working families, seniors, veterans, and rural communities. He says he has worked to connect families to the internet and to deliver results in all 33 counties.

U.S. representative for Mississippi's 2nd District. His campaign says he has a long record of bringing federal funding home, and that in 2024 and 2025 that work totaled nearly $4 billion. He won the 2026 Democratic nomination for the seat. The campaign says that funding covered health care, infrastructure, agriculture, and education. It also says the money covered broadband, public safety, clean water, and disaster recovery. He presents that record as results on the issues that matter most in the district.

Long-haul trucker and small-business owner running for Congress in Arizona's 8th District. Her campaign says she is a mother who grew up in a union family, earned a commercial driver's license in 1997, and logged more than 4 million miles over 27 years while running a small trucking business. She says a car accident ended an Army ROTC scholarship at the University of Arizona. She says she will lower the cost of groceries, fuel, and housing, protect Social Security and Medicare, and force drug companies to renegotiate prices. She says she will secure the border and stop trafficking, and support an earned path to citizenship for people who follow the law. She says she will fight lease-purchase deals that trap truck drivers in debt, defend the right to organize, and protect reproductive care and contraception.

Small-business owner Bernadette Wilson is a lifelong Alaskan who started a commercial waste company in 2016 and has led the Alaska Policy Forum and worked with Americans for Prosperity. She also served as a senior advisor on Nick Begich's congressional campaign. She says Alaska should move from talk to construction on projects including AKLNG, ANWR, Willow, the Ambler Road, and West Susitna access. She says she will restore the statutory Permanent Fund Dividend. She says Alaska's children should be able to attend strong schools in the state.

Retired Air Force lieutenant colonel running for Congress. Berney Flowers's site says he served nearly 21 years in the Air Force, with later work in national defense and cybersecurity, and that he was raised in a working-class family. He describes himself as a father, mentor, and veteran rather than a career politician. He says he advocates term limits, fiscal responsibility, and working across party lines. He says he supports taking politics out of public schools, parental involvement, and local control of education. He says he supports strong immigration enforcement, national defense, and public safety.

Retired Army major general and attorney running for the U.S. Senate. His campaign says he graduated first in his West Point class, earned a law degree from Harvard, and commanded troops in combat, including a joint task force in Afghanistan. It says he later held senior civilian posts in the Army and as an adviser at the CIA. He says he would focus on balancing the federal budget. He says he would lower the tax on selling a home and the broader tax burden on Virginia families. He says he would protect veterans' health benefits, ban members of Congress from trading stocks, and support new nuclear plants to bring down household energy costs.

Stay-at-home parent running for Congress in Pennsylvania's 13th District. Beth Farnham says she is a stay-at-home parent running again for the 13th District, with the support of her husband, Rob. She says she wants a representative who is accessible across the district. She says she would defend reproductive freedom, public education, gun safety, universal health care, and immigration reform. She also lists affordability and the environment, and says climate change requires action to protect agriculture and communities.

Author and former Roanoke Times reporter running for Congress. Her campaign says she grew up poor in a small Ohio town, was the first in her family to go to college, and spent 25 years at The Roanoke Times. She says her books include Factory Man, Dopesick, and Paper Girl, and that Dopesick became a Hulu series she helped produce. She says she is running to make life affordable for working families, expand health and mental health care, and invest in rural communities. She says every child should have a real chance by rebuilding the ladder that helped her leave poverty. She says she has stood with people overlooked by a system that benefits billionaires, including families hurt by addiction and workers whose jobs disappeared.

Former mayor running for Congress. Beth Van Duyne's campaign says she is a single working mother who left home at 17, put herself through college, and became the first woman mayor of her hometown before serving in a presidential administration. She says she is running in the 24th District so her children have the same opportunities she had, and she warns about socialism, the border, and hostile nations. She says she is a conservative who has fought government corruption, supported removing criminal noncitizens from North Texas, and backed growth and the Constitution.

Scientist and working mother running for Missouri's 3rd District. She grew up in Foristell, lives in St. Peters, and has worked as an environmental chemist testing crops and checking communities for lead and forever chemicals. She supports full, equal funding for public schools from pre-K through college and union apprenticeships. She wants affordable physical and mental health care, and federal infrastructure money for rural roads, bridges, broadband, and water. She ties her environmental work to clean air and water, and she supports the Women's Health Protection Act, the Equal Rights Amendment, and Medicare for All.

U.S. representative for Minnesota's 4th District. Betty McCollum's office says she has represented Saint Paul, Ramsey County, and most of Washington County since 2001, and that she was the second Minnesota woman elected to Congress since statehood. She serves as the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Defense Subcommittee. Her office says she champions education, environmental protection, health-care access and affordability, fiscal responsibility, and international engagement that pairs diplomacy and development with a strong national defense. She says she wants higher education kept affordable and public schools accountable to parents and local officials, and she supports universal health coverage and the Affordable Care Act. On defense, she says funding should keep the armed forces trained and equipped, with priority for military health care and ending military sexual assault.

U.S. senator running for re-election. He says he is a businessman and a former U.S. ambassador to Japan, and that serving Tennessee in the Senate has been the honor of his life. He says his business career shapes how he approaches the debates in the Senate. He says he is running to keep fighting for lower taxes, energy independence, secure borders, and the rule of law. He says his Senate work has included securing the southern border, supporting small businesses, and strengthening national security. He says he will keep pushing an America First agenda and treat the Chinese Communist Party as a serious adversary.

U.S. representative and small-business owner from Ottawa County. His campaign says he is a lifelong Ottawa County resident who built and ran a local business before Congress, and that he and his wife Natalie raised five children in southwest Michigan. He attended Holland Christian High School and earned a political science degree from Calvin College. He says he has pushed to rein in federal spending to fight inflation and lower the cost of energy, groceries, and housing. He supports more American energy production and fewer regulations so small businesses can hire. He says he backs limited government, secure borders, and safe communities, and that he has worked on Great Lakes and PFAS issues.

Former prosecutor and U.S. representative for southeastern Massachusetts. He says he was elected to the state House at 23, later served as a state senator and Norfolk district attorney, and won this U.S. House seat in 2010. He and his wife Tevis live in Bourne and have two adult children. He says he is challenging tariffs that raise prices and hurt small businesses, and that he wants health care that is more affordable and accessible. He says he has fought to protect Social Security, Medicare, reproductive rights, and veterans and military families. He says he serves on Foreign Affairs and Armed Services and has brought home federal money for coastal resiliency, public safety, clean energy, and jobs.
District 21 · U.S. House · New York · Democratic

Dairy farmer running for Congress in New York's 21st District. His campaign says his parents started a North Country dairy farm after the Peace Corps, and that he has run Twin Mill Farms with his wife and three sons for 22 years. It says he has also coached junior-varsity basketball, served on the Lisbon school board, and founded a nonprofit for children with cancer. He says he would repeal costly regulations, support fair trade, and bring manufacturing back so prices fall for families and for seniors on fixed incomes. He says this border district needs more Border Patrol staffing, a harder path for illegal entry and an easier legal one, and fixes to the guest-worker programs farms rely on. He says farms and Main Street businesses also need fewer burdensome rules and investment in rural roads and bridges.

Election-reform advocate running for U.S. Senate. Blake Huber says he has worked on campaigns since he was 17 and spent more than 30 years in management, including apartments, a small business, a motel, and teams of network engineers. He says he later chaired the Libertarian Party of Colorado, served on its national committee, and now focuses on how elections are run. He wants approval voting, so people can support every candidate they like and elections are not decided by fear of wasting a vote. He says immigration should pair orderly borders with a simpler legal path for people who pass background checks and want to work. He says federal rules bury small businesses in cost and paperwork, and that old rules should expire while new ones face a test of their economic impact.

State senator and oil-and-gas business owner running for Congress. A seventh-generation Louisianian and LSU graduate, he says he has owned a home in Baton Rouge for more than 25 years, expanded his family's oil and gas business, and is raising four children with his wife Ashley, a special-education teacher. He was elected to the state Senate in 2023. He says he passed a law so Louisiana can prosecute corrupt politicians after they leave office, and in Congress he would push term limits and a permanent ban on members trading individual stocks. He says he wrote the state law forcing New Orleans to follow immigration law, and he would finish a border wall, mandate E-Verify, and treat cartels as foreign terrorist organizations. He says he authored constitutional carry, banned Big Tech money in Louisiana elections, and banned ultra-processed food in school cafeterias.

U.S. representative for northern Utah. He says three terms in Congress have centered on costs, immigration, the military, and what he calls the Utah way of life, and he notes a constituent-service award for his office. He says he is pushing border security, American energy, fiscal discipline, and conservative social policy. He points to work strengthening Hill Air Force Base, expanding the charitable tax deduction, protecting the Great Salt Lake, and funding local water, roads, trails, and education.

Candidate for railroad commissioner. He says he was raised in Midland by a father in the Texas energy business, entered the industry in 1994, and worked as an energy trader. He says he is also a rancher and mineral owner and has chaired the Tarrant County Republican Party. He says the Railroad Commission oversees oil and gas plus uranium, coal, and salt, and that the seat should be held by a conservative who will back the president. He says he will end diversity, equity, and inclusion programs, regulation he calls overbearing, and influence from radical Islam and the Chinese Communist Party in Texas oil. He says he will enforce the Legislature's ban on hostile foreign ownership of land in order to protect the Texas oil industry.

Union leader running for Congress in Pennsylvania's 7th District. Bob Brooks is a union president who says he has spent his career fighting for workers. He says he is running so Washington works for working people. He says that as a union president he pressed politicians for higher wages, better health care, and stronger benefits. His issues page lists affordability, health care, a higher minimum wage, stronger unions, housing costs, and ending corruption.

Former Navy submarine officer running for U.S. Senate. Bob Chew says he served as a Navy submarine officer during the Cold War and has spent three decades creating jobs. He says he is an independent candidate running for people who are tired of the two parties. He says he will measure success by problems solved and people helped, not by how much public money is spent. He says he cannot be bought or bullied, and that his promise is to Coloradans rather than to parties or donors.

Former teacher and Bucks County commissioner running for Congress in Pennsylvania's 1st District. Bob Harvie taught for 26 years before serving on the Bucks County Board of Commissioners. His campaign says he is running because working families are paying the price while Washington is in chaos. He says families deserve a fair shot to earn a living, afford a home, raise children, and retire with dignity. He describes the race as a chance to send someone to Congress who will fight for a better deal for working people.

Retired Air Force lieutenant colonel and former state senator running for secretary of state. His campaign says he is an Omaha native who served 21 years in the Air Force, including Desert Shield and Desert Storm and the Looking Glass mission at Offutt, and retired in 2000. It says Gov. Dave Heineman appointed him to the Legislature in 2009, voters reelected him, and colleagues chose him to chair the Executive Board. He says the secretary of state should run elections for every voter, make legal voting easy, make cheating difficult, and certify the results no matter who wins. He calls for public transparency, checks that safeguards against fraud are working, and support for the county officials who run elections. He says he would modernize the office where that improves service without weakening security, so people trust the count.

U.S. representative for Ohio's 5th District. His official biography says he has represented Ohio's 5th District since 2007 and is a senior member of the Energy and Commerce Committee, where he chairs the Energy Subcommittee. He says he has held more than 1,500 meetings in the district since 2012 and has had 35 bills and provisions signed into law. He lists rural broadband, less government spending, a strong national defense, the substance-use crisis, energy independence, and commonsense government reform as top priorities. He points to the INFO Act on opioid data, the Advanced Nuclear Technology Development Act, and the Critical Electric Infrastructure Act to protect the power grid. He highlights the Drinking Water Protection Act on algal toxins, faster processing of VA appeals, and laws on propane supply and precision-agriculture connectivity.

U.S. representative and physician from Missouri. His campaign describes a record in Congress and in Jefferson City centered on immigration enforcement, abortion limits, gun laws, and taxes. He highlights a bill aimed at visa overstays and earlier Missouri legislation against sanctuary cities and employment of people without legal status. He says he co-chairs the Pro-Life Caucus and has backed federal abortion limits, after authoring Missouri clinic rules and helping write the 2019 heartbeat bill. He points to work on constitutional carry and the Second Amendment Preservation Act, and to the tax bill he says he passed with House Republicans.

Retired Navy commander running for Congress. Bob Smith's campaign says he enlisted in the Navy and rose to commander over 26 years, including combat deployments, and was named the Navy's engineer of the year in 2023. It says he holds engineering degrees and lives in Carpinteria with his family. He says he would cut wasteful spending, lower housing, energy, and food costs, and expand homeownership while protecting Social Security and Medicare. He says schools should emphasize reading, math, and STEM, plus vocational paths and research ties to local universities. He says immigration policy should secure the border, remove people convicted of violent crimes, and update farmworker visas.

Candidate for governor of Maine. Bobby Charles says he grew up in Wayne, Maine, the son of a public-school teacher, and later studied at Dartmouth, Oxford, and Columbia Law. He says he is running for safer streets, lower taxes, stronger schools, and a government that works for residents. He says he would cut crime and treat the drug trade as a central threat to Maine communities. He says he would cut taxes and regulation that he argues weigh on businesses and working families. He says schools should improve and that too much state policy has been driven by ideological agendas he opposes.

Musician and small-business owner running for Congress. Bobby Pulido's campaign says he was born and raised in Edinburg, studied political science, and became a well-known Tejano singer while also running businesses. It says he and his wife are raising four sons in the Rio Grande Valley. He says he would challenge corporations raising prices, cut red tape for small businesses, and back apprenticeships and higher-wage jobs that stay in South Texas. He says farmers and ranchers need fair markets and open trade, and that tariffs are raising costs. He says the border should stay secure and violent criminals should be removed, without raids that he argues hurt local workers and businesses.

U.S. representative and ranking Democrat on Education and the Workforce. His campaign says he grew up in Newport News and has represented Virginia's 3rd District since 1993. It says he is known as one of the hardest-working members of Congress and is fighting for students, workers, families, and seniors. He says he authored legislation to raise the federal minimum wage gradually to $17 an hour and the PRO Act on the right to organize. He says he was a lead author of the Every Student Succeeds Act and is fighting to make college more affordable through his College Affordability Act. He says he was the House sponsor of the Post-9/11 G.I. Bill and is leading work on evidence-based criminal-justice reform.

U.S. representative for Minnesota's 1st District. Brad Finstad's office says he is a fourth-generation farmer from the New Ulm area who won a special election in 2022. He and his wife Jackie, who met on the school bus in second grade, have seven children and run an agriculture business alongside their family farm. He earned a University of Minnesota degree in agricultural education. His office says his work as Minnesota's USDA Rural Development director supported rural infrastructure, business development, homeownership, schools, public safety, health care, and high-speed internet. He previously served three terms in the Minnesota Legislature and held executive roles with the Minnesota Turkey Growers Association and the Center for Rural Policy and Development.
District 13 · U.S. House · North Carolina · Republican

Former federal prosecutor and U.S. representative for North Carolina's 13th District. His campaign says he and his wife grew up in Raleigh and are raising two daughters there, and that he resigned as a federal prosecutor in eastern North Carolina to run in 2024. He says he is running again so the district stays safer and more prosperous. He says he would finish the border wall and send an immigrant who commits a felony to prison for at least five years before deportation. He says he supports school choice, a balanced-budget amendment, and police, and he opposes new gun laws aimed at law-abiding owners. He says he is pro-life, supports state laws protecting the unborn, and would defend faith-based pregnancy centers.

Former New York City comptroller running for Congress in New York's 10th District. His campaign says he organized tenants and built affordable housing at the Fifth Avenue Committee and the Pratt Center, then passed wage laws for gig workers on the City Council and later served as comptroller. It says he was arrested by federal agents while defending immigrants from ICE. He says he would be a check on Donald Trump and fight attacks on immigrants, trans kids, the rule of law, health care, Social Security, and working- and middle-class families. He says Congress should help cities end street homelessness, fix public housing, protect tenants, and build more affordable homes. He says he would take on billionaires and corporate power and get money out of politics rather than take Wall Street, crypto, and AIPAC contributions.

Independent American candidate for secretary of state. Brad Lee Barnhill is the Independent American nominee. His campaign says he has worked about twenty years as a systems analyst and about twenty years as a litigation paralegal. He says that if voters approve voter identification, he would carry it out with the office's existing rules and with help for people who have trouble getting an ID. He says possible duplicate registrations should be reviewed by a person before a record is changed, and that poll rules should be the same in every county. He says he would urge repeal of the commerce tax and oversee the move of business filings from SilverFlume to ORION.

Governor of Idaho, first elected in 2018 and reelected in 2022. His campaign says he is committed to leading so Idahoans can thrive, so children and grandchildren choose to stay, and so people who have left choose to come back. The site calls that experienced leadership the state can trust. His campaign says he cut or simplified 95 percent of Idaho regulations and calls Idaho the least regulated state. His campaign says teacher pay rose, literacy funding increased five-fold, and school-facility spending also worked as property-tax relief, along with new school-choice options and the Idaho LAUNCH program. His campaign says he and the Legislature delivered tax relief with a balanced budget and a AAA credit rating, and that Idaho sent more missions to the border than any other state through an effort he calls Operation No Return.

Former Navy civilian engineer and manufacturer running for Congress. A seventh-generation Hoosier from Brownsburg, he says he spent 25 years in local manufacturing and then nine years as a Navy civilian engineer in electromagnetic warfare after moving to Bloomington. He says he walked away from a secure retirement because he could not ignore the country's direction. He says he supports Medicare for All so no one goes broke trying to stay alive, and he wants higher wages, fair taxes, and restored collective bargaining. He says he is focused on making a first home possible again, lowering the cost of education, and an immigration system that respects the dignity of work. He says policy has shifted wealth upward, and he is running so working people are not left behind from their first jobs through retirement.

U.S. representative running for another term. Brad Sherman's campaign says he was born and raised in Southern California and represents the San Fernando Valley and much of the Westside. It says he is a senior member of Foreign Affairs and Financial Services and helped create the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. He says he has a perfect rating from the Brady Campaign and an F from the NRA, and he has pushed an assault-weapons ban and longer background checks. He says he cosponsors a safe-storage bill named for a teenager killed by an unsecured firearm. He says he has championed consumer protections and helped create the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.

Veteran and business owner running for Congress in Wisconsin's 6th District. His campaign says he is a dad, a veteran, and a business builder, and a Democrat running to deliver jobs, affordable health care, and training. He says he wants to protect the Wisconsin he loves. He supports a higher minimum wage, apprenticeships, prevailing wage, project labor agreements, and the right to organize, plus training through tech schools, college, and trades. He says health care should protect people with pre-existing conditions and stay close to home, and he wants transparency before large data centers are built. As a gun owner, he supports background checks, red-flag laws, and secure storage, and he also calls for fair milk prices, farm broadband, reproductive freedom, and LGBTQ+ protections.

U.S. representative running for another term. Brandon Gill's campaign says he was born on an Air Force base, grew up on a cattle ranch outside Abilene, and graduated from Dartmouth before working in finance and starting a conservative news site. It says his father was a fighter pilot and his grandfather a Dallas-area preacher. He says that in Congress he has worked to stop a large tax increase, secure the southern border, and end funding for projects he calls leftist. He says he is running again so children can live in a better Texas and a better America, alongside an America First agenda.

Firearms entrepreneur running for Congress. Brandon Herrera's campaign says he is an entrepreneur and Second Amendment activist with family roots in Texas, including Hispanic heritage and parents from military families. It says he studied pre-law and then built a small firearm-manufacturing business. He says he would take practical steps to secure the southern border and improve support for veterans and their families. He says he would seek national concealed-carry reciprocity, pledge no new taxes, cut waste, and back the REINS Act.

Union leader and Democrat running for Congress. His campaign says he was raised in Copan, returned to Bartlesville as a third-generation union worker, and spent 26 years in leadership with IUOE Local 351. He says he is the son of a Vietnam Army veteran and serves as secretary of the Oklahoma Democratic Party Veterans Federation. He says health care should be affordable for everyone and not tied to a job, and that he would protect women's health care choices and strengthen Social Security and Medicare. He says the economy should grow from the working class up, with fair wages, safe workplaces, and corporations and the wealthy paying their fair share. He says he would fully fund public schools, modernize immigration, and defend the rights of women, LGBTQ+ people, immigrants, and minorities.

Business owner and victims' rights advocate running for Oakland mayor. Brenda Grisham says she is a longtime community advocate and business owner who has stood with Oakland families for safer neighborhoods. She says she announced for mayor in 2025 and is on the November 3, 2026 ballot. She says she will focus on safer neighborhoods and stronger public safety. She says city government should be more accountable and transparent, and that local businesses need support to grow. She says she wants more stable housing, cleaner streets, and stronger neighborhood services.

U.S. representative for Pennsylvania's 2nd District. His campaign says he grew up in a Philadelphia rowhouse, was the first in his family to attend college, and later earned a public-policy degree from Harvard. It says his father was a SEPTA custodian who emigrated from Ireland and that Boyle was elected to the House in 2014. He says his work on the Budget Committee is aimed at a federal budget that expands opportunity. On Ways and Means, he says he wants tax and social policy that matches the priorities of working families. He says the Blue Collar Caucus he co-founded in 2016 looks at wage stagnation, job insecurity, trade, offshoring, and careers in manufacturing and the building trades.

Iowa attorney general and former Guthrie County attorney. The campaign says Iowans elected her attorney general and that she is the first Republican to hold the office since 1979. She was Guthrie County attorney from 2018, a prosecutor since 2016, and president of the Iowa County Attorneys Association, and she previously was counsel to Governor Terry Branstad. She says she has worked to get criminals off the street, advocate for crime victims, and stand with law enforcement. She says that as counsel to Governor Branstad she fought federal health-care policy and rules from other states that she says tried to dictate Iowa farm practices. She says she led a fight against EPA regulations that were hurting Iowa farmers and will use the office to defend what she calls the rule of law.

Insurance agency owner and Republican nominee for Florida's 20th District His campaign says he is a Pompano Beach small-business owner who spent 16 years in insurance and founded Pilgrim Bay Insurance Agency in 2010. He is the son of a public-school teacher and a union worker, holds a finance degree from Nichols College, and is raising a daughter in Pompano Beach with his wife, Yula, who was born in Venezuela. He says housing and insurance costs are pricing Broward families out, and that 16 years in insurance is what he would take to Congress. He says he would fight the higher grocery, energy, and health-care bills hitting working families. He says he supports legal immigration and a functioning asylum system, and opposes what he calls open borders.
