State senator and funeral-business owner running for Congress in Tennessee's 9th District. His campaign says he is a small-business owner in the funeral business and a West Tennessee state senator. He says he is ready to take that work to Congress. No 2026 issue list was found for this candidate.

Hawaii Senate minority leader The campaign says Brenton Awa is Hawaii's Senate minority leader, representing Kaneohe through the North Shore, and that he was first elected in 2022. He says he is running for the U.S. House so the 2nd District has more leverage in Washington. He wants to limit corporate purchases of single-family homes and open suitable federal land for local workforce housing. He says federal infrastructure money should be tied to housing for people who live and work in Hawaii, and he wants down-payment help for first-time local buyers. He says he refuses gifts and has founded roadside food forests and other land-restoration projects.

U.S. representative and chair of the House Energy and Commerce Committee. After Army service he joined a Bowling Green manufacturing business his father started, represented Kentucky's 32nd Senate district, and was elected to the U.S. House in 2008. He says representing the Second District is the honor of a lifetime. He says he is focused on lower health-care and prescription costs, energy independence, and cutting taxes and regulations. He says he wants to protect seniors, strengthen domestic manufacturing, and keep government out of the doctor-patient relationship. The campaign says he is pro-life, has an A rating from the NRA, and has been called a friend of the Farm Bureau.

Candidate for governor. His campaign describes a governing approach built on practical problem solving, personal responsibility, and what it calls stewardship for the next generation. He says cities and rural communities succeed together rather than against each other. He says he would expand paths to success through education, workforce training, and entrepreneurship. He says policy should be predictable and institutions reliable, with results ahead of spectacle. He says the state should be held in trust for the people who come after, not only for the next election.

Candidate for governor whose site publishes a plan written with the Pacific Green Party. He says corruption is the most important problem and that the major parties will not fix the system that keeps them in power. The plan thanks Matt Rowe, Seth Woolley, and the Pacific Green Party. He proposes a surcharge on large employers whose wages leave workers needing public assistance, with small employers exempt and the money directed to health coverage, food aid, and wage support. He proposes expanding the Oregon Health Plan into a public option open to every resident, with private insurance still available. He also says he is the only candidate against data centers, and he backs a state limit on sending the National Guard into combat without a congressional declaration of war.

U.S. representative running for another term. Brian Babin's campaign says he is an East Texas dentist who served in the National Guard, Army Reserve, and Air Force, was mayor of Woodville, and was sworn into Congress in 2015. It says he serves on Transportation and Infrastructure and on Science, Space, and Technology. He says securing the border, including support for a border wall, is his top immigration priority. He says he is running to keep the country safe, strong, and economically secure for his children and grandchildren.

Independent candidate for U.S. Senate Brian Bengs is running as an independent for the U.S. Senate. His site says he was a National Park Ranger and that he has signed a pledge against money from artificial-intelligence data centers. He says he wants a constitutional amendment to ban unlimited corporate political spending that he traces to the Citizens United decision. He says local communities should be able to refuse a new data center, and that he will not take data-center money. He says he supports term limits for Congress and that he would not vote to continue what he calls an unnecessary war with Iran.

School board member running for Congress. Brian Burley's campaign says he is running because Washington is stuck in partisanship and he has tried to get things done by listening. It says that as a school board member he has worked to protect parents' voices, help students succeed, and watch taxpayer dollars. He says he would advocate tax relief for families and business owners. He says he would take a stand against illegal immigration and fully support law enforcement and the military. He says he would fight to restore what he calls American family values.

U.S. representative for Pennsylvania's 1st District. His campaign says he spent nearly 15 years as an FBI supervisory special agent focused on political corruption before coming to Congress. It says he chairs the Problem Solvers Caucus and calls himself the most bipartisan member of the House for five years running. He says that on his first day in office he proposed congressional term limits, no pay if Congress misses a budget, and a requirement to balance the budget. He highlights a law he wrote to give law enforcement more resources to stop drugs at the border. He says he wants people with serious terminal illnesses to have access to treatments that might save their lives, and that institutions should serve the public rather than career officials.

U.S. representative and former White House political director. He says he is a sixth-generation Georgian raised in Fayette County, a Woodward Academy and Pepperdine graduate who worked at Peachtree City Hall and later for Ben Carson. He says he joined Donald Trump's 2016 campaign and served as White House political director through that administration. He calls the border the country's most pressing issue and says he will push to finish the border wall, fund ICE and the Border Patrol, deport people he calls criminal immigrants, and rewrite immigration law around working-class prosperity. He says he will return to tax cuts and energy production he credits with an earlier economic boom, arguing that spending and energy policy have driven up gas and grocery prices. His issues list also names stopping crime, ending what he calls the weaponization of justice, and leading on digital innovation.

U.S. representative running for another term. Brian Mast's campaign says serving the country is what he always wanted to do, following his father and uncles, and that he and his wife, Brianna, hope their children find the same purpose. It says he represents Florida's 18th District and tries to serve without regard for personal gain. No 2026 issue list was found for this candidate.

Democratic candidate for Montana's 2nd District. His campaign says he has lived in Montana for nearly 25 years and has practiced general civil litigation in state and federal courts across the state for nearly 15 years. He says he is an independent-minded Montanan and not a politician. He says prices are higher, jobs are fewer, programs that help people are being destroyed, and government debt is ballooning, and he describes an attack on the Constitution from what he calls an overgrown executive. He names data centers in Montana, the war in Iran, health care, affordability, and agriculture as the top issues. He says he would apply common-sense judgment with the people of Montana first and use evidence-based solutions.

Union ironworker and city council member running for Congress in Ohio's 7th District. Brian Poindexter says he is the son of a union machinist and the grandson of a union autoworker, one of six children who grew up in Cleveland, and a Brook Park council member since 2017. He says he has worked on a shop floor and on Cleveland skyscrapers. He says companies that benefit from America should invest in American workers instead of sending jobs overseas for cheaper labor. On the council he says he has opposed right-to-work laws and school vouchers and supported the postal service and public schools.

Attorney General of the District of Columbia He says that as attorney general he has worked to protect residents' rights, make neighborhoods safer, and keep businesses competing on a level field. He says he is running for reelection to continue that work. He says the office has prosecuted juvenile crime, pursued opioid companies, and sued landlords over dangerous housing. He says he has opposed a federal takeover of the Metropolitan Police Department and filed cases against federal orders, including a National Guard deployment in the District. He says the office has gone after unpaid wages and benefits, won rent refunds, and sued what he calls a housing cartel for illegally raising rents.

Teacher and city council president running for Congress in Ohio's 5th District. Brian Shaver says he was born and raised in Fostoria, still lives on a small family farm there with his wife and daughter, teaches social studies, and is president of the Fostoria City Council. He says representatives should put people before party. He supports campaign-finance limits, term limits, stronger checks and balances, and transparency in legislation. He also wants guardrails so elected officials cannot profit from their positions, and he says they should stay present and accountable to their communities.

Georgia state senator, Senate Judiciary chairman, and practicing attorney. He was born and raised in Henry County, still lives in McDonough, and says he practices law there. He was first elected to the Georgia House in 2012 and to the state Senate in 2018. He says that as judiciary chairman he handles the state's laws on courts, crime, and criminal procedure. He says he wrote the law that fixed long delays in competency hearings and has been a leading voice for mental-health reform. He says he worked to stop foster children from being housed in state offices and supported stronger laws on gangs, counterfeit drugs, and human trafficking.

Omaha city councilman and candidate for Congress in Nebraska's 2nd District The campaign says Brinker Harding is a fourth-generation Omahan, a business leader, and the Omaha City Council member for District 6. It says he was chief of staff and economic-development director for Mayor Hal Daub and has been on the council since 2017. His campaign says he would work on wages and inflation, year-round E15, and prescription prices matched to other developed countries. The site says he would protect Social Security, Medicaid, and Medicare for single mothers, veterans, older people, and people with disabilities, and make care including IVF more affordable. He says he supports term limits, a ban on congressional stock trading, halting congressional pay during shutdowns, deporting people here illegally who commit violent crimes, and nationwide voter ID.

Former Colorado legislator running for Congress. Brittany Pettersen says she was born in Colorado, grew up in a working-class Jefferson County family, and was the first in her family to finish high school and college. She says her mother's addiction after a back injury shaped her, and that she then served 10 years in the Colorado legislature. She says she will keep working on small-business capital, job training, and rural broadband, and that she wants to stop price gouging and lower costs for families. She says she supports a fast shift to wind, solar, and geothermal power, and that she will protect public lands and water levels in the Arkansas River. She says she will defend Medicare and Social Security, let Medicare negotiate drug prices, and protect the right to vote.

Nassau County executive running for governor. His campaign describes him as a lifelong New Yorker who has also served as a Port Authority commissioner. It says that as county executive he hired more police officers and did not raise county property or sales taxes. He says public safety is the center of the campaign, including opposition to sanctuary policies and work with federal immigration officers to remove people he calls criminals. He says he blocked scheduled property-tax increases in Nassau County and would seek relief for homeowners and renters as governor. His site names Madison County Sheriff Todd Hood as his lieutenant governor running mate and describes Hood as a career law-enforcement officer.

U.S. representative for Arkansas's 4th District The campaign says Bruce Westerman was born and raised in Garland County, played football at the University of Arkansas, and earned a master's in forestry from Yale. He worked in engineering and forestry for more than 22 years, served in the Arkansas House, and now chairs the House Natural Resources Committee. He says he wants lower taxes so families and small businesses can keep more of what they earn, and he points to tax cuts passed while he has been in Congress. He says he has helped roll back regulations he argues hurt jobs. As the only forester in the House, he says he wants science-based management of national forests and points to the Resilient Federal Forests Act.

Attorney from Benton Says he is not a politician and that his only client would be the taxpayer. He argues a Democrat who voted for the current budgets cannot be the watchdog of a Democratic governor and legislature. Spending decisions still sit with those two branches. The comptroller’s leverage is disclosure and which bills get paid when. Rebuild the office website so a resident can see, in plain language, where money went. Track grants to nonprofits and use artificial intelligence to flag waste, fraud, and abuse. Treat transparency as the path to lower spending and lower taxes. Says he would help the legislature if it takes up pension changes.

U.S. representative for Wisconsin's 1st District, seeking another term. His campaign says he is a lifelong resident of southeast Wisconsin who was first elected in 2018 after work in the private sector. It says he chairs the Committee on House Administration and a Financial Services subcommittee on digital assets and artificial intelligence. He says he is cutting wasteful spending to lower prices, securing the border against fentanyl and human trafficking, and working with local law enforcement. He says he will protect Social Security and Medicare, including their solvency, and work to lower prescription prices for seniors. He also says he is working so service members, their families, and veterans get mental-health care and the benefits they earned.

District 17 · U.S. House · New York · Democratic

Army special operations veteran running for Congress in New York's 17th District. Her campaign says she is a fourth-generation Hudson Valley native, a West Point graduate, and a decorated combat veteran who was one of the first women to lead in Army special operations. It says she is running because the politicians who created today's problems will not be the ones to fix them. She says she would lower drug and premium costs by holding pharmaceutical and insurance companies accountable and creating a public insurance option. She says she would ban members of Congress and the White House from trading stocks, and stop utility monopolies from passing private-jet, lobbying, and campaign costs on to ratepayers.

Army officer running for Congress. Caitlin Rourk's campaign says she is an Army intelligence officer and a mother who has lived and worked in Central Texas for more than a decade. It says she was raised by public-school teachers, worked on energy and deficit policy, and most recently led communications at Dell. She says she would lower costs, restore government accountability, and expand access to health care. She says she would strengthen public schools and child care, set rules for communities facing artificial intelligence, and fix immigration. She says foreign policy and national security should be practical rather than driven by headlines.

Community organizer running for Georgia's 9th District. Her campaign says she holds a bachelor's and a master's from the University of Georgia and a master's from the London School of Economics. She says she organized for women's rights and criminal justice reform, and that she helped unionize her workplace. She says she would fight for a livable minimum wage, more affordable housing, and Medicare for All so people in the 9th District can save and buy a home. She says the wealthiest people, whom she calls the Epstein Class, are not paying their fair share of taxes, and that the revenue should fund social programs. She says she would fund the Forest Service and protect the Roadless Rule, replace lead water pipes in rural North Georgia, and have Congress reclaim its war and taxation powers.

Attorney and veterans advocate running for Congress in Michigan's 1st District. Her campaign says she was born and raised in Traverse City and Cheboygan, taught school, and became the primary caretaker for her husband Matt after he came home from the Marine Corps with combat injuries. That work led her into veterans advocacy and law. She says health care should be a right, wants Medicare available from birth, and wants Medicaid cuts restored and drug prices lowered. She wants homes people can afford, less red tape for local builders, and a balance between short-term rentals and year-round residents. She says work should pay enough to live in the district, and she supports unions, Social Security, childcare, farms, and broadband.

Radio host running for Congress in Ohio's 13th District. Carey Coleman says he is a longtime northeast Ohio radio host on WNIR and a former television meteorologist. He says he is running because rising costs, insecure borders, and government overreach have made it harder for families to get ahead. He says he will rein in federal spending, expand American energy to lower fuel and utility costs, and protect middle-class families from new taxes. He also says he will defend the First and Second Amendments and religious freedom, back law enforcement, secure the border, and give parents a stronger say in education.

Air Force veteran running for Congress. Carlos De La Cruz's campaign says he was raised by a single mother in South Texas, enlisted in the Air Force at 17, and served 20 years, including deployments to Iraq, Afghanistan, and the southern border. It says he and his wife later built a San Antonio business. He says he would keep securing the border, give Border Patrol more support, and welcome legal immigration. He says he would lower costs for working families, expand Texas energy, and vote to ban members of Congress from trading stocks.

U.S. representative for Florida's 28th District His office says he was born in Cuba in 1954, came to the United States after the communist takeover, and grew up in Miami's Little Havana. He joined the Miami Fire Department in 1975, served 25 years, and was the department's first Cuban American chief. He later was Miami's city manager, a county commissioner, and mayor of Miami-Dade before his election to Congress in 2020. He and his wife, Lourdes, have three children and six grandchildren. He says small businesses need lower taxes, less legal liability, and fewer regulations. He says immigration shaped South Florida and that the border should be secured in a way that keeps that community intact. He says China is America's most aggressive adversary, and he supports domestic energy that stays environmentally conscious.

Former Spokane County deputy prosecutor and Foreign Service officer running for Congress. She is a third-generation eastern Washingtonian whose family worked on farms, in trades, and on the railroad, and she says she later served under six presidents overseas. She wants lower everyday costs and more investment in housing, child care, education, and infrastructure for families, new workers, small businesses, and farms. She says her prosecutor and diplomatic work shapes a focus on public safety and steady leadership abroad. She wants Medicare, Medicaid, and Social Security protected, health costs lowered, rural hospitals strengthened, and veterans supported.
District 10 · U.S. House · New Jersey · Republican

Small-business owner running for Congress in New Jersey's 10th District. Her campaign says she grew up in foster care, has lived on the streets, and built a small business, a home, and a foundation called Bucco's Rising Stars. She says public service should be about people rather than politics. She says she would focus on local needs, refuse to vote for personal gain, and fight irresponsible spending. She says her priorities are roads, schools, public safety, mental-health support, and holding the line on property taxes. She says schools should return to the basics and taxpayer dollars should reach people who need help.

U.S. representative for West Virginia The campaign says Carol Miller is a small business owner, farmer, and job creator, and a wife, mother, and grandmother. It says she is in Congress to lower costs. Her campaign says she is pro-life, pro-jobs, pro-energy, and for lower taxes. The site says taxes, spending, and regulation from Washington hurt West Virginia families and businesses. It says she has worked to lower taxes, create jobs, protect energy industries, and secure the border.

Candidate for secretary of state Caroleene Dobson is running for secretary of state. Her campaign says the job should serve Alabama voters and businesses. She says she will reduce fees on Alabama businesses. She says she will streamline government services for the public. She says she will oppose groups she calls liberal activists who want to weaken election security.
District 12 · U.S. House · New York · Republican

Lawyer and economist running for Congress in New York's 12th District. Her campaign says she lives in Midtown, majored in economics at MIT, and worked at the Federal Reserve and at central banks in Europe and Israel before earning a law degree from Harvard. It says she then advised businesses and financial institutions at a New York law firm. She says she would protect paychecks and push schools to treat every student like an honors student while using innovation to improve results. She says she would back law enforcement and first responders, fight antisemitism, and stand with Israel and the city's Jewish community. She says she would restore competition and price transparency in health care and pass the Access to Breast Cancer Diagnosis Act.

Republican state senator running for Nevada's 1st District. Her campaign says she grew up working on a small farm, taught fifth grade in North Las Vegas, and as a principal turned a low-performing school around before leading the growth of Pinecrest Academy charter schools. She says she then won a state Senate seat and lives in Nevada with her husband, Eric, a retired deputy police chief, and their four sons. She says she will protect parents' rights, secure the border, and fully fund police. She says tips should never be taxed. She says she will work with the president to hold Washington accountable for every taxpayer dollar.

Business owner and Republican nominee for Florida's 22nd District His campaign says his family immigrated legally to the United States after fleeing religious persecution, and that his first jobs were at McDonald's and mopping floors at CVS. He enlisted in the Marine Corps after high school. He says he is chairman of Askar Family Office, employing thousands of people in South Florida, and a married father of seven. He says grocery and gas prices are his top priority, and that he would cut taxes and regulations he says are driving those costs up. He says he would keep deporting people here illegally who have committed crimes, secure the border, and keep a merit-based immigration policy. He says he would ban members of Congress from trading stocks and defend parents' say over their children's education.

Criminal defense lawyer running for Congress. Casey Shepard's campaign says he is a seventh-generation Texan who returned to Waco in 2010 and has practiced indigent criminal defense in Central Texas since 2011. It says that work means enforcing constitutional duties for clients who cannot afford a lawyer. He says Congress should be able to check the executive branch, and that courts should stay independent enough to review those decisions. He says he would fully fund SNAP and school meals, restore Medicaid and Medicare support, and expand the health-care workforce. He says tax incentives and rental aid should produce affordable homes, and that tariffs are raising the price of food and building materials.

Independent candidate for the U.S. Senate. She says she is on the ballot as an independent, worked in insurance, and has spent the last 20 years as a life coach, pastor, and mentor. She says she is running to spend her time on what Tennesseans want rather than on rehearsing what is wrong. She says she would lower costs, seek high-paying jobs, back local small businesses, and promote cleaner energy, safe water, and recycling. On health care, she says she would cut prescription prices, protect rural hospitals, and use existing law to help people who do not have group coverage. She says she would boost public-school funding and vocational training, support private and home schooling, and push for safe, affordable housing and child, adult, and elder care.

Working Class Party candidate for governor of Maryland. Cathy White says she is not a professional politician and has spent 40 years as a factory production worker. She says she cared for her mother and for a sister with Down syndrome while working full time. She says workers need their own political organization because neither major party represents them on jobs, low wages, and rising prices. She says child care and elder care cost more than most workers can pay, and that many older workers cannot afford to retire. She says workers have no reason to support the current war in the Middle East, which she argues enriches defense and energy companies while raising the price of gas.

Candidate for Colorado secretary of state. Celeste Landry says the secretary of state works for every Coloradan, regardless of party. She describes herself as a longtime election champion campaigning to be the next secretary of state. She says her campaign is for the right to vote. She says she wants better representation. She says she is fighting for election integrity.

U.S. representative campaigning on taxes, the border, and federal spending. Her campaign says she has made it a priority to slow inflation so a paycheck covers more, and she highlights a tax bill she says cut taxes on tips, overtime, and Social Security. She says she voted to fund a border wall and to give Border Patrol more technology against drugs and trafficking. She says she will defend religious practice, the Second Amendment, and legal protections for the unborn. She says she has voted to cut wasteful spending and to ease rules she believes have held back American energy production.

Grovetown council member, former Army medic, and union leader running for Congress. She says she served nearly a decade as a U.S. Army medic, then spent twenty-five years in labor, civil, and human rights work as a federal employee and national union leader. She says that as a city council member she has championed children and held local government accountable. She says her vision for the 12th District is good jobs, strong schools, and healthy communities, with investment in new industries and infrastructure. She says she will seek fair wages and health care now, and longer-term resources that keep the district thriving. She says government should work for people rather than special interests, and that dignity, fair pay, and opportunity should not depend on ZIP code.

Vermont attorney general running for another term. Her campaign says she was sworn in as attorney general in January 2023 and is running to keep challenging federal actions, polluters, and companies that harm children. She says she has sued the Trump administration 49 times for violating the Constitution or federal law, and that she has sued Meta and TikTok over harm to children. She says she has defended abortion access, including a case about medication abortion, and sued pharmacy benefit managers over drug costs. She says the office prosecutes violent crimes and sexual crimes against children, and that she sued Monsanto over PCB contamination of water and schools.

Former Kentucky state representative running for the U.S. Senate. Charles Booker's site says he is a lifelong Kentuckian and the son of a West Louisville family, and that he grew up rationing insulin. He says he built a campaign that reaches from the city to the hollers around health care, jobs, and leaders who fight for people instead of corporations. He says Kentucky needs a senator who treats poverty as an emergency, because families can be one medical bill, layoff, or storm from losing everything. He says health care is a human right and that he wants union jobs in every county. He also calls for clean water, clean air, and a politics grounded in the dignity of the people it serves.

Mayor of Surfside and candidate for governor He says he was raised in Miami Beach, has lived in Surfside since 1996, and was elected mayor of Surfside, including a 2024 reelection. He says he owns a national investment company and is running for governor. He says homestead property taxes should phase out for long-time Florida homeowners, with the benefit able to pass to a spouse or children. He says property and auto insurance laws should be rewritten to bring more competition into the market. He says a data center should be allowed only after voters in that county and city approve it.

Conservative candidate running for Congress. Charles Hoelter's campaign describes him as a conservative advocate for faith and family who has spent years listening to families, small businesses, veterans, and law enforcement. It says he is running to restore accountability and constitutional freedoms. He says he would secure the border, lower taxes, support law enforcement, and defend constitutional rights. He says immigration should be legal and controlled, and that parents should have a voice in what schools teach. He says veterans need better health care and support, and that government spending should come down.

Farmer and former agriculture commissioner running for Congress in Tennessee's 5th District. His campaign says he is a fifth-generation dairy farmer and livestock veterinarian who started several businesses, including Hatcher Family Dairy, and served as state veterinarian and agriculture commissioner. He says the family has worked the same land for more than 200 years. He says he would fight inflationary spending and rules that raise energy and business costs, and let families keep more of what they earn. He says food security is national security and that he would protect farmers from foreign disease threats and dependence on other countries for food. He says he would enforce immigration law, defend the Second Amendment for law-abiding owners, and make constituent service a priority.

Mayor of Columbia running for Congress in Tennessee's 5th District. His campaign says he was born and raised in Tennessee, attended Columbia's public schools, the University of Tennessee, and the University of Memphis law school. Elected mayor in 2018, he says he was then the youngest mayor in the state. He says he would ban stock trading by members of Congress and restore trust through transparency and accountability. He says he would lower the cost of health care, housing, and groceries, and stand up for the right to organize. He says affordable health care is a basic right and that rural hospitals need support so they can stay open.

U.S. representative for Maine's 1st District The campaign says Chellie Pingree has lived on the island of North Haven since she was a teenager, where she farmed organically, raised three children, and started small businesses including North Island Yarn and Nebo Lodge. She later chaired the local school board, served in the state Senate, and was elected to Congress in 2008. She sits on the Appropriations Committee. She says her Appropriations work has focused on opportunities for working families, support for farmers, veterans, and wider access to health care. The campaign says she knows meeting payroll and offering benefits is hard because she has run an organic farm and island businesses.

East Texas parent running for Congress. Chelsey Hockett's campaign says she is a mother of two from a union family in Terrell who is not a career politician. It says she is running because Washington is ignoring the cost of food, housing, health care, and child care. She says she would end tariffs she argues raise prices, enact Medicare for All, and create universal child care. She says the minimum wage should start at $25 and be tied to the cost of living, and that Social Security should keep up with prices. She says billionaires and corporations should pay more so public schools, Title I, special education, and Head Start are fully funded.

Conservative candidate running for Congress in Maryland's 8th District. Her campaign says she is a Christian conservative who grew up in Montgomery County and is running on an America First platform. She says she has watched schools, taxes, and crime move in the wrong direction. She says safety comes first and that she will push to keep people who commit crimes off the street, especially to protect older people, women, and children. She says she will back pro-growth policies that put American businesses and workers first, and she argues for limited government rather than what she calls democratic socialism. She also says she will defend the Constitution, the Second Amendment, veterans, and law enforcement, and she calls for sealed borders, more energy production, and parents' rights in schools.

Former national-security official running for Congress in Nebraska's 1st District. His campaign says he was born and raised in Lincoln, graduated from Lincoln East, and comes from a family whose farms were homesteaded in Cass County. It says he served in national security at the highest levels of government and is running to lower costs for families. He says that work included the Situation Room, bipartisan legislation, and briefing presidents while dealing with China, Russia, and Iran. He says he will bring that same focus on solving problems to the 1st District, with families and lower costs at the center.

Democratic and Independent Party candidate for Congress in Oregon's 2nd District. His campaign says he is an Oregon native and lifelong public servant from Jacksonville, and the grandson of an agriculture teacher at Redmond High School. He says he is running to replace Cliff Bentz and to be a representative who shows up for rural constituents. He says Congress should repeal the bill he calls the Big Beautiful Bill and restore Medicaid and SNAP funding, and he wants wildfire-prevention funding and staffing restored at the Forest Service. He says ending the war with Iran and canceling tariffs would ease fuel and household costs, and he wants low-cost housing folded into small-town Main Streets rather than onto farms and forest land. He says rural hospitals and clinics need protection because Medicaid covers a large share of the district, including many of its children.

Builder and farmer running for Congress in Maryland's 5th District. His campaign says he is a husband, father, and grandfather, the son of a veteran, who started as a union electrician, studied at the University of Maryland, and has run a home-building business since 1991. He says he is also a farmer and a conservative running in Southern Maryland. He says high costs have pushed taxpayers out of Maryland and that he would work to bring resources back to the 5th District. He points to the delay rebuilding the Baltimore bridge and says the state should also look at a new crossing from Calvert County toward St. Mary's County and the Patuxent River Naval Base.

U.S. senator from Delaware He says he grew up in Hockessin and, before the Senate, spent a decade in New Castle County government, including as county executive. He says he previously worked as an attorney at W.L. Gore & Associates. He says he has fought cuts to Medicaid and to affordable health care for Delawareans. He says he has secured funding for affordable housing and for protecting the state's natural areas. He says he has backed bipartisan laws on housing access, children's online safety, and health-care research.

U.S. representative for Pennsylvania's 17th District. His campaign says he is a Thornburg native, Naval Academy graduate, and Iraq war veteran who later worked as a voting-rights lawyer at the Brennan Center and at the University of Pittsburgh. It says he has represented western Pennsylvania since 2022 and lives in Allegheny County with his wife and four children. He says he is fighting powerful interests he argues have taken the American Dream away from working people. Before Congress he says he worked on voting rights and election security, and he helped University of Pittsburgh faculty win a union with the United Steelworkers.

Lawyer and business owner running for Congress. Chris Gober's campaign says he is a seventh-generation Texan, a Texas A&M graduate, and a Harvard-trained lawyer who grew up in Throckmorton and Graham. It says he worked on national security and border issues at the Justice Department, then built businesses in Texas, and is a husband and father of two. He says he would make life affordable, secure the border against cartels, and stop what he calls the weaponization of government against conservatives. He says he would grow defense and technology jobs in Austin and the Brazos Valley so the country outcompetes China. He says rural communities need fewer regulations, nearby health care, and data-center rules that do not drain water or raise electric rates.

Attorney and small-business owner running for Georgia's 11th District. His campaign says he grew up in a trailer park in Rossville, worked full time while going to school at night, and drove a forklift and loaded trucks before becoming an attorney. He says he is a husband and father of triplets, and that for more than fourteen years he has worked as a parent-defense attorney. He says he would make health care more affordable, expand Affordable Care Act premium tax credits, lower prescription costs, and improve access in rural communities. He says he takes no corporate PAC money, would ban members of Congress and their immediate families from trading individual stocks, and would cut taxes for working and middle-class families. He says data centers should not shift water and power costs onto ordinary customers, and he would invest in affordable energy and modernize the grid, roads, and bridges.

U.S. Senate candidate of the Oregon Progressive Party and the Pacific Green Party. His site lists his work as a long-haul truck driver and a UAW aircraft mechanic, and civic roles that include the Oregon Consumer League, a neighborhood association, and union shop steward. He says no special interest is funding the campaign. He says he would cut the military budget, support Medicare for All, and raise wages while rejecting both broad tariffs and trade deals that override labor and environmental rules. He proposes a federal fund for earthquake retrofits, backup power, and supplies ahead of a Cascadia earthquake. His site says state law can end a smaller party that misses a statewide vote threshold, and that this Senate race is the Progressive Party's contest this year.

Candidate for Congress The campaign says Chris Jones grew up in Pine Bluff as the son of a minister and built a career in science without leaving Arkansas behind. He says he is running to expand opportunity, strengthen schools and health care, and give more Arkansans a seat at the table. He says the economy should mean good jobs, fair wages, small-business growth, reliable internet, and rural hospitals that stay open. He wants stronger schools, maternal health care, addiction recovery, and food security for families. He supports early childhood education, apprenticeships, and training in both technology and the trades, plus fair maps and elections people can trust.

Former police officer and prosecutor running for attorney general. Chris Mann's site says he followed his father into law enforcement, left uniformed work after a drunk driver hit him during a traffic stop, and then prosecuted cases as an assistant district attorney in Wyandotte County and as a senior staff attorney at the Kansas Securities Commission. He says the attorney general should answer when local departments ask for help investigating and prosecuting major crimes, including drug distribution and child sexual abuse. He wants officer training held around the state, mental-health care for first responders, and workers' compensation coverage for PTSD. He says he will prosecute scams, push treatment access outside the northeast corner of the state, and fund shelters for people leaving domestic violence.

Fourth-generation Iowan and military veteran running for Congress. He says he was born and raised in Iowa's 4th District, that his children are the fifth generation in northwest Iowa, and that his family has farm ties around Fonda. He says he took an oath when he entered the military, is the son of a Vietnam veteran, and studied law. He says he will work with the Trump administration to secure the border, stop fentanyl, and support immigration enforcement. He says standing up for agriculture means protecting markets, defending landowner rights, and backing trade agreements for what farmers produce. He says he will put America first, stand up to China, bring jobs back, restore energy independence, and defend life from conception to natural death.

U.S. representative running for the Senate. Chris Pappas's campaign says he is in the House and will take on corporate interests, Donald Trump, or his own party when he thinks New Hampshire is better served. He says he forced a House vote on banning stock trading by members of Congress, including against his own party's leadership. He says he took on drug companies to lower prices and cap insulin at $35. He says he is challenging polluters of drinking water and companies he describes as taking advantage of veterans.

State representative running for Congress in Pennsylvania's 3rd District. Chris Rabb is a five-term Pennsylvania state representative from Philadelphia. His campaign says he is running to put working people ahead of corporate power. His platform calls for housing people can afford, a living wage, and Medicare for All. He also says he will fight for food security, clean air and water, and a foreign policy that prioritizes peace.

Disabled Army veteran and IBEW Local 1 member running for Missouri's 8th District. He says he is a second-generation union electrician from Arnold running a grassroots campaign that takes no corporate PAC or dark money. He supports the PRO Act to protect organizing and the Major Richard Star Act so combat-injured veterans receive full benefits. He wants the United States kept out of another long war and supports a bill to count the full human and financial cost of war up front. He wants Citizens United overturned and backs the Equality Act, and he says rural hospitals and public schools in the district are underfunded.

Retired Navy SEAL and Republican nominee for Congress The campaign says Chris Shea is a Watertown native, retired Navy SEAL, firefighter, former small-business owner, and the Republican nominee in Connecticut's 5th District. He served with SEAL teams and at the Pentagon over a career of more than 30 years, and he and his wife, Anita, raised their daughter in Watertown. His campaign slogan is lowering costs, growing wages, and protecting America. He says that experience, from a small business that employed six people to helping veterans start new careers, is what he would bring to Congress.

Candidate for Congress campaigning on north Missouri farms, taxes, and rural hospitals. His issues page presents a conservative platform he ties to President Trump, aimed at gun rights, small-town hospitals, abortion, taxes, and agriculture. He says the Second Amendment is not negotiable and that he will oppose federal gun restrictions aimed at law-abiding owners. He wants less red tape for rural hospitals, and he opposes taxpayer funding of abortion. He supports making the Trump tax cuts permanent and giving farms more market access with fewer regulations.

U.S. representative for Pennsylvania's 6th District. Chrissy Houlahan is a third-generation veteran, an Air Force Reserve captain, and a former AND1 executive and Teach for America corps member who was the first woman elected in Pennsylvania's 6th District. She serves on Armed Services and Intelligence and chairs the BIOTech Caucus. She says her work in Congress is aimed at the cost of living for families in Chester County and the district. Through the BIOTech Caucus she says she is working to grow jobs tied to biotechnology.

Former county attorney running for Congress. Christian Menefee's campaign says he was raised in the 18th District by two military parents, used a Pell Grant to become the first in his family to finish college, and earned a law degree at Washington University. It says he was a commercial litigator and then the youngest person, and the first Black person, elected Harris County attorney. He says he would seek Medicare for All, protect public schools and abortion rights, and make daily life more affordable. He lists workers' rights, jobs, gun-violence prevention, immigration, veterans, and criminal-justice reform among his priorities. He says he went to court against voting restrictions, pollution in Black and Latino neighborhoods, and disaster price gouging.

Teacher and union organizer running for Congress in Michigan's 5th District. His campaign says he was born and raised in Michigan, the son of an immigrant family on his father's side and of Michigan ministers on his mother's, and that he worked his way through school as a bricklayer. He says he is a husband, father, and teacher. He says he would fight for living wages, union jobs, and an economy that rewards hard work. He says quality, affordable health care is a right, and he wants housing working families can afford. He also calls for education and job training, and says he would put people ahead of corporate and billionaire interests.

Law professor, engineer, and former state representative running for Congress. She says she is a mom running so Iowa's working families come ahead of the wealthy and well-connected. After 26 years teaching constitutional law at the University of Iowa, she says she feels a duty to defend self-government against money and partisanship. She says her top priority is lowering the cost of living: end tariffs she says raise family costs, stop hedge funds from buying family homes, build more housing, let Medicare negotiate more drug prices, and cap insulin at $35 a month. She says she takes no corporate PAC money and would ban stock trading by members of Congress and other high officials, seek a constitutional amendment to overturn Citizens United, and set term limits. She says her father's insurer canceled coverage after he became ill, and she wants a health system that does not drop people when they get sick.

Prosecutor running for Congress in Michigan's 10th District. Her campaign says she grew up in Macomb County, attended the University of Michigan and Wayne State University Law School, and worked as a prosecutor on homicide, trafficking, and sexual-assault cases. She and her husband David are raising three children in Macomb County. She says she would lower the cost of groceries, gas, and health care and fight for good-paying Michigan jobs. She says she would support safer communities, schools, and law-enforcement resources to prevent violent crime and protect children and seniors online. She says she refuses corporate PAC money, would ban members of Congress from trading stocks, and would work with either party against corruption.

Candidate for governor of Oregon. Her campaign says Oregon should be the best place to raise a family, start a business, buy a home, and get a strong education, and that those goals are out of reach for too many people. She says the cost of living, jobs leaving the state, homelessness, schools, and state spending are leadership problems. She says she would order agencies to find rules and fees that raise the cost of housing, energy, food, child care, health care, and running a business, and that she would veto new tax and fee increases. She says she would speed housing permits, expand help for first-time buyers, and make it easier to build more kinds of homes. She says homelessness spending should be audited and shifted toward addiction recovery, mental-health treatment, and programs measured by how many people reach stable housing.

Candidate for Michigan secretary of state. She says the office should administer elections and serve residents, and that it should not be a partisan platform or a step toward higher office. She says more than a decade in health care shaped her view that individual rights and dignity are not negotiable. She says she would keep voter rolls accurate, let people verify how elections are run, and treat independent and minor-party candidates fairly. She wants government limited to protecting rights, maintaining essential services, and enforcing laws consistently. She says she would restrict mass surveillance, including vehicle-tracking cameras and unchecked data collection, and push open records and plain-language budget reports.

Retired Approval Voting Party candidate for the U.S. Senate. He told the Fort Collins Coloradoan he is retired and is running to publicize approval voting. He does not have a campaign website. He says people should be able to support a lesser-known candidate without taking a vote away from a major-party candidate. He says government should be smaller. He says the national debt should be eliminated.

Kentucky Party candidate for U.S. Senate. Christopher Campbell's site says he is a dues-paying member of a labor union, served in the Kentucky National Guard, and is a Kentucky Colonel. He supports Medicare for All and says the federal government should provide basic medical care. He says workers need safe conditions, strong benefits, good pay, and a way to raise grievances without retaliation. He wants a constitutional environmental amendment and a ban on carbon credits that he says let facilities keep polluting.
District 1 · U.S. House · New York · Democratic

Military pilot and union leader running for Congress in New York's 1st District. His campaign says he joined the New York Army National Guard at 17, deployed to Kuwait, and later worked as an FAA air traffic controller, a union leader, and a volunteer firefighter. He says he is running to bring that same discipline to Congress for the Long Island district where he grew up. He says he would seek federal investments that reduce the cost of housing, energy, and basic goods for Long Island families. He says he would protect Medicare and Medicaid and push changes that expand access and lower out-of-pocket costs for older adults. He also says he would press for long-term investment in the shoreline and for the tools first responders need to keep neighborhoods safe.

Coast Guard veteran and federal law enforcement officer running for Congress The campaign says Christopher Lancia was born and raised in Bridgeport, served in the Coast Guard, and later worked as a federal law enforcement officer. He now lives in Milford and says he is running to give Connecticut a voice in an America First agenda. He says border security is national security and that he wants the border chaos stopped. He says he will fight for lower taxes, a balanced budget, and an end to spending he ties to inflation. He supports term limits, the Second Amendment, and law enforcement, and says parents should control decisions about their children's education.
District 4 · U.S. House · New Jersey · Republican

U.S. representative for New Jersey's 4th District. His campaign says he has served 46 years and is running again after Ocean and Monmouth County Republican conventions endorsed him. It says he is known for constituent work and for turning local problems into national law. He says his laws cover veterans' health care and benefits, autism, Lyme disease, Alzheimer's, and international parental child abduction. He says he wrote the Trafficking Victims Protection Act and later anti-trafficking laws, and that he is worried crowded events such as the World Cup raise trafficking risks. He says he backed the Working Families Tax Cut and has fought offshore wind projects he says endanger the Jersey coast.

Republican candidate for U.S. House in Colorado's 1st District. Christy Peterson's campaign says she is the Republican candidate for Congress in the 1st District, covering Denver and parts of northern Arapahoe County. She says she is running on common sense, safe cities, a strong economy, and safe schools. She says she stands for low taxes, limited government, and peace through strength. She says she would review Social Security's finances so the program can stay solvent, and that she would cut the federal debt. She says she supports Colorado's Taxpayer's Bill of Rights.

America First Party candidate for U.S. Senate in Nebraska. His campaign says he has lived in Nebraska his whole life, the oldest of seven in an Irish Catholic home, and that he has worked since he was 12, including in management, sales, and as a vice president of a meatpackers and butchers union. He says his views line up with the America First Party. He says he would secure the southern border, expand immigration enforcement, deport people he says have no claim to remain, and put citizens, veterans, and workers first for taxpayer resources. He says Social Security must be protected with no benefit cuts before a 2032 insolvency date, and he opposes endless foreign wars and blank checks to other governments. He also calls for affordable college, an end to crushing student debt, a return of trade schools, lower health-care costs, and help with child care for working parents.

U.S. representative for Tennessee's 3rd District. His campaign describes him as a fiscal and social conservative representing Tennessee's 3rd District. He says massive federal spending meant to stem unemployment is counterproductive, and that the tax system does not support the growth the economy needs. He says the country's founding values still matter to him, and that environmentally safe energy exploration should be part of energy policy.

Wyoming secretary of state and candidate for Congress The campaign says Chuck Gray served six years in the Wyoming House before becoming secretary of state, an office that also serves as lieutenant governor. It says he has focused on election administration, energy, and abortion limits. His campaign says he will protect coal, oil, and gas jobs, oppose what he calls woke wind projects and ESG rules, and fight inflation with lower taxes and less spending. The site says he sponsored Wyoming's voter ID law, required proof of citizenship to register, and banned ranked-choice voting and foreign funding of elections. It says he supports securing the border, the Second Amendment, and pro-life policies, and opposes taxpayer-funded abortion.
District 5 · U.S. House · North Carolina · Democratic

Journalist running for Congress in North Carolina's 5th District. His campaign says he is a Wilkes County native who started at his grandfather's paper, the Wilkes Journal-Patriot, and spent more than 40 years as a local journalist after graduating from Wofford College. He and his wife Shari live in Wilkesboro. He says he would raise the minimum wage, shift taxes toward the wealthy, and support public schools, small businesses, and farms. He says he would protect Medicare, Medicaid, Social Security, and veterans' benefits, and add a public option so rural towns have a hospital nearby. He says abortion belongs between a patient and a doctor, and he wants to overturn Citizens United and ban members of Congress from trading stocks.

Former mayor and retired law-enforcement officer running for Congress. Chuong Vo's campaign says he is a husband, a father, a former mayor of Cerritos, and a 28-year law-enforcement officer who answered 911 calls for nearly three decades. It says his wife is a classroom teacher and that his family, like many immigrant families, was given a chance in this country. He says he is running to keep families safe, lower costs, and hold government accountable. He says that on the council he focused on safe neighborhoods, responsive city services, and balanced budgets. He says he returned campaign contributions after a council election and supports ending insider stock trading in Congress.

Democratic candidate for governor and a former executive councilor. Cinde Warmington is the Democratic nominee for governor. Her campaign says she was the only Democrat on the Executive Council and is running on the cost of living. She says she would repeal the private-school voucher program, which she argues drives up property taxes and hurts public schools. She says she would push back on higher health-care costs and tariffs, and would reject an immigration detention site in Merrimack. She says she would not support a sales or income tax, and that she would work for small businesses.

Kansas state senator running for governor. Cindy Holscher's site says she was raised on a farm and that her work in the Legislature included cleaning up after a failed tax experiment, lowering costs, and making health care more accessible. She says she will lower the cost of living, including health care, housing, child care, and groceries, and fully fund public schools. She says she will expand Medicaid, protect rural hospitals, and protect Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid. She calls for a pause on new data centers until guardrails are set, and she supports legalizing recreational and medical marijuana.

U.S. senator from Mississippi seeking another term. She says rumors that she would not run again are false and that she is definitely planning to campaign for reelection. She says the campaign is a grassroots fight for conservative leadership for Mississippi. Her campaign issues page highlights Second Amendment rights and balancing the budget. It also highlights health care and defending unborn life. It lists stopping illegal immigration and supporting the military and veterans.

Attorney running for Congress. Claire Reynolds's campaign says she grew up in central Illinois, studied journalism at Northwestern, and earned a law degree at the University of San Diego. It says she moved to Texas in 2007, raised her children here, and is the Democratic candidate in a district that now stretches from north Austin to Midland and Odessa. She says wages have not kept up with prices and that nobody should go bankrupt over a broken hip or cancer. She supports moving toward single-payer coverage like Medicare, a strong border with a faster legal immigration process, and abortion that is safe, legal, and rare. She says Texas needs both oil and gas and renewable energy jobs to stay competitive.
District 7 · U.S. House · New York · Democratic

State assemblymember running for Congress in New York's 7th District. Her campaign says she is a union organizer, artist, and democratic socialist, and a dual citizen of the Ysleta del Sur Pueblo Nation and the United States. It says she worked low-wage jobs, helped democratize UAW Local 2110 at Columbia, and has used her Assembly seat to tax the rich and protect tenants. She says she would strengthen the PRO Act, give active federal support to union organizing, and end at-will employment. She says everyone should be able to count on a living-wage job, paid parental and sick leave, health care, and a dignified retirement. She says the campaign will not take corporate PAC or dark money.
District 24 · U.S. House · New York · Republican

U.S. representative for New York's 24th District. Her campaign says she is an attorney and businesswoman whose view of public service was shaped by running a small business while raising her son as a single mother. It says she served six years in the state Assembly before her election to Congress. She says she has led efforts against Chinese theft of American intellectual property and against China's grip on the financial system. She says the border has to be secured now, that Social Security and Medicare are personal because her parents relied on them, and that the Second Amendment is a way of life in Upstate New York. She also says the health-care system is not working and that Congress has to deliver solutions, and she highlights veterans' issues as what she calls a Marine mom.

U.S. representative for Georgia's 14th District. His office says he was district attorney for the Lookout Mountain Judicial Circuit and is a lieutenant colonel in the Air National Guard. He says he was a White House Fellow in 2018 and 2019, serving in the vice president's office and the Defense Department. Raised in the North Georgia mountains, he captained the basketball team at Emory, then earned a master's from Cornell and a law degree from Southern Methodist University. He says he is fighting for President Trump's agenda to bring manufacturing jobs back to northwest Georgia. He says he supports removing people who are in the country without permission, and that border security is national security. He says he would defend the First and Second Amendments, and keep working to stop fentanyl trafficking in northwest Georgia.

Candidate for Congress in Louisiana's 3rd District. His campaign site says he is a lifelong Louisiana resident who served in Acadiana law enforcement and trained as a military police officer in the Army. It calls him a defender of the Bill of Rights. He says a sworn officer's oath is to the Constitution, not to a sheriff, chief, or marshal. The site says that, as a Christian, he focuses on the power of an individual to be redeemed.

Community volunteer running for Congress in Ohio's 3rd District. Cleophus Dulaney says he lives and works in the district and has spent years helping people who are homeless, encouraging young people, and backing candidates in both parties. He says he is running because politics has too much party loyalty and not enough listening. He says he will push Medicare to negotiate drug prices, take on pharmacy middlemen, and support tax relief for working and middle-class families. He also wants infrastructure, manufacturing, and clean-energy jobs, apprenticeships, and fewer rules that do not make small businesses safer, plus voting-rights protections and fair maps.

U.S. representative for Oregon's 2nd District, seeking another term. His campaign says he is a third-generation Oregonian raised on cattle ranches in Harney County, a lawyer who has practiced in Ontario since 1977, and a former chair of the Oregon Water Resources Commission. It says he served in the Oregon House and Senate before running for Congress. He says he will back tighter border security and finishing a border wall, and he describes himself as a right-to-life candidate who believes life begins at conception. He opposes government-run health care and says he will direct investment toward rural Oregon while holding the federal government accountable for how it manages forests and wildfire. He says he supports the Second Amendment and the wise use of Oregon's water and land.

Democratic nominee for Mississippi's 1st District. His campaign says he is a fifth-generation Mississippian living in rural Lafayette County with his wife of 35 years, and that his career has been spent speaking up for people who are vulnerable. A campaign release calls him a civil rights attorney. He says he wants to combat inflation and the policies driving up costs for Mississippians. He says he will protect and expand affordable health care. He says north Mississippi should get its fair share of federal dollars for economic development, infrastructure, and struggling schools, and he wants the right to have a vote counted preserved.

Retired Army first sergeant running for Congress The campaign says Clyde Jones served 21 years in the Army Signal Corps, retired as a first sergeant, and received a Bronze Star for service in Desert Storm and Iraqi Freedom. He later worked in process safety for DuPont and FMC in south Alabama and serves as an associate minister. He says he will focus on lowering prices for gas, health coverage, rent, and groceries. He says Congress should check the White House, and he says he will not take corporate PAC money. He supports expanding Medicaid and Affordable Care Act premium tax credits so people who earn too much for Medicaid can still get coverage.

Republican candidate for Nevada's 4th District. His campaign says he is a fourth-generation Nevadan, a small-business owner, and a rancher who has also coached young athletes. He says he is running because Washington is not working for Nevada. He says he wants housing, health care, groceries, and energy to be more affordable. He says tipped workers should not be taxed on tips and that overtime pay should be defended. He says waste, fraud, and abuse should be eliminated so Medicaid and Social Security last, and he wants more quality schools and career pathways.
District 8 · U.S. House · North Carolina · Democratic

Small-business owner running for Congress in North Carolina's 8th District. His campaign says he was born and raised in Union County, started in masonry, was homeschooled, and worked in construction and farming before starting a business more than a decade ago. He says he and his wife have two children and that he never planned to run. He says he will not take money from lobbyists for corporate or foreign interests and will not trade stocks in office. He says homeownership should be back in reach and that health care should heal people rather than maximize profit. He says markets should reward work and entrepreneurship, and that corporate monopolies are squeezing small businesses and family farms.

Former U.S. representative running for Congress. Colin Allred's campaign says he was raised in Dallas by a single mother who taught in public school, captained the Baylor football team, played in the NFL, and became a civil rights lawyer. It says he worked at the Department of Housing and Urban Development and later won a House seat. He says he is running to lower costs and stop politicians from rigging the economy against people who work hard. He says his earlier service included work on voting rights and on VA care in North Texas.
Governor and lieutenant governor · Illinois · Independent

With Carolyn Schofield, a former McHenry County Board member · Palatine consultant Owner of Cor Strategies. A Republican strategist for about 20 years who left the party to run. This guide has no separate photo of Schofield. He calls affordability the race and says neither major-party nominee will fix property taxes. Property-tax relief first, then spending restraint, cheaper gas and power, fewer data centers, and more housing. Has proposed taxing some services so property taxes and the sales tax on essentials can come down. Supports abortion rights. Would amend the TRUST Act so police can work with federal agents on violent cases. Supports more gun laws and health-care price transparency, including direct primary care.

Contract manager and farmer Colt Shelby says he worked on drilling rigs for nearly 16 years and has spent the last twenty years managing hundreds of millions of dollars in contracts. He says he got into the race in 2024 after a 3,000-bed prison was proposed near his home. He says he will open government records and restore what he calls honest government. He opposes school voucher plans that he says pull money away from rural public schools. He opposes the proposed Franklin County prison, and he says data-center expansion should not raise utility rates for families and farms.
