Congress votes, added across the communities

San Francisco supervisor running for Congress. Connie Chan's campaign says she was born in Hong Kong, moved to San Francisco at 13, and graduated from Galileo High School and UC Davis. It says she is the District 1 supervisor and has chaired the Board of Supervisors budget committee since 2023. She says Washington should stop cutting public programs to pay for tax breaks for billionaires and corporations, and should rebuild worker bargaining power. She says she would reform the tax and budget system and defend rights she says are under threat. She points to her work on affordable housing, small-business and union protections, and legal help for immigrants facing enforcement.

First-generation farmer from north Louisiana running for Congress. He says he knows hard work and keeping his word, and that he cannot be bought by lobbyists or billionaires. He is running so someone in Washington fights for people he calls hard-working patriots who are tired of being left behind. He says he would raise wages, protect the right to organize, and shift power from corporations to the people who do the work. He says more than a third of the district relies on Medicaid, that he supports Medicare for All, and that health care should depend on need rather than income. He says he would open public grocery stores stocked with local food that SNAP and WIC can buy, and he supports overturning Citizens United and banning congressional stock trading.

Candidate for U.S. Senate. Cory Booker's campaign calls him a fighter for New Jersey and says the effort is aimed at justice and opportunity. The site says the campaign takes no money from federal lobbyists, corporate PACs, or executives in the fossil-fuel and pharmaceutical industries. It asks supporters to give directly and says the campaign is powered by grassroots donors.
District 4 · U.S. House · South Carolina · Democratic

Civil-rights advocate running for Congress. Her campaign says she was born and raised in Spartanburg, in a family that has lived there for more than two centuries, and that she holds degrees in journalism and communications and a master's in political science from Howard University. She says she has worked as a legislative page, a Clyburn Fellow, and a lobbyist on reproductive health, public education, elections, guns, and criminal justice. She says her Upstate First agenda would expand health care, build affordable homes, manage rapid growth, invest in small businesses, and stop data centers from coming into local communities. She says she would fight for stronger schools, fair wages, safer communities, the power of every vote, and veterans. She says she is committed to a more affordable and inclusive future for Greenville and Spartanburg.

U.S. representative running for another term. Craig Goldman's campaign says he is a fifth-generation Texan and fourth-generation Fort Worth native who spent 12 years in the Texas House, including as chair of Energy Resources, before his election to Congress. It says he serves on Energy and Commerce, which covers energy, health, and telecommunications. He says his first bill signed into law rolled back regulations he argues would have cost Americans billions, and that he voted to extend the 2017 tax cuts. He says he supported the Laken Riley Act so immigration authorities detain people in the country illegally who are accused of theft or assault. He says border security is the federal government's first duty and that he backed more defense spending to keep building the F-35.

Manufacturing executive running for Congress. Cristian Morales's campaign says he was born in Guatemala, came to the United States with his family in the 1970s, and earned degrees from Purdue and Cornell. It says he has spent more than 20 years in automotive, aerospace, and defense manufacturing. He says he wants better education and job skills, a state where business is affordable, and more work for blue-collar families. He says immigration, housing costs, crime, homelessness, health care, and civil rights are the pillars of his campaign. He says government should protect freedoms, secure the border, and stay accountable rather than grow larger.
Second votes in the whole country · Germany
Second votes in the whole country

Former city commissioner and Democratic nominee for Florida's 18th District His campaign says he is a former Lake Wales city commissioner, the manager of Eagle Ridge Mall, a restaurant owner, and a husband and father of five. He says that under his management the mall grew from 35 to 71 stores, and that he and his wife are raising their children in Lake Wales. He says he would push a federal reinsurance backstop to bring down property-insurance premiums. He says veterans should get timely local care, including covered local providers when the VA cannot see them nearby soon enough. He says he would keep property taxes from pushing out homeowners, seniors, and working families, and support citrus growers against disease and unchecked development.
No 2026 issue list was found for this candidate.

Candidate for governor of Oklahoma. Her campaign says a campaign should be about people, and she is asking Oklahomans to send stories, photos, and letters about why they love the state. She says those stories would guide her if she becomes governor. No 2026 issue list was found for this candidate.

Teacher and small-business owner running for Indiana's 6th District. She says she is a seventh-generation Hoosier who, with her husband Trent, raised two children in Columbus and has owned a community business for more than 20 years. She taught biology and environmental science for more than a decade at Columbus Signature Academy and later served as a science and education fellow in the U.S. House. She earned a biology degree from the University of Evansville, a master's in anthropology from Indiana University, and a doctorate in education policy from Ball State in 2025. She says working-class Hoosiers should have good-paying jobs, affordable housing and child care, and access to sick time and paid family leave. She says she would support professional teachers and neighborhood pre-K through 12 schools that are safe and welcoming for students of all backgrounds and abilities. She says health care should be affordable enough that no one skips treatment because of cost, job loss, or discrimination, and she would invest in cleaner energy and oppose data centers that consume large amounts of fuel, water, and electricity.
District 6 · U.S. House · North Carolina · Democratic

Mayor of High Point running for Congress in North Carolina's 6th District. His campaign says he is a husband, father, former teacher, small-business owner, and mayor who was raised in the district. It says he was the youngest person elected mayor of High Point. He says his priorities are affordability, health care and hunger, democracy and accountability, education and the workforce, economic development, and immigration. He says that as mayor he focused on violent crime, workforce funding, housing, and small businesses. He says Washington should make paychecks, schools, neighborhoods, and businesses better, not score political points.

Candidate for Congress The campaign says Dale Strong was born and raised in Monrovia in Madison County and worked as a volunteer firefighter and paramedic before serving as a district commissioner and chairman of the Madison County Commission. He says he is running to continue a conservative agenda he associates with Donald Trump. He says he is a pro-life Christian, a lifetime NRA member, and that he will defend the Second Amendment. He says raising taxes is not an option and that cutting waste and shrinking government should be a priority. He says he supports building a border wall, returning people in the country illegally, and enforcing immigration law.
District 1 · U.S. House · New Jersey · Republican

Union carpenter running for Congress in New Jersey's 1st District. His campaign says he is a working husband, father, and tradesman, not a career politician, who started Americas Pulse Network and the Jersey Sure podcast after an earlier run for Congress. He says South Jersey families are working harder and falling behind. He says he would cut unnecessary federal spending and regulations, support American energy, and secure the border. He says he would require proof of citizenship and voter identification, and give parents more say over school curriculum. He says he would expand apprenticeships, back law enforcement against fentanyl trafficking, and make health prices and prescriptions more affordable, including through health savings accounts.

Business owner and former state legislator running for governor Dan Ahlers's campaign says he is a business owner, a former Dell Rapids Chamber of Commerce administrator, and a former state legislator who served on the Appropriations Committee. He says he would use that experience as governor. No 2026 issue list was found for this candidate.

Richardson council member running for Congress. Dan Barrios's campaign says he grew up in a working-class family in Brownsville and has lived in North Texas for more than 25 years. It says he was elected to the Richardson council in 2023 and is a husband and father. He says he would confront rising grocery and housing costs by strengthening consumer protections. He says nobody should be left without affordable medical care, and he would oppose extremism and defend the Constitution.

Candidate for governor of Maryland. Dan Cox's campaign describes him as a husband, father, and small-business owner who says he has taken on leaders in both parties. He says he is running because high prices and the cost of living are weighing on Maryland families. He says he would cut taxes and fees and limit property taxes so retirees are not taxed out of their homes. He proposes down-payment help and tax credits for first-time and younger buyers, and says building and permitting costs should come down. He says Maryland should reopen closed power plants, study small modular reactors, and give households more energy choices so electric bills stop climbing.

Navy reserve officer and Republican nominee for Florida's 9th District His campaign says he was working in the Pentagon on September 11, then joined the Navy and completed four tours in the Middle East and Central Asia, plus a State Department tour in southern Afghanistan. He says he holds the rank of commander, has been selected for promotion to captain, and served with SEAL team deployments in Iraq and Afghanistan. He says he would safeguard constitutional rights and work with President Trump to keep the military funded. He says he would take on overdevelopment and rising property-insurance rates. He says he would lower grocery, gas, and housing costs.

Former White House and Labor Department aide running for Congress. Born and raised in Andover, he says his family came from Korea and Lebanon. He says he was a senior White House aide, chief of staff at the Labor Department and for Boston's mayor, and an Andover Select Board member, and that he and his wife Amy have two young children. He says he is running to defend democracy, protect rights, and reduce the cost of living against what he calls a dismantling of the country. He says that in the Biden administration he worked on infrastructure, clean-energy jobs, education, and lower prescription costs for seniors. He says that at the Labor Department he helped recover wages, improve workplace safety, and increase union participation, and that he takes no corporate PAC money.

U.S. representative for Pennsylvania's 9th District. Dan Meuser describes himself as a job creator who was first elected in 2018 and is serving a fourth term. He sits on Financial Services, where he chairs an oversight subcommittee, and on Small Business. He says his priorities are an America First agenda, border security, the economy, and energy. He says his committee work is aimed at oversight of the financial system and support for small business.

Industrial mechanic, union leader, and Navy veteran. His campaign says he is a Navy veteran, a Nebraska National Guardsman, an industrial mechanic, and a union leader. He says no institution needs fixing more than the Senate, and that he would bring that work history to it. He says people have more in common with each other than with the partisans who run Washington. He says he would protect small businesses, family farms and ranches, and middle-class jobs. He says he would bring Nebraska values to Washington, drawing on his years as a sailor, a guardsman, a mechanic, and a union leader.

Lieutenant governor of Texas, running for re-election. His campaign says he was first elected lieutenant governor in 2014 and re-elected in 2018 and 2022. It describes him as a national voice for conservative policy. He says he fights to protect liberty, lower property and business taxes, create jobs, and grow the economy. He says he wants a stronger electric grid through more reliable thermal power and a high-quality education for every student. He says he works to secure the border, support law enforcement, and protect life, religious freedom, and the Second Amendment.

U.S. senator from Alaska Dan Sullivan has served in the U.S. Senate since January 2015 and was reelected in 2020. He was a Marine Corps infantry officer for more than 30 years, retired as a colonel in the Reserve in early 2024, and sits on the Armed Services, Commerce, Environment and Public Works, and Veterans' Affairs committees. He says he is running again to keep developing Alaska's energy resources. His campaign points to a large tax cut and says families and businesses should keep more of what they earn. He cites military investment and a stronger Alaska health-care system as reasons for another term.

Consumer advocate running for Congress in Maryland's 1st District. His campaign says he is a Democrat who has spent more than 14 years working with state banking regulators and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to challenge financial fraud. He and his wife Megan live in Bellevue, and he says her work as a nurse practitioner in Dorchester County shapes his view of health-care costs. He says he would hold monthly town halls and support a ban on members of Congress trading stocks, options, and crypto. Attorney · former Illinois Republican Party chair · won the primary with 40% Springfield lawyer and former chair of the Illinois Gaming Board, from Mt. Sterling. He says he is running on costs, safety, and a voice for the whole state, not only Chicago and Cook County. Lower taxes, energy bills, and health-care costs, with an all-of-the-above energy policy so rates fall and the lights stay on. Back police, hold violent offenders accountable, and enforce immigration law. He opposes taxpayer-funded benefits for people here illegally. Less federal regulation on small business, manufacturing, and farms, and tighter control of federal spending.

U.S. representative and former Virginia lieutenant governor. His official biography says he is in his sixth term representing Arlington, Alexandria, Falls Church, and parts of Fairfax County, and that he serves on Ways and Means and the Joint Economic Committee. He was lieutenant governor from 1990 to 1998 and ambassador to Switzerland and Liechtenstein under President Obama. His biography says his signature work as lieutenant governor included advocacy for Virginians with disabilities and protections for vulnerable people during welfare changes. It says he chaired Jobs for Virginia Graduates, a high-school dropout-prevention program, and served on the D.C. Campaign to Prevent Teen Pregnancy. As ambassador, it says, he pressed for stricter sanctions to push Iran toward nuclear talks and worked against Swiss bank secrecy used by wealthy Americans.

Electrician and U.S. representative for New Jersey's 1st District. His campaign says he is an electrician who attended community college and a skilled apprenticeship, and that he raised his first son as a single father. He says he has relied on unemployment and disability insurance, has a son in the military, and is now a grandfather. He says he supports higher wages, jobs in skilled trades, and fair pay and safe workplaces. He says students need affordable education that does not leave them in debt, and that every American should have affordable health care, including reproductive freedom. He says he will protect Social Security and Medicare and keep seeking South Jersey funding for water, clean energy, and community projects.

Candidate for California secretary of state. Don Wagner says he is running for secretary of state so every eligible voter can take part and only eligible voters cast ballots. He says elections should be secure, efficient, accurate, and accessible. He says the office's business division should be friendly to small business. He says he supports the voter-identification initiative on the November ballot.

State representative running for Congress in Michigan's 13th District. His campaign says he is a lifelong Detroiter who grew up in northeast Detroit, was raised by his mother and grandmother, and was the first in his family to graduate from college. It says he led SEIU Healthcare Michigan and now serves in the state House. He says he would defend the right to form a union, fight for a living wage, tax billionaires, and support a universal basic income. He calls for a Green New Deal, clean air and water, and more public transit, and he says Detroit's lead pipes and pollution are personal. He supports Medicare for All, a national housing guarantee, an end to cash bail, and federal protection of abortion access, including repeal of the Hyde Amendment.

U.S. representative running for another term. Doris Matsui's campaign says she was born in a Japanese American incarceration camp, grew up on a Central Valley farm, and graduated from UC Berkeley. It says she has served in Congress for more than two decades and is running in the redrawn 7th District. She says she has secured billions for flood protection, including Folsom Dam and levee work, and helped pass the Affordable Care Act and Medicare drug-price provisions. She says she would expand telehealth and mental-health clinics and keep pushing clean-energy and grid programs that lower bills. She says she opposes immigration raids she calls unlawful, votes against funding ICE, and objects to masked agents operating outside the rule of law.

Video-production business owner running for Congress. He founded Prologue Digital, has worked in media and sales training since 1990, and has been a Republican precinct officer and a volunteer with Seattle rescue missions. He says families are being priced out by gas, energy, groceries, housing, insurance, and taxes, and he argues the Climate Commitment Act raises energy costs. He wants an economy in which people can start a business, buy a home, learn a trade, and advance. He says public safety should hold people accountable for crime and disorder while still offering compassion to people in crisis.

Election-administration expert and attorney running for Congress. Doug Chapin's site says he is a father, educator, and attorney who has spent almost 40 years on election policy, including a decade at the University of Minnesota's Humphrey School, where he founded a certificate program in election administration. He says he has also worked in Congress, the executive branch, and the courtroom. He says he will fight for single-payer health care so people can get care without going broke, and to reverse Medicare and Medicaid cuts. He says he will eliminate the income cap on Social Security taxes and repeal tax cuts for billionaires in the White House budget bill. He says he will defend Congress's power over spending, taxes, tariffs, and war, and support immigration laws with a clearer, less costly path to citizenship.
No 2026 issue list was found for this candidate.

Former U.S. senator and former U.S. attorney Doug Jones is a lawyer who served as U.S. attorney for the Northern District of Alabama and, in that job, prosecuted two former Ku Klux Klan members for the 1963 bombing of the Sixteenth Street Baptist Church. He was elected to the U.S. Senate in 2017 and is now the Democratic candidate for governor. He says he will declare a one-year moratorium on data centers and reject tax breaks, secret deals, and nondisclosure agreements for those companies. He says he would suspend the state gas tax when prices spike, eliminate the grocery tax, end taxes on overtime, and raise the minimum wage. He says he would expand Medicaid to cover more than 154,000 working Alabamians and stop turning down roughly $182 million a year in federal health-care funding.

Republican candidate for Michigan attorney general. Doug Lloyd's campaign says he has been a prosecutor for more than 30 years, led cases involving fraud and financial crime, and was chosen by fellow prosecutors to lead their state association. He says he is running to prosecute cases and make communities safer. He says he would prosecute crimes fairly, without political favor or bias. He says he would advise lawmakers as they write what he calls strong, commonsense laws. He says he would protect constitutional rights, oppose politically motivated prosecutions, and root out corruption.

Retired Army lieutenant colonel and consultant running for Congress. His campaign says he is a husband and father of seven who lives in Culpeper County, served two combat tours in Iraq, advised coalition forces in Afghanistan, taught at West Point, and was director for Iraq at the National Security Council. He says he now leads a consulting firm that combats corruption. He says he is focused on restoring fiscal responsibility, rebuilding American industry, and ensuring food security. He says he would protect the values that shape both rural communities and fast-growing suburbs, and build a stronger, safer, and more affordable America.
No 2026 issue list was found for this candidate.

Community journalist running for the U.S. Senate. He says he is a community journalist who drives a 2010 Subaru Outback and built the campaign site himself. He asks what would change if working-class people wrote the law. He says he would advocate a universal basic income of $1,000 a month for every adult citizen and $1,500 a month for descendants of chattel slavery. He supports single-payer health care, and he says private-equity firms should not own homes, with rents tied to local wages and leases based on need. He calls for an end to U.S. hostilities with Iran and for ceasefires in Gaza and Ukraine, and he wants accountability for Flint's water and a stop to Line 5.

Marine veteran running for Congress in Indiana's Fourth District. He says he is a lifelong Hoosier and veteran raised by a farmer and a public schoolteacher. He says the campaign refuses corporate PAC donations so it answers to residents rather than corporate interests. He says he supports a single-payer Medicare for All system and would overturn Citizens United to get big money out of politics. He says he would raise the minimum wage, support unions, and fight poverty, and he wants affordable-housing legislation. He says that as a Marine veteran he would vote against further wars he calls needless, rein in unilateral military action, and fund the VA.
No 2026 issue list was found for this candidate.

Green Party candidate for Arizona secretary of state. His Clean Elections statement says he grew up in a small farming town in California, worked in construction, labor, sales, and service, and settled in Arizona with his wife and two children. He says he supports strong borders and legal immigration, including more lawful pathways so farming and construction have a workforce. He says he supports renewable energy, including fusion, and securing Arizona's share of Colorado River water. He says he would hold corporations accountable for clean air and water and work to bring manufacturing and higher-paying jobs to Arizona.

Army veteran and business owner running for U.S. House in Colorado's 3rd District. Dwayne Romero says he is a husband, a father, and an Army engineer officer who was raised by a single mother on low wages and food stamps. He says he has also been a small-business owner, a school board president, a city councilman, and a state economic-development director. He says affordability comes first, and that he would start by repealing tariffs and expanding family tax credits. He says he would pass a farm bill, keep foreign buyers out of Colorado water and farmland, and defend the district's water. He says the district should keep using the energy it already produces while newer sources come online, and that rural hospitals and public-land staff need to be protected.

U.S. representative for Hawaii's 1st District The campaign says Ed Case is the U.S. representative for Hawaii's 1st District, covering Honolulu from Makapu'u to Mililani and Kapolei, and that he is asking voters to return him to Congress. He says another term would move him into the top quarter of House seniority and keep him on Appropriations. He says the country needs experienced leadership to defend democracy and deliver practical solutions. He says he will keep speaking honestly, listening, and representing all of Hawaii, pointing to his work through COVID-19, Red Hill, and the Maui wildfires.

Navy SEAL, farmer, and Trump-endorsed candidate for Congress. A fifth-generation Kentucky farmer, he says he served three decades as a Navy SEAL officer, rising to captain, including SEAL Team Six, and earned three Bronze Stars. He says he returned home to keep farming and support veterans. He says he would cut taxes and regulations, stop spending he blames for inflation, and bring jobs back to Kentucky. He says he would finish a border wall, fund Border Patrol and ICE, and rebuild the military. He says he would defend gun rights without compromise, that he is pro-life, and that he would eliminate DEI programs in schools, the military, and government.

U.S. senator from Massachusetts, first elected to the Senate in 2013. Ed Markey's campaign says that since he entered the Senate he has refused to compromise progressive values and has focused on costs, opportunity, rights, and a safer and more sustainable future. He says he is fighting to lower costs, protect workers, and expand opportunity in education and jobs. He says health care is too expensive and that he wants lower costs, wider access, stronger public health, and corporations held accountable. He also lists clean energy and transit, civil rights for LGBTQ people and immigrants, stronger gun laws, and a fairer justice system.
No 2026 issue list was found for this candidate.

Attorney and veteran running for Congress. Edgardo Baez's campaign says he has been a soldier, a critical-care nurse, and an attorney for more than 20 years, and that he saw government overreach while in Cuba. It says he is running in the San Antonio area. He says he would defend constitutional rights, reject socialism, and protect freedoms. He says he would stimulate local business, attract investment, and champion tax changes that help neighborhoods.

U.S. Senate candidate, Marine, and school board member. Edmond Laplante's site describes him as a father, grandfather, Marine, and a mechanic for more than 40 years. He says he qualified for the November ballot by petition. He says the Constitution is a set of limits on power, not a tool for politicians to redesign society. He says a government that stays inside those limits is more trustworthy than one that promises to fix everything.

Candidate for Congress who grew up on a Whatcom County dairy farm. He says the district needs a representative focused on economics and public safety, and he argues that high taxes and a larger government created the affordability crunch. He supports tying federal public-safety grants to local cooperation, labeling cartels as foreign terrorist organizations, and ending sanctuary policies. He wants faster energy permits, more nuclear and hydroelectric power, and a repeal of federal carbon taxes. He wants Title IX to define sex as biological sex, a federal ban on irreversible medical procedures for minors, and immigration rebuilt around nuclear families and job skills.
No 2026 issue list was found for this candidate.

Army veteran and former police officer running for Congress. His campaign says he was raised in poverty and foster care, then by his grandparents in Puerto Rico, worked as a police officer there, and served combat tours in the Middle East before retiring as a disabled veteran. It calls him a grassroots conservative and a supporter of the Second Amendment. He says responsible gun ownership is both a right and a responsibility, and that he would protect the constitutional rights of law-abiding citizens. His site lists education, public safety, affordable health care, veterans, youth mentorship, Social Security, and small-business job growth as his priorities. He says he is committed to strengthening families, expanding opportunity, and building safer communities in the 3rd District.

Retired Navy rear admiral running for U.S. House in Colorado's 4th District. Eileen Laubacher says she served 34 years in the Navy, graduated from the Naval Academy, and raised five children in Colorado. She says she retired in 2024 and is running because the district needs someone focused on costs and on making government work. She says lowering costs comes first, including ending tariffs that raise prices, a middle-class tax cut, and making data centers pay for the power and infrastructure they use. She says she would fight for rural hospitals, pass a long-term farm bill, and build water supplies so farms are not sold off and dried up. She says she takes no corporate PAC money and supports term limits, a ban on members trading stocks, a secure border, and a path to citizenship.

Former member of Congress, Navy veteran, and small-business owner. Her campaign says she joined the Navy at 17, spent 20 years on ships with six deployments, then built the Mermaid Factory from her kitchen table in Hampton Roads. She says she previously served the district in Congress, including on Veterans' Affairs. She says she would restore Affordable Care Act subsidies, expand Medicare drug negotiation, cap insulin at $35, and restore Medicaid funding she says was cut. She says she would strengthen Social Security and Medicare, fight offshore drilling, fund the Chesapeake Bay program, and ban members of Congress and their families from trading individual stocks. She says she helped pass the PACT Act, would reverse cuts to veterans' care, repeal tariffs that raise prices, and serve as a check on the war in Iran.

Former Navy SEAL and U.S. representative for Arizona's 2nd District. His campaign says he enlisted after September 11, served 13 years including five wartime deployments with SEAL Team 3, and later started Bottle Breacher with his wife. He says he is a father of two raising his family in Arizona. He says he is pro-life and pro-Second Amendment, and that he voted to end taxes on tips, overtime, and Social Security while expanding the child tax credit. He says he would finish the border wall, hire more immigration judges, and stop fentanyl, and he supports a national voter-ID law. He says rural Arizona should come first, including copper, water, tribal entrepreneurs, and veterans' care, and he opposes wind and solar farms he says raise utility bills.

Washtenaw County prosecuting attorney, running for Michigan attorney general. Eli Savit's campaign says he grew up in Ann Arbor, taught eighth-grade history, and later clerked at the U.S. Supreme Court for Justices Sandra Day O'Connor and Ruth Bader Ginsburg. It says he was elected Washtenaw County prosecutor in 2020. He says his office built units for sexual assault and domestic violence and pursued cold-case rape prosecutions. He says that after Roe v. Wade was overturned he went to court to challenge Michigan's abortion ban and has kept arguing for reproductive freedom. He says he created a unit aimed at wage theft and consumer harm and has sued large companies over pollution of air and water.

Journalist and Democratic nominee for Florida's 27th District His campaign says he spent forty years telling South Florida's story and recently left the anchor desk. He says he is the son of Cuban immigrants and that his family has lived in the district since the 1960s. He says his daughters moved away because housing in South Florida had become unaffordable. He says he would turn unused federal land into mixed-use housing, expand workforce housing, and seek a federal backstop for homeowners' insurance. He says he would protect Medicare, Social Security, and Medicaid, oppose raising the retirement age, and let people ages 55 to 64 buy into Medicare. He says he supports a secure border, faster immigration courts, protection for Dreamers, and removal of people who pose a genuine threat.

Governor on the Kane County list. Not on the Will County list.

Candidate running for Congress in Ohio's 6th District. Elizabeth Kirtley's campaign says due process and the freedoms of speech, assembly, and religion should be treated as rights, not privileges. She says she is running to defend those rights and a woman's ability to make medical decisions. She says ICE should be abolished because she believes an agency that blocks constitutional rights should not exist. She wants abortion rights written into federal law so they do not change at state lines, and she says each person should have one vote that cannot be bought.

Nurse and patient advocate running for Congress in Arizona's 5th District. Her campaign says she grew up in poverty in Ohio, became a nurse, and was 37 when she was diagnosed with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. She and her husband Sean became parents through adoption and IVF, and she says she has spent more than a decade in reproductive health care. She says she would cosponsor Medicare for All, cap insulin at $35 for everyone, and let Medicare negotiate the price of every drug. She says billionaires should not pay a lower tax rate than a nurse, and she wants the expanded child tax credit restored and tariffs that raise grocery and medicine prices stopped. She says she would protect abortion and fertility care, and she supports early voting, vote by mail, and the John Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act.

Lawyer and mediator running for Idaho's 2nd District. Her campaign says she is a lawyer and mediator, not a career politician, and that she has spent more than twenty years helping businesses, schools, and communities work through conflict. She says she took an oath to uphold the Constitution when she was sworn in, and that her family chose Idaho and raised their children here. She says she would ban corporate purchases of single-family homes, expand the ROAD to Housing Act, and give counties the last word on data centers so they do not drain local water and power. She says she would keep public lands public, protect the Roadless Rule, and pass farm bills that give Idaho farmers and ranchers a stable plan. She says Congress should check executive power, ban stock trading by members and their immediate families, and ban dark money.

U.S. representative for Missouri's 5th District. His campaign says he grew up in public housing and has treated affordable housing as a lifelong cause, including work on a major federal housing law. He says Social Security and Medicare should be kept solvent, and he supports expanding Medicaid so rural patients do not have to travel hours for care. He supports the Affordable Care Act, wants it strengthened, and says he has fought to lower prescription drug prices. He opposes the decision overturning Roe v. Wade and supports bipartisan gun laws that he says can protect children while allowing responsible ownership.

U.S. representative for Ohio's 13th District. Emilia Sykes says she grew up on Akron's west side and has worked with members of both parties to bring federal resources back to the 13th District. She serves on Transportation and Infrastructure, including its water resources subcommittee. She says clean water, clean air, and a healthy environment are basic rights, and that environmental policy can also create jobs and hold down utility costs. She says every northeast Ohioan deserves to have their voice heard and their vote counted.

Candidate for Congress who grew up in Washington's 6th District. She says she is the daughter of a shipyard worker and a paraeducator and that those roots connect her to the district's working-class families. The campaign says it does not accept corporate PAC money and is funded by working people. She frames the race as a bid to change conditions for the families in the district where she was born and raised.

Rancher, large-animal veterinarian, and Marine veteran who served as speaker of the Wyoming House and then in the State Senate. His campaign says he is a fourth-generation Wyomingite raised on a Campbell County ranch who returned after the Marines, earned a veterinary degree, and kept the family ranch with his wife, Kelly. He says his legislative work has centered on Wyoming energy independence, rural health access, and water infrastructure. He says he is running to offer leadership rooted in service, and that the campaign is counting on Wyoming residents rather than special-interest money.

Green Party candidate for Michigan secretary of state. His campaign says corporate-funded debates have replaced nonpartisan League of Women Voters forums and left people convinced elections are rigged. He argues Michigan should expand democratic choice. He wants ranked-choice voting so people can rank the candidates they support and so third-party votes are not dismissed as wasted. He says he would lower the voting age to 16, arguing that youth political power matters more than claims of voter fraud. He says the stations that sell candidate ads should not control debate questions, and he points to Green Party pickets of those studios.

U.S. representative campaigning on taxes, health care, and the border. His campaign calls him a conservative family man and says the agenda is meant to put Missouri families first. He wants spending cut so Missourians keep more of their pay. He says health care should be affordable and directed by patients rather than bureaucrats. He wants the southern border secured, constitutional rights of law-abiding people defended, and federal waste investigated.

Walnut mayor and business owner running for Congress in California's 31st District. His campaign says he served nine years on the Walnut City Council, including a term as mayor in 2016 and 2017, after leading the Chinese American Association of Walnut. It says he has 30 years of business experience and has volunteered with churches, food distributions, and treatment centers. He says he will defend speech, religion, and the right to keep and bear arms, and secure the border against illegal weapons, drugs, and people while keeping legal trade and tourism moving. He says he supports term limits, reasonable pay for officials, and restitution from people convicted of crimes. He says he supports school choice, opposes identity-based admissions and racially divisive curriculum, and wants fewer regulations on U.S. businesses.

Air Force veteran running for Congress in Ohio's 1st District. Eric Conroy says he grew up on Cincinnati's west side, graduated from the Air Force Academy, served as a captain in special operations, and later worked as a CIA case officer. He says he is running to fight for working families and safer communities. He says he will lower inflation, cut red tape, and back pro-growth policies for Ohio workers and small businesses. He also says he will stand with law enforcement, secure the border, protect Social Security and Medicare from benefit cuts, and support parents and local control of education.

Former prosecutor and Army officer running for Congress. Eric Flores's campaign says he grew up in the Rio Grande Valley, served as a Texas Army National Guard infantry captain on the border, and was an assistant U.S. attorney who prosecuted trafficking cases. It says he is a husband and father of two. He says he would lower the cost of living, oppose spending that feeds inflation, and fund roads, ports, broadband, and water supplies. He says he would shorten VA waits, protect seniors' earned benefits, and back South Texas farmers, ranchers, and small businesses.

Democratic candidate for Alaska's at-large U.S. House seat. His candidate statement, which he filed with the Alaska Division of Elections, says he studied criminal justice at Denver College and Pacific Island, ethnic, and women's studies at City College of San Francisco. He describes work on Native Hawaiian and Native American legal defense, public-education campaigns, and the Fight for $15. He says war should be avoided, both for service members and for families caught in it. He says higher education should stay open, including Indigenous history, Black history, and women's medical choices. He says Alaska's lands, including the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, should not be used for short-term exploitation.

Retired Army colonel running for Congress. Eric Jenkins's site describes him as a retired Army colonel with 34 years of military service and more than 20 years of public service, running in Kansas's 3rd District. He says he will fight wasteful spending, push a balanced-budget framework, oppose new broad-based tax increases, and make Trump-era tax cuts permanent. He says he will fully fund and modernize the military, support veterans' health care, and strengthen Kansas installations including Fort Leavenworth. He says secure borders are a national-security need, and he lists the Second Amendment, free speech, and religious liberty as rights he will defend.

Business leader running for Congress. Eric Jones's campaign says he grew up in rural Maine, attended Yale, and helped build companies in health care, banking, and education before moving to Napa with his family. It says he accepts no corporate PAC money, has signed a term-limits pledge, and is running in the 4th Congressional District. He says corruption and corporate money drive the cost of living, and he wants corporate funds out of politics, a ban on congressional stock trading, and an end to gerrymandering. He says he would cut taxes for working people, challenge utility monopolies, add Medicare coverage for vision, dental, hearing, and in-home care, and lower prescription prices. He says he would defend Social Security, secure water and family farms, and refuse blank checks for war.

Libertarian nominee for governor of Colorado. Eric Mulder says he is a U.S. Army veteran who served in Afghanistan as a chaplain's assistant. He says that work showed him people from very different backgrounds can pull together when the mission comes first, and that Colorado should govern in that spirit. He says programs should be judged by the results they deliver, not by how many dollars they spend, and that communities closest to a problem should be free to solve it. He proposes a one-year break from the state sales tax for places in economic distress, with local voters deciding whether to replace it with a local tax for schools, roads, water, emergency services, or other needs. He says he would oppose government cameras that track every passing car, and he wants the state to clear a path for small nuclear reactors, including reactors that large power users could run themselves.

Democratic candidate for lieutenant governor, and an entrepreneur. He describes himself as a moderate Democrat, a father, and a brain-health advocate who wants government in the style of the late Governor Cecil Andrus. He says he came to Idaho after marrying Lesley, who is from Idaho Falls, and that they are raising two boys in the Treasure Valley. He says taxes should stay low, but that roads, schools, and senior care cannot be met by cuts alone. He says he will fight House Bill 328, which he says adds Medicaid work rules, shifts care to profit-driven companies, and lets officials cut benefits overnight. He says he will fully fund public schools, repeal the voucher program, and connect career training to jobs that keep young people in Idaho.

Minnesota state senator running for Congress. Eric Pratt's site says he has lived in Prior Lake since the 1970s, worked in banking, served on the Prior Lake–Savage school board, and has been a state senator since 2012. He and his wife, Tina, have been married 34 years and raised two children in the district. He says he will focus on lowering costs, supporting small businesses, and restoring an economy that working families can afford. He says he supports law enforcement and first responders, and that laws should be enforced consistently from neighborhoods to the U.S. border. He says he will crack down on fraud and abuse, pointing to his banking work against financial scams and his Senate work on taxpayer accountability.

Fond du Lac County district attorney running for attorney general. His campaign says he has prosecuted human trafficking, homicide, sexual assault, drug trafficking, and financial crimes, and that he is a past president of the Wisconsin District Attorneys Association. It says he was named the state's district attorney of the year in 2024. He says he would back police, keep violent offenders off the street, and put public safety ahead of politics. He says he would go after cartels and dealers tied to fentanyl and meth. He says he would modernize the state crime labs and clear the testing backlog.

Small-business owner and Democratic nominee for Florida's 6th District His campaign says he was born in Florida, raised in the 6th District, grew up in Citra, and graduated from North Marion High School. His father was an Ocala police officer and his mother leads a local Realtor association. He says he managed big-box stores in the district for more than 20 years, hiked the Appalachian Trail in 2022, and started a business renovating vintage Airstream trailers. He says families should be able to afford a home, health care, insurance, and everyday essentials, with more workforce housing and a steadier insurance market. He says economic growth should reward work, support local businesses, and include wages and schedules that match the cost of living. He says Medicare and Social Security must stay strong, and he would negotiate prescription prices.

County employee and former small-business owner running for Congress. Erik Osberg's site says he is a husband and father, a former small-business owner, and a county employee who has worked in finance, the public sector, media, and the trades. He says he and his wife have lived in Wadena for about 20 years, where they raised three children, and that he graduated from Hamline University. He says he will defend constitutional rights and fair elections, and he supports a constitutional amendment to end Citizens United and a ban on members of Congress trading individual stocks. He says health care should be more affordable and accessible for rural families, seniors, and towns that depend on local clinics and hospitals. He says he will back federal funding for public schools and support for farms, small businesses, housing, child care, and public safety.

Candidate for governor of Colorado. Erik Underwood says he has fought corporate fraud, including eight years in federal court against Bank of America, and that he holds a patent on an artificial-intelligence product. He says he would bring that same fight to the governor's office. He says he has a plan for home loans with a down payment capped at $2,500. He says he would fund child care with 25 cents on each purchase and wants universal health care in Colorado. He says he would offer free college and trade school and would fight for the state's water rights.

U.S. representative and House Republican Conference secretary from Salem, Indiana. Born and raised in Scottsburg, she says she interned in the Indiana Senate while at Indiana University, worked in child services and for Senator Dan Coats, and later built a small business helping law enforcement communicate with communities. She lives in Salem with her husband Dustin and their three children. She says she supports finishing a border wall, backing law enforcement, and deporting people she calls criminal illegal aliens. She says the federal government spends too much, and she backs a balanced-budget amendment and opposes late-term abortion. She says parents should direct their children's education, that she would not defund the police, and that cutting red tape and taxes is how small businesses create jobs.

Mayor of Troy running for Congress in Michigan's 11th District. His campaign says he and his wife Bethany moved to Oakland County 17 years ago, and that he was elected to the Troy City Council in 2015 and mayor in 2019. He says he has spent seven years as a nonpartisan mayor focused on rebuilding trust in local government. He says he is running because constant political division is unhealthy, and that people can hold their principles while still listening to one another. He says most people want stability for their families, opportunity for their children, and safe communities, and that he would bring that approach to Congress.

Republican nominee for North Carolina's 2nd District. His campaign brochure says he was raised in Swarthmore, Pennsylvania, earned a PhD in fiber and polymer science at North Carolina State and a master of divinity, and taught college chemistry before retiring as a chemistry and education consultant. He says he moved to Wake County in 2023 and is running to replace Deborah Ross. He proposes a flat tax with minimal deductions for people and businesses, and less federal regulation so states handle more local affairs. He says human life should be protected from conception to natural death, and he calls for a ban on partial-birth abortion and for states to limit what he describes as gender surgeries on children and euthanasia. He wants elementary and secondary education controlled by states and localities, with the focus on reading, writing, science, and math.

U.S. representative, refugee, and Army veteran. He says he was born in Soviet Ukraine to a Jewish family, left at age three after his mother died, and arrived in New York as a refugee in 1979. He says he attended public schools in Brooklyn, SUNY Binghamton, and Army ROTC at Cornell, and that he served 25 years in the Army, including in the Iraq War. District 8 · U.S. House · New York · Democratic

House Democratic leader representing New York's 8th District. His campaign says he has represented the Brooklyn-based district since 2013 and was elected House Democratic leader in 2023, the first person of color to lead a major party in Congress. It says the district includes neighborhoods such as East New York, Brownsville, Bedford-Stuyvesant, Canarsie, and Coney Island. He says he is working to lower child care, health care, education, and prescription costs, including a $35 monthly insulin cap for people on Medicare. He supports universal background checks and a ban on assault weapons, and he highlights a law that made gun trafficking a federal crime. He says he wants more affordable and public housing, better-paying jobs through infrastructure and manufacturing investment, and protection of abortion access.

Dean of the U.S. House, representing southern and eastern Kentucky since 1981. Born in rural Kentucky, he says he has been elected to 23 consecutive terms and became the longest-serving House member in 2022. He points to Operation UNITE, the Center for Rural Development, and SOAR as regional projects he helped build. He says that as Appropriations chair from 2011 to 2016 he cut discretionary spending by $126 billion and pushed oversight of federal agencies. He says he led the first Homeland Security appropriations subcommittee and pressed for immigration enforcement and border security. After winning the 2026 primary he said he would keep fighting for conservative values, jobs at home, and energy independence.

Sixth-generation farmer Hallie Shoffner says she is a sixth-generation Arkansas farmer and that she has lived through a farm shutdown. She describes the farming community of Shoffner, named for her family, as a place that is now empty buildings and abandoned fields. She says she will cut taxes for working families and lower the cost of groceries, child care, housing, and health care. She says she will protect and strengthen Social Security and Medicare, lift the payroll-tax cap on the very wealthy, and reverse cuts to those programs. She says a farm bill should help farmers diversify, sell into regional markets, and supply food to public schools.

U.S. representative for Georgia's 4th District. His campaign says he is in his tenth term representing parts of DeKalb and Gwinnett counties, and it describes him as a legislator focused on delivering results for the district. He says he supports DACA, temporary protected status, refugees, and immigrants who come to build a better life for their children. He says he has delivered more than $350 million in federal investment for district job creation since January 2009, including $98 million he says saved more than 1,000 teaching jobs in DeKalb, Rockdale, Newton, and Gwinnett counties. He says he will oppose efforts to take away affordable health insurance and will stand with consumers seeking coverage.

Candidate for governor of Maine. Hannah Pingree says she was raised on the island of North Haven, became Speaker of the Maine House, and later directed the Governor's Office of Policy Innovation and the Future. She says she still lives on North Haven with her husband and two children. She says her record includes expanding access to health care and affordable housing and helping lead the state's climate work. She says that in the Legislature she worked on rural broadband, clean energy, lower health costs, reproductive rights, and Maine's working waterfronts. She says that work included the Kid-Safe Products Act, aimed at keeping toxic chemicals out of products children use.

Member of Congress and lawyer whose campaign says she has fought federal regulators in court. Her campaign says she has spent her career challenging rules that affect ranchers, farmers, and energy producers, and that Congress should take back power it has given to federal agencies. She says she will defend speech, gun rights, and private property, and that she wants voter identification and an end to mailing ballots to people who did not request them. She says she will fight tax increases, cut federal spending, and defend oil, gas, and coal production. She says federal land agencies have mismanaged forests and that she wants multiple-use rules that answer to the people who live with those decisions.
Secretary of State · South Dakota · Republican

State representative and small-business owner Heather Baxter's campaign says she has been the state representative for District 34 since November 2024 and owns a small business in Rapid City and Custer. She says she is a lifelong South Dakotan running for secretary of state. She says she would push secure and transparent elections and restore trust in how votes are run. She says she would give small businesses easier access to office resources and cut red tape through what she calls SD DOGE. She says she would improve customer service in the secretary of state's office.

Retired Ford employee running for Congress in Michigan's 6th District. Her campaign says she is a Christian mother of two, married 30 years, and the first in her family to attend college, earning a bachelor's and a master's from Central Michigan University. She says she recently retired from Ford after more than 32 years in product development, planning, and analytics. She says she would cut wasteful spending, balance the budget, and limit spending bills that bundle unrelated items. She wants schools focused on academics, elections limited to citizens, and energy independence through the free market. She says she would close the border, protect the right to self-defense, and restrict foreign ownership of land.

Candidate for Congress in Tennessee's 8th District. Her campaign says the district needs fresh ideas and leaders who show up for people, and she is asking voters to make a plan for Election Day. She says data centers should not get a blank check. She says communities deserve a say in whether and where data centers are built, and in how much water and power they use.

Former CVS retail president running for governor Helena Foulkes's campaign says she is a lifelong Rhode Islander who spent 25 years at CVS and became president of its retail division. It says that as retail president she worked to lower prescription prices and took tobacco off the shelves. She says she would create good-paying jobs and make Rhode Island more affordable, and she criticizes the state's handling of housing and the Washington Bridge. She says she would push back against federal funding cuts aimed at states like Rhode Island. Her plans page lists health care, jobs, child care and transportation, career and technical education, and a housing program called Rhode Home.

U.S. representative and former Texas secretary of state. His official biography says he was born in Laredo, the eldest of eight children of migrant farmworkers, and was the first in his family to attend college. He has worked as a lawyer, customs broker, and educator, and served as a state representative and Texas secretary of state. He says education is the key that opens the door to opportunity for every child. He says his Appropriations work, including as ranking member of the Homeland Security Subcommittee, is meant to strengthen national security while delivering results for South Texas. He says a bipartisan reputation keeps him at the table fighting for Texas families no matter which party is in power.
District 3 · U.S. House · New Jersey · Democratic

Physician and U.S. representative for New Jersey's 3rd District. His campaign says he is a lifelong Burlington County resident, the son of a teacher and a nurse, who earned degrees from Princeton, Jefferson Medical College, and Rutgers Law School. He says he served 25 years in the Assembly, including as health committee chair, before his first term in Congress. He says government does not belong in the exam room and that he is fighting to keep health care, including abortion, affordable. He says he wants safe communities, strong public schools, good jobs, and a healthy environment. He says he has worked to ease taxes on middle-class families, protect small businesses, and open manufacturing pathways for students.

County supervisor and former labor secretary running for Congress. Hilda Solis's campaign says she has stood up for working people as a county supervisor and is now running for the House. It says she served as secretary of labor in President Obama's Cabinet and helped implement the Affordable Care Act. She says she is running to defend workers, immigrants, educators, affordable housing, reproductive rights, veterans, unions, Medicaid, and democracy. She says she has prioritized clean air, water, and open space, and she cites environmental-justice laws recognized with a Profile in Courage award. She says she wants to create and preserve affordable housing and find better ways to help people who are homeless.
District 6 · U.S. House · New Jersey · Republican

Civil servant running for Congress in New Jersey's 6th District. Her campaign says she is a Monmouth County mother of three and the spouse of an Army veteran, with a criminal-justice degree and years of civil service in police, military, veterans, agriculture, and immigration agencies. She says she attended school in New Jersey and is running because the district needs new leadership. She says she will fight for parental rights and transparency in education, lower taxes, and medical freedom. She says she wants fair immigration reform, respect for veterans and seniors, and clean water and air. She also lists equal rights and expanded liberty under the Constitution.

U.S. representative for Michigan's 3rd District. Her campaign says she is a former Justice Department attorney, a Christian, and a mother of two, and that in 2022 she became the first Democratic woman to represent West Michigan in the House. She says she is running for a third term focused on costs, health care, and government corruption. She says she is working to lower health-care and drug costs, defend the Affordable Care Act, and stop insurers from dropping people who get sick. She says decisions about pregnancy belong with women, and that she will protect the right to choose. She wants well-paying jobs, semiconductor manufacturing in Michigan, and protection of drinking water from PFAS.

Council vote, added across the regions

South Bay native and Marine Corps veteran running for Congress. Houston Brignano's campaign says he was born and raised in the South Bay, joined the Marine Corps out of high school, and deployed twice to Iraq. He says student debt and housing costs, including a first-time homebuyer age he puts at 40, are shutting people out of a stable life. He says he would train young people to use artificial intelligence and protect jobs from automation with reskilling programs.

Georgia state representative running for Congress. He says he was born and raised in Athens, where he still lives, and has served in the State House since 2019 for Barrow, Clarke, Jackson, and Oconee counties. He says his work has been helping small businesses grow, and that he now works with Carter Engineering in Oconee County. He says immigration enforcement should keep cooperating with ICE, deportations should continue, and the border should stay secured. He says he led opposition to defunding the police in Georgia, backed hundreds of millions of dollars for law enforcement, and took on district attorneys he says endangered public safety. He wants spending cuts and tax cuts to match what he calls Georgia's balanced budgets, more American manufacturing, a military rebuilt around strength, and a block on Chinese purchases of U.S. farmland.

U.S. representative and the first African refugee elected to Congress. She says her public service started at 14 interpreting for her grandfather at DFL caucuses, and that in 2016 she became the first Somali-American Muslim legislator in the country. In 2018 she became the first woman of color to represent Minnesota in Congress. She says she has fought to codify Roe v. Wade, pass climate legislation, address opioids, and ban assault weapons. She says she negotiated a public-safety bill with local investment and accountability, and funding that fed more than 30 million children during the pandemic. She says community projects she brought home include veteran housing in Robbinsdale and help for entrepreneurs in north Minneapolis.

Pritzker campaigns on wages, abortion access, schools, and budgets he says are balanced, along with credit-rating upgrades. Points to the $15 minimum wage, the ended state grocery tax, a doubled child tax credit, a $35 insulin cap, and medical-debt relief. Wants more housing. Abortion-access laws that made Illinois a destination for care. He says health care is a right and opposes federal Medicaid cuts. Signed limits on civil immigration arrests near courthouses, hospitals, colleges, and day cares. Says people convicted of violent crimes should be deported, and that he is open to changes in SAFE-T pretrial rules.

Indiana state senator running for Congress in the 5th District. He says he entered the state Senate in 2018, flipped a long-held Republican district, and is the first openly LGBTQ+ legislator in Indiana history. He says he is not independently wealthy and knows the pressure of rising health-care and grocery costs. He says he would cap health-care and prescription costs and push corporations to account for prices on groceries, housing, and energy. He says Washington needs a Democratic check so federal agencies are not above the law. He says he grew up in a union family, with a father who drove trucks and a mother who was a school secretary, and that he is running because that middle-class promise is no longer guaranteed.

Air Force officer and lawyer running for Congress. Jace Yarbrough's campaign says he is a seventh-generation Texan, an Air Force major, and a constitutional lawyer with degrees from UT Austin and Stanford. It says he and his wife founded a classical Christian school and are raising five children. He says he would back immigration enforcement and oppose amnesty, and keep legal immigration from being used to push down wages. He says he would seek national concealed-carry reciprocity and repeal of the National Firearms Act.

U.S. representative and retired Marine lieutenant general. His campaign says he rose to lieutenant general in the Marine Corps, ran a small business, and spent 22 years as a commercial airline pilot. He and his wife Cindy live in Watersmeet, and the campaign says family roots in the Upper Peninsula go back to iron miners in the late 1800s. He says he has worked to expand rural broadband, including a bill that would account for short construction seasons in northern Michigan. He says his veterans work includes suicide-prevention grants, more home and community care, and a burial-benefit fix he calls Gerald's Law. He says he backs Michigan farms, including cherry growers, opposes taxpayer funding of abortion, and wants a military strong enough to deter adversaries.
District 12 · U.S. House · North Carolina · Republican

Financial professional running for Congress in North Carolina's 12th District. His campaign says he is a Christian and a financial professional who decided to run because of housing costs, personal debt, and what he calls an erosion of civility. He says America should work for everyone. He pledges not to accept PAC money and not to trade individual stocks. He says he would hold more than 10 town halls a year.

U.S. senator Jack Reed's campaign says he grew up in Cranston, graduated from West Point, served as an Army Ranger, and commanded paratroopers in the 82nd Airborne. It says he serves on the Appropriations and Armed Services committees. He says he voted against the Iraq War, opposes the Iran war, and is using his Senate vote to stop that war and other military operations he calls unnecessary. He says he wants housing, education, health care, and environmental spending paid for by higher taxes on billionaires and changes to the tax system. He says he has worked to bring federal money to Rhode Island for housing, coastal research, Coast Guard ships, Quonset jobs, the airport, roads, and transit.
District 18 · U.S. House · New York · Republican

Hudson Valley resident running for Congress in New York's 18th District. Her campaign says she was born in the Hudson Valley and is running because the region is becoming too expensive for the families who built it. It says she is not a career politician and does not owe favors to party bosses or special interests. She says she would work on taxes, energy, everyday bills, and health care so more income stays with families and small businesses. She says she would focus on good-paying jobs, skilled trades, and education connected to careers in the region. She also calls for congressional ethics, government transparency, and protection of local rights and public safety.

State assemblymember running for Congress. Jacqui Irwin's campaign says she is a mother, an engineer, and a community leader with two decades in local public life. It says she is running for the new 26th District to focus on public safety, affordability, and Ventura and Los Angeles counties. She says she would stand up for the district against what she calls an assault on democracy and California values. Her campaign highlights laws she wrote on housing and services for homeless veterans, a state climate law, and gun-safety measures. It says she has worked to create jobs, balance budgets, and keep communities safe.

U.S. representative for Connecticut's 5th District The campaign says Jahana Hayes, a teacher named National Teacher of the Year in 2016, was elected in 2018 as Connecticut's first African American congresswoman. She sits on Education and Labor and on Agriculture, where she is ranking member of the nutrition subcommittee. She supports Medicare for All and says she has worked to curb surprise bills and cap prescription drug costs. She wants housing help for first-time buyers and an economy that lowers grocery, gas, and energy costs rather than serving only the very wealthy. She supports red-flag laws, expanded background checks, and other steps to reduce gun violence.

Marine and U.S. representative on the Energy and Commerce Committee. He says he is a dad, a Marine, and a lifelong student of American history who represents 35 cities and towns from Fall River to Brookline. He says leaders fight from the front, own hard decisions, and eat last. He says he works in Washington to defend democracy and lower prices against corruption that makes the American dream too expensive. He describes a New American Dream as an excellent education by 18, a home by 30, and a dignified retirement by 65. He says housing, health care, and utility costs should be treated by cutting rules that block starter homes, using technology to lower hospital prices, and fixing Social Security so the wealthiest pay more in.

U.S. representative running for another term. Jake Ellzey's campaign says he is a Naval Academy graduate who flew fighters, served on the ground with a SEAL team, and finished as air boss on the USS Ronald Reagan. It says he later became a businessman, a Texas Veterans Commission member, and a commercial pilot, and that he and his wife are raising two children in Ellis County. He says he will defend gun ownership, opposes leaving families unarmed at home, and supports a legal right to life. He says Congress should finish a border wall, back Border Patrol, and stop projects he says seize private land, including a proposed high-speed rail. He says he serves on Appropriations and Small Business and advocates for veterans, small firms, and taxpayers.

Math teacher running for Congress. Jake Johnson's site says he grew up in Stewartville, is a math teacher and father of four, and that he and his wife Molly, a paraprofessional, are raising their boys in southern Minnesota. He says he will vote to end tariffs and the Iran war that he says are raising grocery, gas, and fertilizer prices, cut taxes for working families, and raise taxes on big corporations and the very wealthy. He says he supports a balanced-budget amendment, term limits, a ban on members of Congress trading stocks or becoming lobbyists, and recovering money lost to fraud in Minnesota. He says he will push a bipartisan farm bill, a right to repair for farm equipment, protection of Social Security, Medicare, and veterans' benefits, and a moratorium on data centers until protections are guaranteed.

Lawyer and former deputy prosecutor running for Congress. An Elkhart native and daughter of businessman Art Decio, she says she was among the first women admitted to Notre Dame and one of the first to graduate from Notre Dame Law. She says eight years in court to adopt her son taught her persistence. She says gas, groceries, housing, utilities, and health care should be affordable, and that tax dollars should go to Indiana families rather than Wall Street or endless foreign conflicts. She says universal health care alongside private payers would help small businesses compete and improve life for Hoosiers. She says data-center growth should not raise utility bills or silence local voices, and that the president and members of Congress must be held to the Constitution.

Wyoming legislator running for the U.S. Senate. His campaign says he is a native of Wyoming whose family roots in the state go back to homesteading in 1862, and that he has worked across the aisle in the Legislature. He says he will try to lower energy costs by backing domestic production, cutting red tape, and ending foreign wars he says are driving prices up. He says he will keep public lands public and open for hunting, fishing, grazing, and recreation, rather than selling them.

U.S. representative and chair of the House Oversight Committee. He grew up in rural Monroe County, studied agriculture at Western Kentucky University, and bought his first farm after graduating in 1993. He served six terms in the Kentucky House, was state agriculture commissioner, and was elected to Congress in 2016. He says that as Oversight chair he is leading major investigations and pushing to reduce government waste, fraud, and abuse. He says he wants a balanced federal budget, rebuilt infrastructure, and business-friendly policies that create opportunity for families. He says his record includes work on the 2018 farm bill and legislation to lift regulations and increase government accountability.

California assemblymember running for Congress. James Gallagher's campaign says he was born in Yuba City, earned degrees from UC Berkeley and UC Davis School of Law, and has represented an Assembly district since 2014, including as Assembly minority leader. It says he previously served on the Sutter County Board of Supervisors and works as an attorney and in his family's farming operation. He says he would lower taxes, fees, and regulations to make life more affordable for North State families. He says he would pass tougher crime laws, expand energy production to bring prices down, and continue the president's border security approach. He says he would defend property rights and parental rights and shield farms and businesses from excessive regulation.

Economist running for Congress in Pennsylvania's 12th District. James Hayes is the son of a steelworker, an economist, and a former Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond employee who has lived in the Pittsburgh area since 2005. He says he is running for safer communities, stronger growth, and practical leadership. He says he wants less regulation, a return of good-paying union jobs, support for law enforcement, and accountability for repeat violent offenders. He also supports school choice, an all-of-the-above energy strategy, standing with allies including Israel, and reining in federal spending.

Building-trades worker running for Congress in Michigan's 12th District. His campaign says he grew up on the east side of Detroit, worked at Eastern Market, and later worked in the building trades. It says he also served with Samaritan's Purse and the Billy Graham Evangelistic Association in Liberia, and that he is Wayne County Republican chairman. He says he is pro-life from conception to natural death and that the Second Amendment should not be infringed. He says representative government exists to secure the rights of the governed, and he calls himself an America First conservative. He says he is a conservative Christian and that he will be a voice for those positions in the House.
