Coast Guard veteran and Democratic nominee for Florida's 21st District His campaign says he is a fourth-generation Floridian, born and raised in Hobe Sound, and a U.S. Coast Guard veteran. He graduated from the Coast Guard Academy, commanded two cutters in Fort Pierce, and served at the White House from 2022 to 2025 under both Vice President Harris and Vice President Vance. He holds a commission as a lieutenant commander in the Coast Guard Reserve. He says he would take on grocery prices, property insurance, and health-care costs, including a public option that leaves employer and union coverage in place. He says he would finish Everglades restoration and stop toxic discharges into the St. Lucie Estuary and Indian River Lagoon. He says he would not cut Social Security, Medicare, or veterans' benefits, and would ban members of Congress from trading stocks.

U.S. representative and chair of the House Rules Committee. Born and raised in Worcester, he is the son of small-business owners and has represented the 2nd District since 1996. He says he also co-chairs the Tom Lantos Human Rights Commission and the House Hunger Caucus. He says hunger, housing insecurity, and unaffordable health care are political choices, and that he is running against tax breaks for billionaires. He says his work in Congress is to defend human rights, reform campaign finance, end hunger, and build an economy where everyone can thrive. He says he walks 43 miles each year through the Pioneer Valley to raise money and attention for the Food Bank of Western Massachusetts.

Attorney and Democratic nominee for Florida's 11th District His campaign says that over more than 30 years he has served as a presidential appointee in the Clinton administration, a congressional staff member, an attorney, and a government-affairs executive. Raised in Central Florida, he started as a staff assistant to Senator Bob Graham. He says caring for his aging mother showed him how expensive health care has become. He says he would oppose cuts or privatization of Social Security and Medicare and let Medicare negotiate drug prices. He says he would protect the Affordable Care Act and seek federal funding to ease the housing crisis and lower property insurance. He says he would eliminate income taxes for people making less than $100,000 a year and cut taxes for middle-class families.

Mental health business owner running for Congress The campaign says James Russell, who goes by Rus, has lived in central Arkansas for more than 25 years with his wife, Wendy, and they have run an outpatient mental health business in Little Rock since 2014. He says he is running for the 4th District in 2026. He says wages have not kept up with profits or the cost of living and that he wants higher pay and equal pay for equal work. He wants fairer taxes, with working people paying less and loopholes closed for the very rich. He supports expanding Medicare toward health care for everyone and making college or job training affordable.

Candidate for Maryland attorney general. Jim Rutledge's campaign says he earned a law degree with honors from the University of Maryland and has practiced law in Maryland for decades. It says he served as a Bel Air town commissioner and on the judicial nominating commission for Harford County's district and circuit courts. He says he would fight crime at every level without turning the office into a partisan fight. He says the office should go after hackers, online predators, and scams that target older and vulnerable people. He says he would protect clean water and the Chesapeake Bay.

Candidate for the U.S. Senate. His campaign says he is an eighth-generation Texan, a former middle school teacher, and a Presbyterian seminarian who has served as a state representative. He says that work has been aimed at donors and politicians he believes have taken over the state. He says he has led a fight against billionaire donors and politicians he calls puppets. He says he is running for the Senate to take that fight against corruption to Washington and return power to working people.

Attorney General of Florida He says he previously served as Governor Ron DeSantis's chief of staff and, before that, as counsel to Donald Trump's 2016 campaign and as a senior advisor to Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross. He says he led state legal fights to reopen businesses and schools and to prohibit mask and vaccine requirements. He says he is focused on prosecuting dangerous criminals, combating illegal immigration, and keeping Florida safe. He says he has sued corporations over what he describes as sexualizing and indoctrinating children. He says his work with the governor included education freedom, parental rights, election rules, tax relief, and public safety.

U.S. representative for Virginia's 11th District. He says he grew up in Prince William County, graduated from NYU, and lives in Fairfax with his wife, Yvette, and their son, Mateo. Before Congress he served on the Fairfax County Board of Supervisors and was chief of staff to Representative Gerry Connolly for more than a decade. He says he was elected to Congress in 2025. He says housing, groceries, utilities, and child care are squeezing families, and he blames tariffs and a war with Iran for higher prices, including gas. He says he opposed those tariffs, is working to restore Congress's authority over trade, and cosponsored the Energy Bills Relief Act. He also says his work includes protecting federal workers, health care, Social Security and Medicare, and lowering costs for northern Virginia.

Republican nominee for Colorado secretary of state. James Wiley says he is a fifth-generation Coloradan, born in Colorado Springs, who lived in Kazakhstan as a child and later earned a management degree and an MBA from CSU Pueblo. He says he is the Republican nominee and calls himself the Red Flame of Liberty. He says elections should be held on one day, in person, with voter identification, paper ballots, and citizen hand counts. He says he would put public records, including voter rolls and business filings, on a blockchain he calls Liberty Chain. He says he would cut red tape and fees so it is faster and cheaper to start a business.

Farmer running for Congress in North Carolina's 11th District. He says he is a husband and father of three from Fairview, a graduate of A.C. Reynolds High School and Warren Wilson College, and that generations of his family have farmed at Hickory Nut Gap. He and his wife Amy say they built the farm into a sustainable meat company that supports about 25 employees and works with farmers across the region. He says he is running because of Hurricane Helene recovery, affordability for working families, and the need to preserve the region's environment and culture. He says people in western North Carolina work hard and still struggle to pay bills, and he distinguishes a hand up from a handout. His platform also covers health-care costs, government waste, immigration, veterans, small business, local farms, public lands, and community safety.

Farmer and Tensas Parish Police Jury member running for the U.S. Senate. Jamie Davis's site says he built a business, met a payroll, farms Delta ground his grandfather sharecropped, and served his neighbors on the Tensas Parish Police Jury. He says Louisiana has become unaffordable and that he wants lower grocery, insurance, and utility bills. He says he will work to expand access to affordable care and will not vote for hospital closings. He says he opposes secret nondisclosure agreements in development deals and land takings for industry, and that his campaign is funded by Louisiana donors rather than corporate PACs.

Researcher running for Congress. Jamie Joyce's campaign says she is a Berkeley researcher who has worked on electric-grid policy, democracy technology, and artificial intelligence, including fellowships and tools for reading legislation. It says her mother left school at 13 to work, and that Joyce now opens a community space in the East Bay. She says a bill she wrote, the MAD Act, would set guardrails for artificial intelligence, limit immigration enforcement and surveillance, and require a government plan for how AI affects jobs and the environment. She says she takes no corporate or pro-Israel PAC money and wants more Epstein files released, dark money disclosed, and stronger checks on the presidency. She also says she would seek affordable health care and housing, higher teacher pay, and more support for people who are homeless.

U.S. representative for Maryland's 8th District, sworn in for a fifth term in 2025. He says he proudly represents the 8th District and founded Democracy Summer, a program that trains high school and college students in voter registration, canvassing, and organizing. The campaign asks supporters to help defend democracy in Maryland and across the country. He says Democracy Summer teaches the history of democratic freedom and lessons for political leadership today. The campaign is organizing volunteers to defend what it calls strong democracy and freedom. He is asking voters to send him back to the House for another term representing the 8th District.

D.C. Councilmember for Ward 4 She says she is a third-generation Washingtonian raised in Ward 4, a graduate of D.C. public schools and Howard University School of Law, and a former assistant attorney general who was elected to the Council in 2020. She says her family left a childhood home because the rent went up. She says that as mayor she would side with working people to make the District safe and affordable in all eight wards. She says she has worked to keep tenant protections and to make housing more affordable, and has voted for raises and stronger worker protections. She says she led bills that raised wages for early-childhood educators, ended the subminimum wage for restaurant workers, and increased SNAP food assistance.

U.S. representative for Oregon's 5th District, seeking another term. Her campaign says she is a mother of four and a small-business owner who, with her husband, ran four restaurants, and that she is the daughter of teachers with degrees in electrical engineering and business. It says she served in the Oregon House before Congress, where she has passed bipartisan bills. She says her mission is to lower health-care and housing costs, create jobs, and make sure every child gets a good education. Her issues list also names climate action, protecting reproductive rights, and ending homelessness. She says she is pushing back on what she calls cruelty and chaos from the White House while working with either party on results.

Journalist running for Congress in Pennsylvania's 10th District. Janelle Stelson says she spent more than 30 years telling stories in central Pennsylvania. She is running on term limits that would apply to herself, a ban on congressional stock trading, and a pledge to vote against pay raises for members. She says she wants to lower utility, health care, and housing costs and support small businesses and farms. She says she will protect Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid and defend abortion rights.

Independent American candidate for lieutenant governor. Janine Hansen says she is a native Nevadan who has advocated for families and taxpayers at the Legislature throughout her adult life. She is the Independent American Party nominee. She says she would use the Senate presidency to oppose growth of state government into family and taxpayer life. She says tourism, especially outdoor recreation, should expand because rural counties depend on it, and that Nevada should keep taxes low, including no state income tax. She says the homeland-security role requires watching for terrorism while protecting constitutional rights.

U.S. representative running for another term. Jared Huffman's campaign says he has represented a North Coast district since 2012 and was chosen in 2025 as the top Democrat on the House Natural Resources Committee. It says he previously served in the California Assembly, was a senior attorney at the Natural Resources Defense Council, and lives in Marin. He says he has worked on climate action, wildfire disaster relief, dam removal on the Klamath River, and offshore wind in Humboldt County. He says he has pushed federal money for local infrastructure, tribal clean energy and broadband, salmon habitat, and toxic-site cleanup. He says he has defended democracy and the separation of church and state, and sought stronger school funding for students with disabilities.

U.S. representative for Florida's 25th District His campaign says he was born and raised in Broward County, graduated from Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School, and joined the Parkland City Commission while in law school at Nova Southeastern. He served in the Florida House and on the Broward County Commission, then as director of the Florida Division of Emergency Management under Governor Ron DeSantis, before his election to Congress in 2022. He and his wife, Leah, live in Broward with their two sons. He says he wrote legislation to cut property-insurance premiums and is fighting prescription prices, housing costs, and price gouging. He says he would protect Social Security and Medicare and reverse Medicaid cuts. He says that after the 2018 shooting at his high school he helped pass Florida's school-safety law, and that he supports a ban on members of Congress trading stocks.

Independent candidate for governor Jasjit Gotra, who goes by Jay, is running as an independent. His site says he founded companies, including Alliance Security, and that he would treat the state budget like a business profit-and-loss statement. He says he would cut waste, fully fund teacher and firefighter pensions, and make the state easier for businesses. He says he would end the state tax on Social Security within two years. His listed plans include cutting energy costs, teaching artificial intelligence in every high school by 2028, capping out-of-pocket health costs, and building 20,000 housing units in four years.

Microbiologist and Georgia state representative running for Congress. She says she has served in the Georgia House since 2018 after flipping a long-held Republican seat, and that she has been the legislature's leading science voice. She says she blocked a state school superintendent from banning AP African American Studies and challenged COVID data and an abortion-ban source she says was a fake medical organization. Her agenda lists lowering the cost of living, protecting education at every stage, and building an economy that works for people. She also lists protecting rights and the most vulnerable, building safer communities, protecting democracy, and supporting veterans. She says she is running because funding has been stripped from the CDC and the NIH and health care has been cut, and she says a policy that hits one group affects the whole community.
Secretary of State · South Carolina · Democratic

Democratic nominee for secretary of state Jason Belton's campaign calls him the 2026 Democratic nominee for secretary of state. It describes him as a servant leader who says government should work for every family, business, and community. The site says the campaign takes no corporate PAC money. It says contributions pay for community events and voter outreach in every South Carolina county.

Small-business owner running for U.S. House in Colorado's 6th District. Jason Clark says he was raised in a working-class family in the 6th District, went to Smoky Hill High School, and graduated from West Point in 1992. He says he has been an entrepreneur and small-business owner in Aurora for more than 30 years. He says rent, education, and health care cost too much, and that bringing those costs down is his first priority. He says the campaign is about good-paying jobs, and that he would back entrepreneurs, small businesses, and developers. He says he would go after criminals and clean up Colfax Avenue, and that every Colorado child should be able to thrive.

Combat veteran running for Congress. Jason Crow's campaign says he grew up in a working-class family, the grandson of a bricklayer and the son of small-business owners. It says he joined the National Guard to pay for school, enlisted after September 11, served three combat tours in Iraq and Afghanistan, rose from private to captain, and earned a Bronze Star. He says he is fighting to make daily life more affordable and to lower health-care costs. He says he has never taken corporate PAC money and never will, and that he wants campaign-finance reform and a ban on insider stock trading. He says he does not trade stocks and posts his public schedule so he answers to Coloradans rather than to donors.

Constitutional advocate running for Michigan attorney general. He says he founded WTPN.news to publish the same record on candidates, donors, and officials, including himself. He is running with Anthony Hudson on the Libertarian ticket and says both major parties have protected the same machine of taxes, corporate welfare, and corruption. He says he would build a public-corruption unit aimed at government abuse, retaliation, fraud, and misuse of office, and investigate patterns of courtroom misconduct. He wants to end qualified immunity and stop civil asset forfeiture without real due process, and he says hidden contracts and pay-to-play lobbying should be exposed. He says he would defend homeowners from property-tax foreclosure abuse and treat secret corporate-welfare deals as corruption.

Santa Clarita council member and engineer running for Congress. Jason Gibbs's campaign says he is a mechanical engineer who worked on rocket fueling systems and earned engineering degrees from Cal Poly San Luis Obispo. It says he was elected to the Santa Clarita council in 2020, served as mayor in 2023, and is raising two children there. He says he would oppose new taxes, push energy affordability, and cut wasteful spending to lower the cost of housing, groceries, gas, and energy. He says he would back law enforcement and end what he calls catch-and-release treatment of repeat offenders. He says he is running to put local values and practical problem-solving ahead of party politics.

Plano native and former mortgage and insurance worker running for Congress. His campaign says he was born and raised in Plano, started working as a kid, and often worked two jobs and 80-hour weeks. He says he became a top performer in the mortgage industry, later worked in finance and insurance, and left his job to run. He says he knows what it is like to live paycheck to paycheck and to choose among rent, food, and health insurance. He says leadership should be about service, lifting people up, telling the truth, and making sure no one gets left behind.

U.S. representative for Missouri's 8th District. He says he grew up on a farm, used an FFA project to help pay for college, finished a double major in three years, and later ran the family farm and a small business in Dent County while paying off law-school debt. He describes his state House years as a push for smaller government and fiscal conservatism, and his colleagues later chose him as majority whip and speaker pro tem. On Ways and Means he says he has focused on simplifying the tax code and lowering the federal tax burden on small businesses, farmers, and families.

Former NFL kicker running for Congress in Arizona's 1st District. His campaign says he played 14 seasons in the NFL, including for the Arizona Cardinals, and later worked as a CBS analyst. He and his wife Rebecca have lived in the Valley for 15 years and are raising four children. He says he will protect Arizona's water, stand with farmers and ranchers, defend Second Amendment rights, and oppose federal mandates he says hurt families, small businesses, and schools. He says he will fight to finish the border wall, back Border Patrol and ICE, and work to keep fentanyl out of neighborhoods. He says he will cut red tape, extend the Trump-era tax cuts, and back domestic manufacturing so the Valley keeps higher-paying jobs.

Software entrepreneur and U.S. representative running for another term. Jay Obernolte's campaign says he is a business owner who started FarSight Studios in a dorm room in 1990 and has lived in the 23rd District for more than 25 years. It says he earned engineering degrees from Caltech and UCLA, served as mayor of Big Bear Lake, and was elected to Congress in 2020. He says he is fighting to balance the federal budget and stop spending he argues is driving up prices. He says he has worked to lower taxes, repeal gas taxes, help small businesses, and expand the child tax credit. He says he wrote a bill to hold fentanyl dealers accountable, voted to fund the military and a border-security bill, and wants the border wall finished.

Wisconsin native and business graduate running for secretary of state. His campaign says he was born and raised in Clintonville, earned a business degree from UW-Stout, and was the first student elected to the Menomonie City Council. He says Wisconsin should move election administration from the Wisconsin Elections Commission to the secretary of state, by legislation or by referendum. He says voters can hold an elected secretary accountable for how elections are run in a way they cannot hold an appointed commission. He says the office should also stand for transparency in public records and in the land funds it oversees.
District 4 · U.S. House · New York · Republican

Hempstead Town receiver of taxes running for Congress in New York's 4th District. Her campaign says she was first elected receiver of taxes in 2019, overwhelmingly reelected in 2023, and has practiced law for more than 30 years, including as an associate village justice in Bellerose. It says she is running to keep fighting for Nassau County taxpayers. She says she would restore the full state-and-local tax deduction and seek more relief for families and seniors. She says she would support law enforcement and keep the southern border from being opened again.

Navy veteran and former elected official running for Congress. Jeff Belle's campaign says he is a Navy veteran, a private-equity executive, and a former elected official with 25 years in public service. It says he lives in Chula Vista and is running to accelerate growth in South Bay San Diego. He says he would safeguard constitutional rights, secure the border, and provide financial relief to families and small businesses. He says housing policy should add supply, speed approvals, and make starter homes and apartments easier to build. He says he would invest in public schools and make federal small-business programs easier for neighborhood employers to use.

U.S. representative for Colorado's 5th District. Jeff Crank says he was born and raised in southern Colorado and has spent more than 30 years working to strengthen El Paso County. He says he is in Congress and is asking voters in the 5th District to send him back. He says he is focused on the district's military installations and its veterans. He says he is working to make the community more resilient to wildfires. He says he wants conservative change so Colorado stays a place to live, work, and raise a family.

Small-business owner running for Congress. Jeff Frese's campaign says he is a husband, father, and coach in Moraga who built a national snack brand from his kitchen and has run consumer companies. It says he is not a politician and is running in the 10th Congressional District without PAC money. He says he would set an eight-year congressional term limit, ban members from trading stocks, withhold pay if there is no budget, and close the lobbying revolving door. He says he would stop deficit spending that raises mortgage rates, cut building red tape, and bar Wall Street and foreign buyers from single-family homes and farmland. He says he would back police and fentanyl prosecutions, require voter ID with paper ballots, put classrooms ahead of bureaucracy, and refuse cuts to Social Security and Medicare.

Grand Junction attorney running for U.S. House in Colorado's 3rd District. Jeff Hurd says he grew up in Grand Junction, is a husband and father of five, and built a law practice for rural electric cooperatives, counties, schools, fire districts, and broadband providers. He says western and southern Colorado need a representative who focuses on results. He says the border should be secured now, legal immigration expanded, and law enforcement given what it needs to stop fentanyl and other drugs. He says his first priority is higher-paying work in rural Colorado, with fewer unnecessary rules and a fairer field for small businesses. He says he supports producing Colorado oil and gas along with competitively priced cleaner power, and that he will press the Lower Basin to live within its share of Colorado River water.

Lawyer and former state representative Jeff McLaughlin was a schoolteacher, then practiced law in Guntersville for more than 30 years, and represented Marshall County in the Alabama House for ten of those years. He says he self-financed those legislative races and led the fight to ban secret PAC-to-PAC transfers. He says he will use the attorney general's office to root out public corruption no matter the party or the connections. He says he will go after scams that target seniors and fraud that drains working families, and that he will stand up for victims. He says he will back local police and focus on fentanyl and other dangerous drugs coming into the state.

U.S. senator from Oregon, seeking another term. His campaign says he was born in Myrtle Creek and has not lost touch with working-class roots. It calls him a workhorse and a progressive who is trying to get the country back on track. He says his daily work is to create opportunity for working families. He says he is trying to stop the corruption of democracy. He says he is trying to tackle the climate crisis.

Unity Party candidate for governor. Jeff Peckman says he is running for governor with T.J. Cole, chair of the Unity Party of Colorado, as his running mate. He says his own campaign is self-funded and is not taking donations. He says Colorado companies can cut air pollution without new electric-vehicle mandates, and that he would declare an air-pollution emergency on his first day. He says he would create a chief coherence officer and a partnership to launch new technology projects. He says he will work to end TABOR, which he calls a limit that is hurting the state.
No 2026 issue list was found for this candidate.
District 2 · U.S. House · New Jersey · Republican

U.S. representative for New Jersey's 2nd District. His campaign says he is focused on middle-class families and retirees in South Jersey, and that health-care costs remain one of his top priorities. He says he is working to lower health-care costs and everyday expenses, including energy bills and delivery fees. He says he will protect veterans' benefits, back law enforcement, and keep investing in South Jersey beaches, aviation, and infrastructure. He says he supports border enforcement and proof of citizenship plus photo identification for federal voting, and that he will not back cuts to Social Security, Medicare, or Medicaid for people who qualify.

Engineer and businessman Jeff Wadlin says he studied aerospace and mechanical engineering at the University of Virginia, worked at Caterpillar, earned an MBA from Northwestern, and later ran membership nationwide at Sam's Club in Bentonville. He says he also co-founded an online auto-parts salvage company and now has his own consulting business. He says broad tariffs should end because they raise prices on food, equipment, vehicles, building materials, and household goods. He says the goal in health care is to cover everyone while cutting the total cost roughly in half, using private delivery with universal access and protection from catastrophic bills. He says antitrust law should challenge mergers and consolidation that leave farmers and workers facing only a few suppliers and buyers.

U.S. representative for Indiana's 6th District. His office says he founded Storage Express, grew it for three decades, and merged it into a company that trades on the New York Stock Exchange. He co-owned a software firm, invested in oil and gas wells and in farm and ranch land, and served two terms on the Indianapolis City-County Council. He sits on the House Appropriations Committee. He graduated from Indiana University, earned a master's from the University of London, and an MBA in agribusiness from Purdue. He and his wife, Mary, live on Indianapolis's south side. His office says he wants policy that encourages economic development, and that he is focused on reining in federal spending and the national debt. His office says he is working to advance border security and to safeguard conservative Hoosier values. His campaign lists making life more affordable, supporting farmers and small businesses, backing law enforcement and the military, protecting the unborn, and defending the Second Amendment.

Scientist and no-party candidate for governor. Jeffrey Datto's campaign says he is a Hialeah scientist with a doctorate in cell and tissue engineering who researched paralysis recovery at the University of Miami and founded DattoAI. It says he is running with no party affiliation after experiencing illness, disability, and homelessness, and that family and faith are central to the campaign. He says he would move toward universal, income-based health care, strengthen public hospitals and clinics, and create a Florida Institutes of Health focused on serious disease, injury, mental health, and longevity. He says he would abolish charter schools and bring them into one state public-education system, with academic freedom and pathways from school into Florida jobs. He says he would open a public-accountability office, require timely and accessible courts, and make renters share in property-tax relief given to landlords.

Democratic candidate for Mississippi's 4th District. His campaign says he was born and raised in Gulfport, served 22 years in the Army, and founded Extend A Hand, Help A Friend, a nonprofit serving Gulf Coast families, children, and seniors. He says he has also represented Gulfport in the Mississippi Legislature. He says South Mississippi needs an economy in which families can earn a living wage, support their children, and build a secure life at home. He says every child deserves a quality education no matter their ZIP code, and that taxpayer money spent on children is an investment in the future. He says no family should go broke to see a doctor or buy medicine, and he points to closing rural hospitals and reduced health-care funding in Mississippi.

U.S. representative, former Navy pilot, and nurse practitioner. She says she flew H-46 and H-3 helicopters for ten years, with two Persian Gulf deployments, and is married to retired F/A-18 pilot Steve. She used the GI Bill to become a board-certified adult-geriatric nurse practitioner and worked in long-term care and a Virginia Beach primary-care practice. In Congress she serves on Armed Services, Natural Resources, and Veterans' Affairs, where she chairs the Oversight and Investigations Subcommittee. She says she has prioritized cutting inflation and helped pass spending cuts, and she supported the Working Families Tax Cuts that made the 2017 tax cuts permanent and ended most taxes on tips and overtime. She says she fights regulatory burdens so small businesses and industries important to Virginia can hire, and she worked to expand the Child Tax Credit. She says spending cuts should still fully fund veterans' benefits, the military, and Social Security and Medicare.

Teacher running for Congress in Ohio's 2nd District. Jen Mazzuckelli says she was raised by a teacher and a federal employee, earned an English degree and a master's in teaching, and worked as a high school English teacher. She says she is in long-term recovery, has multiple sclerosis, and has lived through domestic violence. She says the representative should work for the people rather than campaign donors, and that neighbors who disagree are not enemies. She says public servants should keep promises and that the way to earn reelection is to do the job well.

Colorado secretary of state running for attorney general. Jena Griswold says she grew up in a working-class family in Estes Park, was the first in her family to attend a four-year college, and earned a law degree. She says she has been secretary of state since 2018 and is running for attorney general to stand up to Donald Trump and protect Coloradans' rights. She says she will defend the rights and freedoms of Coloradans and will not be intimidated. She says that as secretary of state she backed laws against threats to election workers, guns near voting centers, and tampering with voting equipment. She says she expanded ballot drop boxes, in-person voting, campus and tribal voting access, and automatic voter registration.

Educator and former Oklahoma Teacher of the Year running for Congress. Her campaign says she taught for more than 16 years, was Oklahoma Teacher of the Year in 2020, and later worked in nonprofit and corporate leadership, including at the Oklahoma Faith Network. She says she and her husband Karl have two children, and that in 2022 she received more votes than any other Democrat in the race for state superintendent. She says Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid should be protected and strengthened, and that Medicare should negotiate lower drug prices. She says a secure border and a fair immigration system both matter, with more agents and sensors against drug trafficking, faster asylum decisions, and more work visas. She says she would expose backroom deals and opposes adding trillions to the deficit to pay for tax breaks for the wealthiest.
District 11 · U.S. House · North Carolina · Republican

State representative and mortgage lender running for Congress in North Carolina's 11th District. Her campaign says she is an eighth-generation western North Carolinian who grew up on her family's apple farm in Henderson County and has worked in banking since 1998. She says she is a mortgage loan officer who represents Henderson County in the state House and lives in Hendersonville. She says working families should be able to own a home and keep more of what they earn. She says she supports local credit unions and helped change state law so more rural towns can be served by them. She says she supports ending the state income tax on tips, overtime, and bonuses.

Former state representative running for secretary of state. Jennifer Day's site says she has 16 years of business experience in technology, real estate, and finance, founded an interior-design company, worked eight years as an election worker, and represented Kansas House District 48. She says voting systems should stay accurate and free of disinformation, and that she will coordinate with county election officials. She says she will look at states with higher turnout and consider similar ways to bring eligible Kansans into voting. She says she will keep modernizing business registration so it is easier to start and run a company.

Former school board member and Democratic nominee for Florida's 8th District Her campaign says she is the daughter of a corrections officer and a mother living with a disability, grew up in a working-class family, and built a career in education. She served on the Brevard County School Board and, in 2020, defeated a co-founder of Moms for Liberty. She lives in Satellite Beach with her husband, a middle-school teacher, and their daughter. She says she would stabilize Florida property insurance with federal reinsurance and oppose tariffs that raise the price of everyday goods. She says she would expand Medicaid, restore Affordable Care Act subsidies, and protect coverage for pre-existing conditions. She says she would protect the Department of Education, fully fund special-education law, and invest in teachers and student mental health.

U.S. representative for Virginia's 4th District. Jennifer McClellan's office says she entered Congress in 2023 after a special election and was the first Black woman elected to Congress from Virginia. Born in Petersburg, she was valedictorian of Matoaca High School and earned degrees from the University of Richmond and the University of Virginia School of Law. She served in the Virginia House beginning in 2005 and the State Senate beginning in 2017, and she lives in Richmond with her husband David Mills and their two children. She says that on the Energy and Commerce Committee she works on access to health care, lower energy bills, and a clean and livable planet. She says that in the General Assembly she passed bills to protect and expand voting rights, combat climate change, preserve reproductive health care, and strengthen worker protections.
District 10 · U.S. House · New York · Republican

Republican candidate for New York's 10th District. Her campaign says she is a lifelong Brooklynite who got on the ballot to give voters a choice after Brad Lander won the Democratic primary. She is the Republican and Conservative nominee for a district that includes parts of Brooklyn and Lower Manhattan. She says she will support the NYPD and first responders and reject policies she says have made streets less safe. She says New Yorkers are being priced out of their neighborhoods and wants practical answers to the cost of living. She says she will stand for working families, parents, and small-business owners.
District 1 · U.S. House · South Carolina · Republican

Attorney, small-business owner, and local Republican official running for Congress. Her campaign says she is a wife, mother, attorney, small-business owner, girls' sports coach, and lifelong Lowcountry resident who has held local elected office. She says that in office she has balanced budgets, stood with law enforcement, and defended the Constitution. She says she would put the Lowcountry first, stand with law enforcement, and secure the border against fentanyl and people she calls criminal illegal aliens. She says she would fight wasteful spending, balance the budget, and defend the Constitution, including free speech, religious liberty, and the Second Amendment. She says she would protect the unborn, keep men out of women's sports, lower family costs, and press for veterans' health care, benefits, jobs, and housing with less red tape.

Business owner running for Congress in California's 47th District. Her campaign says she co-built companies in energy and financial services, then bought and ran a technology services firm. She has an economics degree from the University of Virginia and an MBA from Columbia, and she is executive director of CAL DOGE, the office she says has gone through California spending line by line. She says she will cut waste and fraud so groceries, gas, insurance, and rent cost less. She says federal housing money should go first to cities that cut permit delays and fees, and that energy should be produced onshore rather than drilled off Orange County. She says she will fully fund border security, end catch-and-release, and require federal homelessness grants to show they get people off the street.

Independent candidate for the U.S. Senate. He says he is an independent running with a plan he calls American, and that he wants voters of every party involved. He says supporters may mail a one-dollar pledge and that unused campaign money will be returned on request. He lists his priorities as defending the Constitution, clarifying history, and restoring what he calls equality for people. He says he would draft an Equal Earnings Act and use assets at Fort Knox toward legislation and the national debt. He says he wants economic alternatives to war and protection of what he calls American human freedom.

State Senate president pro tem running for Congress in Michigan's 11th District. His campaign says he is a lifelong Oakland County resident, a Groves High School and Michigan State graduate, and that Southfield voters elected him to the city council in 2011. He says he later led the 2022 campaign that flipped the Michigan Senate and now serves as president pro tem. He says he would lower everyday costs, push back on tariffs he says raise prices, and defend Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid. He says he reduced barriers to voting as elections committee chair, strengthened the state civil-rights law, and acted to protect abortion access after Roe was overturned. He says he passed gun-safety laws, restored labor rights, and returned tax relief to seniors and working families.

State representative running for governor Jermaine Johnson's campaign says he is a state representative who has passed bills on the senior sales tax, a closed bridge, and broadband. The site also introduces Sam Skardon as his lieutenant-governor running mate. He says he would expand the number of families who owe no income tax rather than eliminate the tax, because he says ending it would mainly help the wealthiest, and he says he would work with cities to cut property taxes. He says he would let cities fix roads with transportation-department money, raise law-enforcement pay, and fund more rural hospitals and trade schools. He says he would audit public education, protect reproductive decisions for patients and doctors, and legalize medical marijuana while putting recreational use to a statewide vote.

Navy veteran and software engineer running for Congress in Ohio's 12th District. Jerrad Christian says he is a Navy veteran who served as a meteorologist, a software engineer, and someone who grew up with poverty in rural Ohio. He says that service turned him into an advocate for using less oil. He wants to overturn the Citizens United ruling, cap campaign spending, and stop foreign-linked money in elections. He also supports universal health care, a higher minimum wage, and more housing by changing exclusionary zoning and limiting large corporate buyers.

Candidate for governor of Tennessee. She describes herself as a lifelong Tennessean, a lawyer, an educator, and a mother of three who has lived in Memphis, Nashville, and Knoxville. She says her public work has included public defense, the Memphis City Council, and county government. She says she will expand paid family and medical leave, support collective bargaining, and invest in small businesses, especially in underserved areas. She says public schools should be fully funded, with respected teachers and without what she calls censorship and political interference. She says the state should expand Medicaid, especially in rural Tennessee, and she supports background checks, red-flag laws, and gun locks.

Businessman and former Mobile County commissioner running for Congress The campaign says Jerry Carl was born in Mobile, started his first company at 25, and has launched more than ten businesses over four decades, from real estate and health care to timber. He later served on the Mobile County Commission, where the campaign says he voted against tax increases and skipped a taxpayer-funded salary for his first two years. He says he will work with President Trump on an America First agenda. He says illegal immigration threatens national security and points to border-wall funding and more Border Patrol agents as work he wants continued. He says he is a lifelong hunter who will defend the Second Amendment.
No 2026 issue list was found for this candidate.

Healthcare worker running for Congress in Pennsylvania's 2nd District. Jessica Arriaga is a mother from North Philadelphia who has worked in operating rooms for more than 20 years. She says she is running to put results for the city ahead of party politics. She says public safety, the cost of living, and career and technical education are the issues she hears about most. She argues health care should put patients first and that the city needs practical results rather than partisan fights.

Former Justice Department official running for Congress. Jessica Hart Steinmann's campaign says she is a Christian, a wife, and a mother of two who served in the Trump Justice Department as director of the Office for Victims of Crime. It says she later was executive general counsel at the America First Policy Institute and is the Trump-endorsed Republican for the 8th District. She says she would put Texas and American workers ahead of what she calls global elites, secure the border, and defend the Constitution. She says she has fought diversity programs in higher education, represented service members who challenged a COVID vaccine mandate, and sued to keep boys out of girls' sports. She says parents, not government, should direct how children are raised, and that she led federal work against human trafficking.

Army veteran running for U.S. House in Colorado's 5th District. Jessica Killin says she is a fourth-generation Coloradan, raised in Colorado Springs by two public-school educators, who served as an Army captain and military police officer. She says she later spent more than a decade at USAA on policy for military families, then worked on Capitol Hill and at the White House, and that this is her first campaign for office. She says she would lower costs for housing, groceries, health care, and energy, strengthen VA care, and cut federal spending that does not work. She says she would end tariffs that raise everyday prices, limit corporate landlords, and hold monopoly utilities accountable for high electric bills. She says she would ban members of Congress from trading stocks, support term limits, and let Medicare negotiate prices on more drugs.

U.S. representative for Hawaii's 2nd District The campaign says Jill Tokuda is a lifelong Kaneohe resident who represented Kaneohe and Kailua in the state Senate from 2006 to 2018, including as Ways and Means chair, and was first elected to Congress in 2022. She sits on Agriculture and Armed Services and co-chairs the Bipartisan Rural Health Caucus. She says zip code and income should not decide the quality of care, and she wants rural hospitals, mobile clinics, telehealth, and Medicare for All. She says she is fighting tariffs, wants the federal gas tax suspended, and wants childcare and the child tax credit expanded so families can stay in Hawaii. She says getting sick should not push people into debt.

U.S. representative for Indiana's 4th District. His office says he is a lifelong resident of west-central Indiana, a Purdue graduate in animal science, and a Vietnam veteran who received a Bronze Star and two Purple Hearts. He farmed and ran a home health agency, served as a Putnam County commissioner and for eight years in the Indiana House, and sits on the Agriculture, Foreign Affairs, and Science committees. He and his wife, Danise, have three children. He says his priorities are protecting family farms, cutting federal spending, and expanding rural health care through more competition and telehealth. He says he would secure the southern border and give immigration enforcement the resources to remove people here illegally who have committed crimes. He says he would protect Second Amendment rights and support veterans.
District 6 · U.S. House · South Carolina · Democratic

U.S. representative for South Carolina's 6th District since 1993. His official biography says he grew up in Sumter as the son of a minister and a beautician, graduated from South Carolina State, and taught school in Charleston before becoming the first Black advisor to a South Carolina governor and later Human Affairs commissioner. He is a former House majority whip and now ranking member of an Appropriations subcommittee. He says his 10-20-30 formula sends at least 10 percent of certain funds to communities where 20 percent or more of people have lived in poverty for 30 years. He points to his Rural Energy Savings Program, which lets rural electric cooperatives lend for home energy efficiency, and to a broadband bill funded in the 2021 infrastructure law. His biography says he has worked to make America's greatness accessible and affordable, including preserving historic buildings at historically Black colleges and creating heritage corridors and parks.

Farmer and U.S. representative running for another term. Jim Costa's campaign describes him as a farmer and member of Congress whose priority is the future of the San Joaquin Valley. It says his work has centered on water, health care, crime, and veterans. He says he helped win federal money for drinking water, aging water projects, storage, highways, and wildfire risk reduction. He says he has funded hospitals, community clinics, and a Valley medical school, and sought more officers to fight gangs and drugs. He says he has defended Dreamers, opposed family separations, and supports a path to citizenship.

County supervisor, pilot, and former mayor running for Congress. Jim Desmond's campaign says he is a father, a husband, a Navy veteran, a Delta Air Lines pilot for 33 years, a former mayor of San Marcos, and a San Diego County supervisor. He says he is running to bring common sense back to government and to focus on fixing problems. He says it is time for common sense to return to government and for leaders to fix problems. His site lists the cost of living, homelessness, the border, energy, and vocational and military education among his priorities.

Navy veteran and businessman running for Congress in Georgia's 4th District. His campaign says he grew up with very little, served in the Navy's nuclear submarine force, and then built a business. He describes himself as a husband, father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, and not a career politician. He says he supports the FairTax Act, H.R. 25, which would end the federal income, payroll, estate, and gift taxes, abolish the IRS, and replace them with a national sales tax plus a monthly rebate so households at or below the poverty level pay no net federal tax. He says families should be able to go to school, church, and the store without fear, and he would back law enforcement and first responders. He says he would cut regulations that make it harder for small businesses to hire and grow, and defend the Second Amendment, religious liberty, and free speech.

U.S. representative for Connecticut's 4th District The campaign says Jim Himes has represented Connecticut's 4th District since his election in 2008. Born in Peru to American parents, he later attended Harvard, studied at Oxford as a Rhodes Scholar, worked at Goldman Sachs, and then led a nonprofit office that financed affordable housing in the New York area. He says he is fighting for accessible, affordable health care and to protect Social Security. He says he is taking on the gun lobby to reduce gun violence and wants more economic opportunity for working families. As the lead Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, he says he works against foreign and domestic interference and for peaceful transfers of power.

U.S. representative for Ohio's 4th District and chair of the House Judiciary Committee. His campaign says he was a state and college wrestling champion, grew up in rural Champaign County, and was the first chair of the House Freedom Caucus. It says his focus in Congress is oversight of federal agencies. He says he is using the Judiciary Committee to investigate federal agencies, including the IRS, and to defend constitutional freedoms. He points to a Cut, Cap and Balance plan and says he has offered deep spending cuts and a balanced federal budget. The campaign says that as a state legislator he opposed higher taxes and spending and received awards from Ohio anti-abortion groups.

Insurance professional running for Congress in Georgia's 1st District. He calls himself a lifelong son of southeast Georgia, raised on faith, family, and service. He says his insurance career showed him how federal red tape holds back small towns, farms, and growing communities, and he describes himself as a Trump conservative. He says he will fight to lower taxes so families and small businesses keep more of what they earn, and he wants regular appropriations, balanced budgets, and agency accountability for spending. On health programs, he supports work requirements for able-bodied Medicaid adults, says Medicaid should not cover people in the country illegally, and says he will protect Medicare while rooting out waste and giving seniors more control of their care. He says he is running to defend President Trump, make the district more affordable, and back border enforcement.

Candidate for secretary of state. Jim Marchant says he is running for secretary of state to rebuild trust in elections and to make Nevada a better place to start a business. He says he would require voter identification and proof of citizenship, replace voting machines with precinct hand counts of paper ballots, and end universal mail ballots while keeping absentee voting for military, traveling, elderly, and medically unable voters. He says every voter should re-register and that Nevada should leave the Electronic Registration Information Center. He says he would advocate repeal of the commerce tax and lower fees to form a business.

Governor of Nebraska. His campaign says he is back at work after a horseback accident and that the next stretch is about commonsense conservative solutions. He says the state's overall tax burden is lower than when he took office. He says the next term should keep a focus on protecting children. He says he will promote Nebraska agriculture and defend what he calls Nebraska values. He says he will keep leading efforts to fix property taxes.

U.S. senator from Idaho seeking another term. He is a small-business owner, a farmer and beef producer, and a former county prosecuting attorney. He says that as governor he cut property taxes by 20 percent, and that he is a former chairman of the Senate Small Business Committee. He says he led the Senate fight against selling some of Idaho's public lands and will keep defending multiple use, including hunting, logging, and grazing. He says he will keep cutting taxes and red tape for small businesses and farms, and he cites a 100 percent approval rating from the American Farm Bureau. He says he supports border enforcement, Second Amendment rights, and returning natural-resource decisions to state and local leaders.

Broadcaster and Republican nominee for Florida's 19th District His campaign says he was born at Naples Community Hospital, married his high-school sweetheart, Carly, and raised their children in Southwest Florida. He earned a finance degree at Stetson, worked in Senator Connie Mack's Washington office in 1996, and runs Sun Broadcasting, including 92.5 FOX News Radio. He says he would stand with President Trump to secure the border, enforce immigration laws, and deport people who are here illegally. He says families are paying too much for groceries, housing, and insurance, and he would fight to bring those costs down. He says he would vote to make President Trump's tax cuts permanent so families and small businesses keep more of what they earn.

U.S. representative and former union organizer running for another term. Jimmy Gomez's campaign says he is the son of Mexican immigrants, grew up without health insurance, and worked his way from community college to UCLA and a public-policy degree at Harvard. It says he organized with a public-employee union and a nurses' union, served in the Assembly, and was elected to Congress in 2017. He says he is fighting for Medicare for All so a medical bill does not bankrupt a family. He says he championed an expansion of paid family leave in the Assembly and wants a national paid-family-leave program. He says he voted for the Inflation Reduction Act and has worked to lower prescription prices for seniors.

U.S. representative running for another term. Jimmy Panetta's campaign says he was elected to the House in 2016 and began as a prosecutor in the Alameda County District Attorney's Office in 1996. It says he serves on Ways and Means and the Budget Committee. He says he would ease inflation by investing in roads, rail, research, manufacturing, broadband, and water, and by expanding child care and equal pay. He says he has written bills to block offshore oil drilling, cut carbon emissions, and fund wildfire prevention and reforestation. He says he has pushed housing tax credits for low- and middle-income homes and grants for veterans and people who are homeless.

U.S. representative running for another term. Jimmy Patronis's campaign says he is a fourth-generation Floridian from Panama City who worked in his family's seafood restaurant, served eight years in the Florida House, and was the state's chief financial officer and fire marshal before winning a House seat. He says his House priorities follow an America First agenda: cutting taxes, restraining spending, investing in the military, and reforming veterans' services. He says that as chief financial officer he pushed benefits for firefighters diagnosed with cancer and mental-health care for first responders. He says he fought insurance practices that let contractors take over homeowners' benefits after storms and drive premiums up.

Retired Marine running for Congress in Arizona's 6th District. Her campaign says she is a working mother and retired Marine, the daughter of farmworkers who grew up in rural poverty. She says she is not a politician and has no tolerance for corruption. She says she would crack down on price gouging, modernize the child tax credit, oppose tariffs that raise costs, and strengthen Social Security. She says she would reverse health-care cuts, protect people with preexisting conditions, and expand Medicare drug-price negotiation. She says she would fund police, deport people who commit violent crimes, create a path to citizenship for people who follow the law, and require data centers to bring their own power.

U.S. representative and former Texas state legislator from San Antonio. His official biography says he was born in San Antonio in 1974, raised on the West Side, and is a product of public schools. He graduated from Stanford and Harvard Law, served five terms in the Texas House, and was elected to Congress in 2012. He says he wants to build what he calls an infrastructure of opportunity: strong public schools and universities, a sound health-care system, and good jobs. His biography says that as a state legislator he helped restore funding for health care and education and worked on mental health, teen pregnancy, and juvenile justice. He says he created a college tour for students with few resources and founded SA READS, a San Antonio literacy campaign.

Milwaukee alder and former state representative running for secretary of state. Her campaign says she was born and raised on Milwaukee's south side, served ten years in the Assembly, and is in her second term on the Common Council. It says she was the first Latina and the first openly bisexual member of both bodies. She is using the campaign to call for state investment in affordable child care, housing, and relief on grocery costs. She says the secretary of state sits on the Board of Commissioners of Public Lands and that she would protect the trust funds and land that support public schools and libraries. She says she would push the state to fund public schools so districts rely less on local referenda.

Michigan secretary of state, running for governor. Jocelyn Benson's campaign says she is the daughter of two special-education teachers and, at 35, became the youngest woman to lead an accredited American law school as dean at Wayne State. She says she has been secretary of state since 2019 and is running so children, parents, and older residents can afford to stay. She says she would expand rural health-care options and build more housing. She says she would take on utility companies over the rates they charge. She says she would make child care free so more people can afford to live in the state.

Former assistant attorney general and prosecutor. Her campaign says she spent five years as an assistant attorney general in the consumer-protection bureau and was a deputy county attorney in Dawson and Dodge counties. She says she is running to return the office to serving Nebraskans rather than political fights. She says the attorney general should protect consumers rather than large corporations. She says enforcement should be both strong and fair so public safety and fairness go together. She says the office should respect the will of voters instead of fighting them each election cycle.

U.S. representative for Connecticut's 2nd District The campaign says Joe Courtney, a Connecticut native and lawyer, was elected to the U.S. House in 2006 after serving in the state House and as Vernon's town attorney. He chairs the Seapower and Projection Forces Subcommittee, which oversees submarine and ship construction. He says his first fight in Congress was to keep Electric Boat building submarines, and he still focuses on the shipyard and the region's defense work. He says he has worked to lower college costs, expand vocational programs, support farmers and veterans, and end surprise medical bills. His priorities page also lists infrastructure, agriculture, health care, and education.

Mayor of Randolph running for Congress in New Jersey's 11th District. His campaign says he grew up in a middle-class family in Clifton, played football at Yale, and worked in government and corporate communications, including as an aide to former Governor Chris Christie. He says he joined the Randolph council in 2022, became mayor in 2025, and lives there with his wife and three children. He says he would cut taxes for first-time homebuyers, including a tax freeze and a refundable credit for closing costs. He says he would cap federal student-loan interest rather than cancel debt outright, and invest in vocational and technical training. He says he would expand the child tax credit and childcare tax relief, require upfront health-care prices, and finish the Gateway Tunnel.

Nevada's governor, running for another term. Joe Lombardo's campaign says he grew up in a military family, graduated from Rancho High School and UNLV, served in the Army and the Nevada National Guard, and spent 26 years with the Las Vegas police before two terms as Clark County sheriff. He says that as governor he has cut regulation, made large investments in education, and pushed accountability in schools. He says he has backed law enforcement and worked on the housing shortage. He says the unfinished work is a safer, stronger, and more prosperous state.

Marine veteran and city council member running for Congress. Joe Males's campaign says he enlisted in the Marines after turning 18, served in the Philippines and Guam, and later built a computer-networking business. It says he is a Hemet council member and a father. He says he ran for council after his son, also a Marine, was murdered, because he wants the rule of law so other families do not face that loss. He says his council work has focused on infrastructure, business growth, and safer, cleaner neighborhoods. He says he would bring that same results-focused approach to Washington for the Inland Empire and Imperial County.

Former Iowa legislator and housing developer running for Congress. Born and raised south of Cedar Rapids, he says he was sworn into the Iowa House at 21, the youngest state legislator in state history, and later worked on housing at HUD and the Federal Housing Finance Agency. He develops workforce housing in rural Iowa and says younger Iowans should be able to afford to stay. He says he takes no corporate PAC money and supports term limits of 12 years in the House and 12 in the Senate, plus a ban on members of Congress trading stocks. He says immigration policy should put Americans first, including a secure border, removal of people he describes as criminal illegal immigrants, and a temporary ban on H-1B visas. He says deregulating homebuilding would lower home prices, and he wants lower taxes for middle-class families and small businesses and fewer rules on farmers.

U.S. representative for Colorado's 2nd District. Joe Neguse's campaign says he represents the 2nd District and is the first African American elected to Congress from Colorado. It says his parents came to the United States as refugees from Eritrea, and that before Congress he was a lawyer, a CU regent, and head of the state's consumer-protection agency. He says public lands are central to the district, and that he moved a Colorado public-lands bill through the House that would preserve about 400,000 acres and has pushed money toward wildfire preparation. He says climate change is an existential threat, and that he has pressed for more solar power, renewable energy, and deep cuts in carbon emissions. He says health coverage should be available to everyone, and that he is working to lower drug prices, raise the minimum wage, and close the gender pay gap.

Businessman and Republican nominee for Florida's 11th District His campaign says he started as a high-school handyman, entered the skilled trades, and grew a family-owned Central Florida company, Strada Services, that created thousands of jobs and paid training pathways. He and his wife raised their family in Central Florida. He says he is a father and grandfather running as an outsider, not for a career in politics. He says he would investigate congressional insider trading, enact term limits, and pass a balanced-budget amendment. He says he would finish the border wall, back law enforcement, and cut waste before asking taxpayers for more. He says he would lower costs, restore energy independence, bring jobs back, and protect Social Security and Medicare.

Youth worker and community organizer running for the U.S. Senate. Joe Tache's site says he is a socialist based in Boston who has spent more than ten years in movements against worker exploitation, war, police brutality, and gentrification, and that he writes and teaches that capitalism is the root of those problems. He says the largest corporations should be taken into public control and the economy reorganized around housing, health care, food, education, child care, retirement, and a living wage. He says climate policy and meaningful jobs require working people in power, and he wants spending shifted from war to domestic needs. He says immigrants, Black Americans, women, and LGBTQ people should not be blamed for the crisis, and he wants rent capped as a share of income, free health care, and millions of union jobs.

U.S. representative who chairs the Armed Services Readiness Subcommittee. His campaign says he is a veteran leader in Congress who serves on Armed Services, Foreign Affairs, and Education and the Workforce, and as an assistant majority whip. He says he is committed to conservative values and works to enact the Trump agenda. He says he promotes a strong national defense and peace through strength. He says he is working to create jobs and to limit the size and scope of the federal government. He says his commitments also cover the economy and veterans' services.

Brooklyn small-business owner running for Congress in New York's 9th District. His campaign says he is a small businessman in Brooklyn who also coaches men's volleyball at Brooklyn College. It says he graduated from Union College in 2005 with a degree in civil engineering. He says the country should bring manufacturing home and stay out of a major war so it can reinvest in infrastructure, pointing to tensions over Taiwan and Greenland. He warns that artificial intelligence could outrun human guardrails and asks how government stays accountable if machines run more of the market and the state.

Connecticut attorney and former Westport planning and zoning commissioner He says he is a Connecticut attorney and a former member of the Westport Planning and Zoning Commission. He says he grew up as the son of a longtime auditor in the Connecticut State Auditors of Public Accounts. He says he would make utility rate cases a priority and challenge policies that raise electric costs. He says he would investigate AI-driven pricing and pursue consumer fraud, including scams aimed at seniors. He says he would hold neighboring states accountable when pollution harms Connecticut rivers, drinking water, or Long Island Sound.

Navy veteran and small-business owner running for Congress. He calls himself a citizen-legislator who has balanced budgets, signed paychecks, and fought to put parents in control of schools. He wants spending that feeds inflation cut back, and less red tape for small manufacturers and the skilled trades. He supports a federal parents' bill of rights, lower public-university tuition, and more training in the trades. He says he would shut down open-air drug markets, interdict fentanyl, finish border barriers, and continue sea-lion control to help salmon runs.

U.S. representative running for another term. John Carter's campaign says he settled in Central Texas with his wife after law degrees from Texas Tech and the University of Texas, practiced in Round Rock, and was appointed a Williamson County district judge before Congress. His issues page lists border security, protecting the homeland, care for veterans, lower taxes and a stronger economy, the Second Amendment, and protecting children. He says he treats Central Texas as home and comes back after votes rather than staying in Washington.

Neurosurgeon and small-business owner running for Congress. He says his family has been in Bartow County since the 1930s, that he grew up on the family farm, graduated from Cartersville High School, and has cared for patients across the 11th District for decades. He and his wife, Dr. Anne Cowan, are raising four children, and he says he serves as a church elder. On health care, he says he would fix problems he attributes to the Affordable Care Act by lowering premiums, expanding choices, and putting patients in charge of their care. He wants tax relief for families and small businesses, investment in American workers, and stronger domestic industry. He supports proof of citizenship to vote, protections for speech, worship, and the right to bear arms, a ban on congressional stock trading, stronger ethics rules, and term limits.

Former teacher, coach, and local businessman running for Congress. His campaign says he taught at Edison Prep, coached, ran a local business, and is a parent who wants government to be accountable to families. He says he is running to be heard as a voice for hardworking Oklahomans. He says he would lower costs so families are not choosing between bills and care, and that hard work should be enough to own a home, send children to college, and retire with dignity. On schools, he says public money should stay in public schools with accountability, and he supports a program to help people earn education degrees and teach for five years debt-free. He says he would keep illegal guns off the streets, expand affordable care so people are not skipping treatment, and back term limits, an end to congressional stock trading, and tighter lobbying rules.

Navy veteran from Lake Charles running for Congress. Born in Shreveport and raised in Lake Charles, he says he served in the Navy from 1994 to 1998 and decided to run after a house fire nearly took his family's belongings. He and his wife Amanda have four children. He says he wants lower everyday costs, better pay, safer communities, and storm protection, with an all-of-the-above energy strategy that keeps oil and gas jobs and invests in renewables. He says insurance should have fair rates and faster claims, and that homeowners should get the coverage they pay for after storms. He says government should not control a person's body, health care, or personal life, and that patients rather than politicians should be in charge of care.

Trial lawyer and Marine veteran running for the U.S. Senate. John Deaton's site describes him as a trial attorney, Marine veteran, cancer survivor, and father of three daughters. He says affordable health care is a right and that he will work to break up large insurers and pharmacy benefit managers, lower drug prices, and expand telehealth. He wants faster permitting for housing and an energy mix that includes nuclear power, and he says he will not support what he calls blank checks for foreign aid. He says he will secure the border, expand legal immigration, and support an earned path to citizenship for Dreamers who meet strict standards.

Candidate for Washington's 4th District focused on farms, jobs, and rural care. He says he wants practical results for central Washington families, and his platform treats Hanford cleanup work as a job base to protect. He wants tariffs that hurt farmers removed, irrigation rights protected, and the Farm Bill written for small and mid-size operations. He says he will defend Hanford cleanup jobs, raise the federal minimum wage, protect the right to organize, and close tax preferences such as stepped-up basis and carried interest. He wants rural hospitals kept open, ACA subsidies restored, and Medicare and Medicaid protected from cuts.

U.S. representative running for another term. John Garamendi's campaign says he was raised on a ranch in Mokelumne Hill, served in the Peace Corps, and held office as a legislator, insurance commissioner, and lieutenant governor before his election to Congress in 2009. It says he and his wife still raise cattle and grow pears. He says Make It In America rules should steer federal purchases to U.S. manufacturing, and he highlights a higher Buy America share for buses and rail. He supports a national public option, rural hospitals and clinics, and letting Medicare negotiate drug prices. He says he would stop Delta tunnel projects that could drain the estuary and keep pushing water storage such as Sites Reservoir.

U.S. senator and former Colorado governor. John Hickenlooper's campaign describes him as a former brewpub owner, a former governor, and a sitting senator. He says he takes no corporate PAC money and supports overturning Citizens United, tighter disclosure of political money, and protection of vote-by-mail. He says he is working on housing costs, small-business capital, and union rights, including the PRO Act. He says health care is a right, and that he supports a public option, Medicare negotiation of drug prices, and restoring Roe v. Wade.

Republican nominee for governor of Michigan. John James's campaign says he entered West Point at 18, became a Ranger-qualified Apache helicopter pilot, and served with the Army in Iraq. He says he is the father of three sons and is running so more young people can build a life in Michigan. He says he would bring down the cost of housing, energy, groceries, and car insurance. He says schools should put reading, math, and skilled trades first, with parents in charge of their children's education. He says he would back police and prosecute violent crime from Detroit to the Upper Peninsula.

U.S. representative for Pennsylvania's 13th District. John Joyce is a physician who has practiced with his wife in Blair County and has served in Congress since 2019. His campaign says he focuses on the economy, affordable health care, and constitutional rights. He says he is working to strengthen the economy and make health care more affordable. He also says he will defend constitutional rights.

Columbus lawyer and Upper Arlington city council member running for attorney general. He says the attorney general should be independent of Columbus politics and should work for the people who pay the office. He says he would take on corrupt politicians and restore transparency and accountability. He says he would pursue price-fixing, scams, robocalls, and fraud by Medicaid providers and nursing homes.

Republican candidate for lieutenant governor John Loughlin's site says he was raised in Rhode Island and educated in the Portsmouth and Lincoln public schools. It says he attended Rhode Island College and the University of Rhode Island, where he was a student firefighter, and later earned a bachelor of science degree from Excelsior University. He says he would restore cuts to Medicare and Medicaid, bring back a public health-care option, and negotiate lower drug prices, including a broader cap on insulin. He says he cosponsors a bill to restore Roe v. Wade and would expand access to reproductive care and mental-health treatment.

Strength coach running for Congress. John McBride's campaign says he moved from Connecticut to California in 1989 to be the first strength and conditioning coach at the University of the Pacific and later coached at St. Mary's High School. It says he has been married since 1994, has five children, and is running in the 9th Congressional District. He says he would remove dangerous chemicals from food and water, emphasize medical freedom and natural healing, and oppose what he calls death boards. He says he would back local police, prosecute crime, support youth mental health, and strengthen the southern border. He says farms need water rights and less federal control, and he wants lower taxes, no tax on Social Security, and deep cuts in spending.

U.S. representative for Virginia's 5th District. John McGuire's office says he is in his first term and serves on Armed Services and Oversight. He was born in central Virginia, spent his early childhood in foster care, served 10 years as a Navy SEAL, and then founded a fitness business, SEAL Team PT. He was elected to the Virginia legislature in 2018. He says he is focused on keeping costs low for families, defending the country, shrinking the federal government, and supporting infrastructure and agriculture.

U.S. representative for Michigan's 2nd District. His campaign says he represents 20 counties and chairs the House select committee on competition with the Chinese Communist Party. He says he is running again to keep cutting taxes, secure the border, and protect Michigan communities. He says he opposed a Chinese-linked battery plant in Michigan and wants to stop adversaries from buying American farmland. He says he will defend the Second Amendment, protect the unborn, and preserve Social Security and Medicare, including tax relief on those benefits for seniors. He says he has worked to support farmers, protect Line 5, and improve patient safety and rural health care.

Retired Minnesota State Patrol lieutenant running for Congress. John Nagel's site says he is a lifelong Saint Louis Park resident who spent 30 years with the State Patrol, including highway patrol in Hennepin County and the governor's security detail. He says he has been married to Connie since 1988 and is a father and grandfather. He says he will cut taxes, fight inflation, and eliminate fraud and waste that he says are driving up prices. He says he will work with the attorney general so violent criminals are kept off the streets, schools are protected, and law enforcement is funded and supported. He says he will keep the border secured, support legal immigration and faster processing for people who follow the rules, and treat border security as national security.

Lieutenant governor, farmer, and small-business owner.
