He says affordability comes first, and that he opposes taxes, mandates, and spending he considers unnecessary burdens on families, seniors, farmers, and small businesses. He says he will defend property rights and traditional land uses for farmers, loggers, sportsmen, and landowners. He wants it to be easier to build housing, and he wants more career and technical education, apprenticeships, and workforce programs.

U.S. representative running for another term. John Rutherford's campaign says he grew up in Northeast Florida, graduated from the FBI National Academy and Florida State in criminology, spent 40 years in law enforcement as Duval County sheriff, and now represents the 5th District. He says he would fight inflation by blocking and cutting taxes, cutting red tape for small businesses, and lowering grocery, gas, and electric costs. He says he has backed VA reform, higher troop pay, veterans' mental-health care, and a school-safety law he authored.

Candidate campaigning as Bongo for Georgia's 5th District. His campaign says he went undercover in what he calls a journalistic pursuit, did not like what he found, and concluded that neither party is giving people proper representation. He says members disappear after they are elected, and he points to dropout rates and pockets of unemployment as a failure of representation. He says he wants attention on what he calls poison in food, and he describes FedNow as a tracking program that would eliminate cash.

Former Idaho Supreme Court justice running for governor as an independent. He is a lifelong Idahoan raised in Grangeville who served as a Latah County district judge and then on the Idaho Supreme Court, a judicial career he puts at 26 years. Candidate for U.S. Senate. He says he would take a practical approach and put New Hampshire first.

Retired Navy command master chief and small-business owner running for Congress. His campaign says he is a husband, father, career Navy veteran, and small-business owner running for the 7th District. He says he would work to pass a war-powers measure on the war in Iran and to end tariffs he says are making life more expensive for farmers and small businesses. He says he would introduce an All American Healthcare Act for low-cost optional insurance and a plan to bring federal spending under control without adding to the debt.

Chairman of the Alabama Republican Party John Wahl became chairman of the Alabama Republican Party in 2021 after earlier work as a party field director, and he runs a butterfly farm in Limestone County. Governor Kay Ivey appointed him to the Alabama Public Library Service board, and the board elected him its chairman in 2024. He supports tax relief and says that as party chairman he helped lead a cut in the state grocery tax. He supports school choice, wants classrooms focused on reading, writing, math, history, and civics, and backs ending the federal Department of Education. He says he will work with Donald Trump's border plans so Alabama is not a sanctuary for illegal activity, and he wants post-election audits and tighter oversight of voting machines.

Western Kentucky boat-dock builder running for Congress. He says he has spent his life in western Kentucky, graduated from Murray State in 2016 with a history degree, and has built boat docks on Kentucky Lake and Lake Barkley since he was 14 while working in the family business. He says neighbors and elders shaped him and that he is running to take those values to Washington. The campaign says it is grassroots and does not take corporate money. His site says he stands for farm resilience, congressional accountability, workplace dignity, fairer drug prices, and veterans' services. He also lists infrastructure, data-center rules, child care, tax policy for everyday Americans, and health-insurance reform among the issues he is running on.

Sheriff's deputy running for Congress. Johnny Garcia's campaign says he was raised on San Antonio's West Side by his mother, worked construction while at community college, and has spent nearly 20 years with the Bexar County Sheriff's Office, including as a SWAT hostage negotiator. He says he would lower everyday costs, end tariffs that raise prices, and stop members of Congress from trading stocks. He says he would secure the border, focus immigration enforcement on criminals, keep police funded, and reverse health-care cuts.

Tennessee House majority whip running for Congress in the 6th District. His campaign says he is a Christian conservative, a husband, and a father of three who has served as House majority whip since 2019. He says he first ran for the state House in 2018 to back an America First agenda. He says he would work with the president on that agenda, including deportations and securing the southern border. He says he would fight inflation, seek lower taxes, and defend the Second Amendment. He also lists keeping men out of women's sports, standing with Israel, backing police, protecting what he calls the sanctity of life, and supporting farmers.

U.S. representative for Maryland's 2nd District since 2025. A lifelong Marylander, he says working-class values from eastern Baltimore County guide him. He serves on Small Business and Foreign Affairs and on the Democratic Steering and Policy Committee. He says he wants higher wages, affordable health care, and fully funded public schools, and he opposed a budget he says gave tax breaks to the wealthy while threatening programs families use. He says he would extend health-insurance tax credits, end tariffs that raise prices, cut drug costs, expand housing, and protect Medicare, Medicaid, SNAP, and the Child Tax Credit. He says he supports expanding voting rights, protecting court independence, and banning stock trading by members of Congress.
District 13 · U.S. House · New York · Republican

Self-financed candidate running for Congress in New York's 13th District. His campaign says he is running in the 13th District on his own money so he owes no private or special interest, and that he turned down super PAC support. It says he rejects communism and anarchism and what he calls toxic politics from the far left and the far right. He says his case is for what he calls universal capitalism rather than socialism, and against a sanctuary city. He highlights the SAVE Act and election-integrity litigation, and says extreme politics are dividing neighbors in Harlem.

Mortgage broker running for Congress. Jon Bonck's campaign says he is a Christian, husband, and father from greater Houston who has worked in real estate and mortgages for more than 20 years with his wife, Laura. It says he is a deacon and Bible-study teacher. He says he would finish the border wall, protect life from conception, and put parents ahead of school ideology. He says he would defend the Second Amendment and religious liberty, cut spending on foreign wars, and reject vaccine mandates.

Candidate for attorney general who says he is a fifth-generation Oklahoman and a small-business owner. His campaign says his family still owns a farm in Okeene, that he and his wife are raising three children in Oklahoma City, and that he earned degrees from the University of Oklahoma and Oklahoma City University's law school. He says he started his first business in college. He says everyone, including political elites, should be treated equally under the law, and that the office should back police and defend liberties. He says he would watch taxpayer dollars and support border and fentanyl enforcement. He says he would defend private property against foreign adversaries and out-of-state interests, work with tribal nations, and back the state's energy industry.

The campaign site calls him Senator Husted and asks voters to send him to the U.S. Senate. An election-eve post on the site describes a Cleveland rally and urges supporters to vote the next day. No 2026 issue list was found for this candidate.

U.S. senator from Georgia seeking another term. His campaign calls him a legislative workhorse and an investigator of corruption and abuses of power. It says he is the only Democratic senator up for reelection in a state Donald Trump won. He says he has worked to cap insulin costs for seniors at $35 a month and to lower housing costs. He says he has worked to upgrade health care for pregnant women, babies, and children, and to crack down on the online exploitation of children.

Candidate for railroad commissioner. He says he is a mechanical engineer who spent 25 years in the energy industry and has served four terms in the Texas House. He says he is the only candidate in the race who knows what the commission regulates and cannot be bought by the companies it watches. He says Texas families need a commissioner who will not bend to the companies being regulated while energy bills climb. He says that in the House he pushed weatherization rules for gas infrastructure after the 2021 grid failure and fought utilities passing the cost of their own failures on to families. He says the commission has bent to special interests while energy bills rise, and that engineering judgment should replace that pattern.

Air Force veteran running for Georgia's 13th District. His campaign says he is a husband and father of four, and a 23-year Air Force veteran who deployed to Iraq. He says he holds a bachelor of science from the University of New Mexico and master's degrees from Harvard and Johns Hopkins in business, finance, and health care administration. He says he would lower taxes on working families, help small businesses add jobs, and cut regulations while still protecting consumers. He says he would expand Medicaid, widen rural and telehealth access, and defend patient choice so care is closer and cheaper. He says he would fund classrooms, work with parents, and strengthen career and technical education, and he supports term limits.

Former Alaska state representative Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, who goes by JKT, was born and raised in Sitka and represented Southeast Alaska in the state House for a decade. He says he left the legislature about three years ago and is running to fund schools, lower energy and housing costs, and balance the budget. He wants public schools fully funded, teachers paid so Alaska can keep them, and a constitutional amendment to forward-fund education. He supports renewables, hydro, and natural gas, and wants the Railbelt utilities to cooperate so electricity costs less. He says the state should cut red tape on housing and open state land in and next to cities and towns for homes.

Former Navajo Nation president running for Congress in Arizona's 2nd District. His campaign says he grew up in rural Arizona in a home without running water or electricity, and that childhood taught him hard work, responsibility, and faith. He says families are paying the price for an economy that puts billionaires first. He says he would lower health-care and housing costs, take on drug-price gouging, and reverse Medicaid cuts that threaten rural hospitals. He says he would secure Arizona's share of Colorado River water, update rural water systems, and protect groundwater. He also lists rural infrastructure, veterans, voting rights, and tribal sovereignty among his priorities.

Marine veteran and Blue Dog Democrat running for Utah's 4th District. He enlisted at 17, served as an infantry rifleman from 2000 to 2004, was in Washington during the attack on the Pentagon, and deployed twice to Iraq. He says veterans in the district drive hours for basic care and that VA staffing cuts, including nurses and doctors, need to be reversed. He credits his grandmother's Teamster pension, Medicare, and Social Security with giving her stability, and he says he will defend those programs. He says there is no VA clinic in Tooele, Sevier, Millard, or Sanpete counties, in a district that includes Camp Williams, Dugway Proving Ground, and the Tooele Army Depot.

Air Force veteran, attorney, and former Missouri assistant attorney general running for Congress. He says he grew up in a working-class Midwestern family, spent nearly 16 years in service, and then went to court for Missourians when the rules were unfair. He says he is running to work on the cost of living with practical proposals. He wants safer communities through what he calls common-sense policy. He says government should treat people with dignity, and he describes the campaign as youth-led and people-powered.

Candidate for Congress The campaign says Joe Arminio was born and raised in Wilmington, earned a political-science doctorate from MIT, and has taught and done policy work tied to defense. He says he is running as an America First candidate who wants Main Street to rise. He says private and public debt are national emergencies and calls for a one-time debt jubilee plus action on the federal debt. He says he wants to stop endless wars, reform education, and restore what he calls constitutional government. He describes the campaign as a populist alternative to an incumbent he says is continuing a failing economy and those wars.
District 6 · U.S. House · New York · Republican

Small-business owner running for Congress in New York's 6th District. His campaign says he was born in Japan in 1964 and lived in Taiwan with his grandmother while his father studied law, and that his father later became one of the first lawyers in Flushing. It says Chou is a naturalized citizen who built a small business in Queens. He says he wants a balanced tax policy that eases the burden on working families and new small businesses, plus fairer interest rates on student loans. He says he would back public, private, and vocational education and improve access to health care and affordable child care. He says he wants a fair immigration system with secure borders and closer cooperation against criminal threats, and he wants to reform cashless bail.
District 16 · U.S. House · New York · Republican

Attorney from New Rochelle running for Congress in New York's 16th District. His campaign says he has lived in New Rochelle and Pelham Bay for 30 years, is the father of triplets who went through New Rochelle public schools, and has practiced law for 32 years. It says he is running to offer ideas rather than a fixed ideology. He says he wants tax relief, lower energy costs, high-paying union jobs, a smaller budget, and lower interest rates so housing is more affordable in Westchester and the Bronx. He says that work will take a generation of cutting federal spending, lowering taxes, producing affordable American energy, and shrinking the administrative state.
Governor and lieutenant governor · Illinois · Write-in
Lieutenant governor on the Kane County list. Not on the Will County list.
District 25 · U.S. House · New York · Democratic

U.S. representative for New York's 25th District. His campaign says he was born and raised upstate and has lived in the same Irondequoit neighborhood for most of his life, the son of a Korean War veteran and a Plumbers and Pipefitters member. It says he served in the county legislature and as Assembly majority leader, and is now ranking member of the House Administration Committee. He says he is fighting to expand child care and affordable housing, strengthen job training, and support local businesses. He says he has worked to end surprise medical bills, lower prescription prices, and protect people with preexisting conditions, and he opposes efforts to dismantle the Affordable Care Act. He also highlights climate action, gun laws, abortion rights, and equal rights for people who live in the country.
No 2026 issue list was found for this candidate.

U.S. representative and fourth-generation rancher from eastern Oklahoma. His official biography says he owned a small excavation and trucking business, served in the Oklahoma Senate from 2010 to 2018, and earlier worked for U.S. Senator Tom Coburn. He is a graduate of Oklahoma State University and was elected to Congress in 2022. He says he is focused on reining in unsustainable debt and deficit spending, which he believes is undermining national security. His House site lists his legislative priorities as deficit spending, border security, traditional values, constitutional adherence, and energy dominance.
District 5 · U.S. House · New Jersey · Democratic

U.S. representative for New Jersey's 5th District. His campaign says he was first elected in 2016 and represents most of Bergen County and parts of Sussex and Passaic. It says he draws on private-sector work and on growing up in New Jersey, including time in his father's store. He says voters sent him to Congress to fight for lower taxes and what he calls Jersey values. He says he works across party lines to find common ground rather than follow a national political agenda.

Governor of Hawaii and a physician. He says he has cared for Hawaii families as a local physician and emergency doctor, then as a legislator, lieutenant governor, and governor. He and Jaime Ushiroda, whom he met in 2005, have two children, Maia and Sam. He says that since 2022 he has worked to lower the cost of living. He says he is working to build affordable housing. He says he is working to reduce homelessness statewide.

U.S. representative running for another term. Josh Harder's campaign says his family settled in Manteca generations ago to farm peaches, and that he worked through Stanford and Harvard before a business career. It says he lives in Tracy with his wife and two daughters and first ran to protect coverage for people with pre-existing conditions, including his brother. He says he would cut insulin and other drug prices, repeal federal and state gas taxes, and get housing costs under control. He says he would bring ag-tech, technology, and clean-energy jobs to the Valley, treat homelessness as an emergency with mental-health and job help, and fund police work against methamphetamine and fentanyl. He says he would stop a Delta tunnel he argues would send Valley water south, build storage, and keep a path to citizenship for Dreamers alongside border enforcement against traffickers.

Wisconsin attorney general and former federal prosecutor. His campaign says he grew up in Oshkosh and Fond du Lac and has led the state Department of Justice since 2019. He says the department has investigated homicides, sexual assaults, internet crimes against children, and drug trafficking, and has sought money from companies tied to the opioid epidemic. He says he supports wider background checks on firearm transfers and more funding for crime-victim services and school safety. He says he is pro-choice, points to a Wisconsin Supreme Court ruling on an old abortion law, and says the office has joined cases against federal funding cuts and weaker environmental rules.

Georgia state senator and attorney running for lieutenant governor. He has been a state legislator for eight years, first in the State House and now in the State Senate, and he represents Senate District 14. He is a Yale-educated attorney and a University of Georgia graduate. He says he passed a bipartisan law that for the first time set statewide rules on the car-booting industry. He says he secured the first $1 million in the state budget for research into therapies for veterans' post-traumatic stress. He says he has fought efforts at the Capitol to advantage corporations and to target vulnerable people for political gain.
District 19 · U.S. House · New York · Democratic

U.S. representative for New York's 19th District. His campaign says he is a fifth-generation Upstate New Yorker from a working-class neighborhood in Endicott, where his mother worked in law enforcement and earlier generations worked at local factories. It says he does not take corporate PAC money. He says utility bills are out of control and that he is taking utility monopolies to court, backing home energy upgrades, and trying to ban foreign ownership of American utilities. He says data centers should pay for the grid upgrades they require instead of passing those costs to Upstate families. He says he backs the Equality Act and mental-health services for LGBTQ young people.

Governor of Pennsylvania The campaign site presents Josh Shapiro as the governor and Austin Davis as lieutenant governor. It asks voters to support Shapiro for governor. His campaign says that as governor he has worked on jobs and money in people's pockets, law enforcement and community groups for public safety, education funding, and protecting freedoms. The site says Pennsylvania has hired hundreds of new officers and created thousands of jobs, and that children can get free breakfast and more mental-health counselors in school. It says high-school graduates have more paths through work, apprenticeships, or college, and that he and Lieutenant Governor Austin Davis are running to continue that work.

Architect and small-business owner from Liberty running for Missouri's 6th District. He is a licensed architect and project professional raising four children, and he says that experience with budgets and deadlines is how he wants government to work. He says voters should judge officials by the plan they propose, the work they do, and what actually changes. He describes the job as planning the problem, building the response, managing the constraints, and finishing it.

Iowa state legislator and two-time Paralympic gold medalist running for the Senate. Born with spina bifida after his father was exposed to Agent Orange in Vietnam, he says he had 21 surgeries by age 12 and later played for the United States at four Paralympics, including a gold medal in Tokyo in 2021. He then won a Council Bluffs seat in the Iowa House, a district he says Donald Trump had carried, by six votes. He says economic policy should benefit the middle class and workers rather than Wall Street and billionaire donors. He says he supports public education and opposes school vouchers. He says Iowa's health care system needs major reform, and he supports protection of air, food, and water.

Small business owner running for Congress in Ohio's 4th District. Joshua Kolasinski says he runs a business that installs, tests, and repairs medical equipment, and that he is a husband, a father of three, and a Christian whose family has lived in Delaware, Ohio since 2012. He says he has voted for both parties and is running as a Democrat so people in the district are heard. He says federal taxes should be used in local communities rather than on more wars or corporate welfare, and that housing, gas, health care, education, and food should be affordable. He proposes a registered-voter lobby and a district think tank, and he says Medicare should negotiate drug prices and patients should see prices before care.

Candidate for Florida attorney general His campaign page identifies the candidate as Jose Javier Rodriguez and says he is taking on the corrupt and powerful. No 2026 issue list was found for this candidate.

Cattle farmer and small-business owner running for Congress. Her campaign says she is a fourth-generation cattle farmer, a Bedford County mother, and the owner of a family farm-equipment dealership who adopted her son Eli through foster care. She says she has taken on monopoly utilities, worked on rural health care and public education, and tried to protect farmland. Her HOME plan says health care should be close to home, with rural hospitals protected and more mental health, addiction treatment, and health workers. She says she would bring industries and small-business investment to the district, rebuild roads and broadband, and fight costs for housing, groceries, and energy. She says she would support teachers, modernize classrooms, and expand higher education and job training so people do not have to leave home for opportunity.

U.S. representative for Ohio's 3rd District. Joyce Beatty says she represents Ohio's 3rd District, serves on Financial Services, and was the first chair of its diversity and inclusion subcommittee. Her campaign describes her as a small business owner and former college administrator who tries to connect people to policy. She says she supports a livable wage, equal pay, workforce training, and lower college costs, and she calls health care a right she would strengthen through the Affordable Care Act. She says she will protect and expand Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid, defend abortion access and civil rights, and support a path to citizenship for undocumented immigrants and DREAMers.

U.S. representative for Arizona's 6th District. His campaign says he is a husband and father of six whose parents were working-class immigrants, and that he is the first naturalized U.S. citizen from Mexico elected to the House from Arizona. It says he grew up in the 6th District. He says his results include more border agents, lower taxes for everyday Arizonans and seniors, and more funding for cancer research. He says he also works to support veterans and law enforcement officers.

U.S. representative and former state legislator running for another term. Juan Vargas's campaign says he was born in National City to Mexican immigrant parents who raised ten children on a chicken ranch. It says he earned degrees from the University of San Diego, Fordham, and Harvard Law, worked with the Jesuits in El Salvador, and served on the city council, in the Legislature, and in Congress. He says he is working to grow good-paying jobs through clean energy, infrastructure, and small businesses. He says he has championed public education and services for communities that have been left out. His site says he is also fighting to protect health care and veterans.

U.S. representative running for another term. Judy Chu's campaign says she was elected to the House in 2009 and represents Pasadena and the west San Gabriel Valley. It says she serves on Ways and Means and the Budget Committee and is chair emerita of the Congressional Asian Pacific American Caucus. She says her Ways and Means work covers taxes, trade, Social Security, and Medicare, including health care and safety-net programs. She says the caucus she led expanded language access in federal agencies and pushed for data that reflects Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander communities. She says she co-chairs a bipartisan caucus on creative rights.

U.S. representative from Louisiana running for the Senate. Julia Letlow's site says she is a Louisiana native, mother, and educator who entered Congress after her husband, Luke, died, and that she was the first Republican woman elected to Congress from Louisiana. She says her work in Congress has been for parents, students, farmers, law enforcement, and Louisiana families. She says she is guided by faith, family, service, and love of the state. She says she is running for the Senate to give Louisiana conservative leadership, and she notes President Trump's endorsement.

Lieutenant governor since 2019 · former state representative · won the primary with 40.4% South Side of Chicago. Daughter of a Navy veteran and a Chicago public-school teacher, and a mother of four. She finished ahead of Raja Krishnamoorthi and Robin Kelly, and she is not taking corporate PAC money in this race. $25 federal minimum wage, a larger earned-income credit and child tax credit, and a middle-class tax cut paid for by higher taxes on income above $1 million. Medicare for All, including home care, hearing, and vision. She opposes the current tariffs, which she calls a tax on groceries and goods. Restore Roe-level abortion protections, pass the John Lewis Voting Rights Act and gun laws, and abolish ICE. Her housing plan targets hedge-fund home purchases and algorithm-set rents.
District 1 · U.S. House · North Dakota · Republican

Candidate for Congress The campaign says Julie Fedorchak is a fourth-generation North Dakotan, born in Williston and a University of North Dakota graduate, who later ran a communications business and served on the Public Service Commission. She says she is running to be a practical voice for the state's energy and farm economy. She says that on the Public Service Commission she pushed to finish the Dakota Access Pipeline and to keep coal and oil energy reliable and affordable. Her issues list includes securing the border, reducing the federal debt, backing law enforcement, and defending the Second Amendment. She says she will work with President Trump to secure North Dakota's energy and agricultural future and to support farmers and ranchers.

Community finance executive running for Oakland mayor. Julius Robinson says he grew up in Watts and has spent more than four decades connecting capital, opportunity, and communities. He says he is running because Oakland needs practical results on safety, housing, and trust in City Hall. He says the city should be safer and cleaner, and that businesses need support to grow. He says housing, homelessness, and economic opportunity have to be handled together. He says local government should operate with more transparency and accountability.

Peace and Justice Party candidate for governor of Vermont. Her campaign says the major parties maintain economic and environmental injustice, and that her platform is a just and inclusive society with wealth and power shared more equally. She wants profitable businesses to pay a living wage and wants Vermont's universal health care law fully carried out. She proposes progressive taxes, including higher taxes on high incomes and on buildings left vacant most of the year, in place of homestead taxes for education. She wants community hubs where people can offer skills and get help, plus housing support such as cooperative ownership and no-interest mortgages for modest homes.

Army veteran running for Congress. Justin Early's campaign says he is a Georgetown father of seven and a cybersecurity architect at Dell whose parents served in the Army. It says he enlisted after Leander High School, served as a paratrooper, and worked at the Defense Intelligence Agency. He says his priorities are affordability, responsible technology and AI, and defending democracy. He says families are squeezed by the cost of living and unaffordable health care, and that he is not a career politician.

Republican candidate for U.S. Senate. Justin Murphy is the Republican nominee. His campaign says it is dedicated to members of the armed forces and publishes a written pledge of his positions. He says he wants the Pinelands kept intact and the Jersey Shore kept free of pollution and offshore wind turbines. He lists parental rights, medical freedom, and Medicare for seniors among his national priorities. He says he would argue conservative positions and calls the race a break from a long stretch without a Republican senator from New Jersey.

State representative running for Congress in Tennessee's 9th District. His campaign says he is the fourth of five sons of teenage parents in Memphis, and that his parents worked their way through college and out of poverty. He says he is a state representative who was expelled after a protest, then reappointed and reelected, and that he is married to Oceana R. Gilliam. He says he would guarantee jobs, raise the minimum wage to a living wage, pass the PRO Act, and make billionaires and large corporations pay more. He supports Medicare for All, rural hospitals, and the veterans' health system, and he wants permits to carry, a ban on assault rifles, and background checks. He says he would pause large data-center construction, overturn Citizens United, and ban members of Congress from trading stock.

Veteran and engineer running for Congress in Pennsylvania's 16th District. Justin Wagner was born and raised in Greenville and Transfer and says his family has lived there for eight generations. He describes himself as a veteran, engineer, and pro-union candidate running for safer and more self-reliant communities. He says housing, health care, power, and food costs are pushing working families into poverty, and that he would fight for affordability, local veterans, and labor. He also says every school needs the tools to prepare the next generation, the justice system should be fair, and the environment should stay safe for future children.
District 22 · U.S. House · New York · Republican

Former Agriculture Department chief of staff running for Congress in New York's 22nd District. Her campaign says she grew up in Auburn in a blue-collar family, was the first in her family to finish college, and most recently was chief of staff to the secretary of agriculture. It says she is a working mother of three running to lower costs for Central New York. She says she would grow good-paying jobs and lower everyday costs so families do not have to leave New York to get ahead. She says her work in government has focused on cutting red tape, strengthening American agriculture, and protecting jobs in the food and energy supply chain.

Mayor of Los Angeles running for re-election. Karen Bass is campaigning for another term as mayor. Her campaign page says she is standing up for Angelenos against federal immigration raids. She says the Trump administration's ICE raids and militarized actions have no purpose other than to create fear. She says those actions damage the city's economy and tear families apart.
No 2026 issue list was found for this candidate.

Educator, author, and Libertarian candidate for U.S. Senate Kasie Whitener's campaign describes her as a community leader, author, educator, and radio personality. She says she would be an independent vote in the Senate rather than a party operative. She says she would simplify the tax code, return to actual budgets, and cut federal spending across agencies. She says she would separate health insurance from employment and remove barriers that keep people from starting medical practices. She says she wants a balanced-budget amendment, no new foreign wars, and no new federal abortion laws or new limits on the Second Amendment.

U.S. representative running for another term. Kat Cammack's campaign says she is in her third term from Florida's 3rd District. It says she and her husband, a Gainesville firefighter and paramedic, are raising their daughter in North Central Florida. She says she is focused on securing the southern border, advocating for small businesses, and defending the Second Amendment. She describes herself as a budget hawk who wants taxes low and federal spending kept minimal.

House Democratic whip representing Massachusetts' 5th District. She says she first ran in 2013 because of the issues facing women, children, and families, and that colleagues elected her Democratic whip in 2022, the highest-ranking woman from Massachusetts in House history. She says the people of the district are why she is running again. She says she is fighting to cancel cuts to Medicaid and the Affordable Care Act, end a war she says raised gas prices, and lift tariffs that made goods more expensive. She says that if Democrats control Congress she would lead efforts to crack down on ICE, stop unauthorized wars, and hold the president accountable for using the office to enrich himself. She says every worker should have a living wage, paid family leave, and the right to join a union, and she highlights the expanded child tax credit in the American Rescue Plan.

Chief counsel to the Alabama attorney general Katherine Robertson is a graduate of Auburn University and the University of Alabama School of Law and has been chief counsel to Attorney General Steve Marshall for nearly a decade. She previously was vice president of the Alabama Policy Institute and worked in Washington as clerk and counsel to Senator Jeff Sessions. She says her work has been to fight what she calls federal overreach. She says she has fought efforts she describes as attacks on women's sports, free speech, and the sanctity of life. She says she is running to defend the rights and freedoms of Alabamians.

U.S. representative running for another term. Kathy Castor's campaign says she is a native Floridian and the first woman elected to represent Hillsborough and Pinellas counties in Congress. It says she was a lawyer and Hillsborough County commissioner before joining the House Energy and Commerce Committee. She says she works to lower family costs, create jobs, and protect Florida's environment, including wetlands and the coast. She says she helped pass the bipartisan infrastructure law, bills expanding care for seriously ill children, and veterans' caucus work.

Governor of New York, seeking another term. Her campaign calls her New York's first mom governor and says she has focused on putting money back in people's pockets, lowering costs, and keeping New Yorkers safe. She is running with New York City Council Speaker Adrienne Adams. She points to inflation refund checks, a larger child tax credit, middle-class tax cuts, and work toward universal child care and lower auto insurance costs. She highlights free school meals, a ban on cell phones during the school day, and gun laws she says are meant to make streets and subways safer. She says the ticket would keep lowering costs, invest in community safety, and protect New York from what she calls MAGA extremism.

Attorney General of Delaware She says she was born and raised in Wilmington, graduated from the University of Delaware and Villanova University Law School, and started as a prosecutor in the Delaware Department of Justice. She says she later served as state prosecutor and chief deputy attorney general before returning to lead the office. She says she is running to make Delaware safer and to make justice fair and equal. She says she prosecuted domestic violence, sexual assault, and homicide cases, and that she built the office's consumer-fraud work. She says that as attorney general she has pursued child predators, opioid manufacturers, corruption, and elder abuse, and is pushing stronger laws on online predators.

Governor of Arizona Katie Hobbs is a social worker who was elected Arizona secretary of state and then governor, taking office in 2022. Her campaign says that before politics she worked with homeless youth and helped run a large domestic-violence shelter. She says she eliminated the tax on rent, offered down-payment help for first homes, and cut red tape to make housing more affordable. She says she created a Border Coordination Office, sent more than $100 million in border-security funding to local police, and that Task Force SAFE has stopped over 19 million fentanyl pills. She says a water compromise passed under her watch will create jobs, lower housing costs, and conserve water, and that she ended a foreign corporation's groundwater leases.

Teacher and attorney running for Congress. Katy Padilla Stout's campaign says she was born and raised in South Texas, taught school, and worked as an attorney for children in foster care. It says she and her husband are raising four children and she is running to be the first woman to represent the 23rd District. She says the cost of living comes from the current administration's economic policies, and that the tax code should help the middle class rather than cut taxes for billionaires while food aid is debated. She says she would expand Medicare toward coverage for everyone and treat gun ownership as a right that still allows commonsense limits.

Attorney and business owner running for Congress. Katy Tyndell's site says she is an attorney and business owner whose family roots in Kansas go back five generations, and that she grew up in a small ranching and farming town. It says she was a staff attorney for the National Congress of American Indians and later co-founded Leading Kansas. She says she will work for affordable health care, including mental health care, after her family navigated a sister's schizophrenia and she watched insurance premiums rise at her business. She says she will look for common ground to lower taxes on working Kansans and bring costs down, instead of tax breaks aimed at corporations and the wealthy. She says tariffs and the war with Iran have hurt Kansas farm markets and raised fertilizer and diesel costs, and that she will fight to reverse those tariff policies and end the war.

Working mother and organizer running for Idaho's 1st District. Her campaign says she is a 36-year-old working mother and a sixth-generation Idahoan. She says she has spent nearly five years, across three election cycles, organizing in a district she describes as about 500 miles long. She says she takes no corporate PAC money, would ban stock trades by members of Congress and their families, and supports term limits of six House terms and two Senate terms. She says she would cut taxes on middle-class families and local businesses, raise the federal minimum wage, repeal right-to-work laws, and direct USDA help to family farms. She says Idaho's public lands are not for sale, and she would fund the Forest Service, local timber, and wildfire work, and move health coverage to a universal single-payer system.

Former Atlanta mayor running for governor. She was Atlanta's 60th mayor and says she is the first mayor in the city's history to have served in all three branches of city government, as a judge, a city council member, and mayor. She says the city balanced four budgets without a property-tax increase, layoffs, or furloughs, and that reserves stood near $181 million at the end of her term. She says that as mayor she secured major investments in affordable housing and a historic pay raise for Atlanta's first responders. She says she supported small businesses and became a national voice on civil-rights reforms. She says the city balanced its budgets through a downturn without property-tax increases, layoffs, or furloughs.

Attorney general of Minnesota. His campaign says Minnesotans first elected him attorney general in 2018 and that he calls the job the people's lawyer. The site says the office has gone after insulin prices, opioid companies, scams, and medical debt. He says the office has lowered costs, including cutting the price of insulin, and has taken on price-gouging, medical debt, and opioid companies. He says he is protecting tenants, going after scammers, and standing up for student borrowers. He says he is challenging the Trump administration because no one is above the law, and that he is defending reproductive rights and access to gender-affirming care.

Ohio auditor of state running for attorney general. His campaign says he was elected auditor after more than two decades that included private-sector work and public office, and that he keeps a law practice in Celina. It says his audit team has pursued criminal cases against public officials and findings to recover taxpayer money. He says he would defend constitutional rights, including religious liberty, and challenge federal actions he argues exceed federal authority. He says he would fight the drug epidemic with treatment, prosecutions, and efforts to cut supply chains, and that he would work with police on human trafficking and survivor services. He says he would enforce consumer-protection laws against fraud, scams, and deceptive businesses, especially cases that target seniors, and he proposes a program to help patients challenge health-insurance denials.

U.S. representative running for another term. Keith Self's campaign says he is a native Texan, West Point graduate, and retired Army lieutenant colonel who served in the infantry and Special Forces. It says that after the Army he was Collin County judge and is seeking another term in Congress. He says he voted to restart border-wall construction, offered a bill to use seized cartel money on border security, and wants the federal government to repay Texas for its border spending. He says he cut the county property-tax rate, opposes stopgap federal budgets, and wants lower taxes, less spending, and energy permitting that expands American production. He says he started a caucus to stop what he calls the spread of Sharia law in Texas and the country.

Candidate for U.S. House in Colorado's 2nd District. Kelley Dennison says she is a Colorado native with roots in mountain towns and the Front Range, and a business owner. She says she is running so those communities have a voice in Congress on costs, energy, and the state's land and water. She says families are squeezed by housing, gas, inflation, and property taxes, and that the district should do better by veterans and seniors. She says parents should be partners in their children's education, and that responsible gun owners should not be punished for crimes committed by other people. She says she has signed a pledge to cosponsor and vote for a constitutional amendment limiting how long any person can serve in Congress.
District 1 · U.S. House · Rhode Island · Republican

Republican candidate and public-health worker running for Congress. Her campaign says she was born and raised in Boston, is a mother of three daughters, attended Boston Latin School and Suffolk University, and served in AmeriCorps. She says her career began at the nation's first community health center and grew into public-health operations. She says she would lower everyday costs and energy bills, offer tax relief for working families and seniors, and make housing more affordable. She says she would cut red tape for small businesses, expand workforce training, invest in community health centers, and support the ocean economy. She says she supports a parental bill of rights, curriculum transparency, school choice, stronger public safety, and secure borders.

New Hampshire's governor, running for another term. Kelly Ayotte is the state's 83rd governor. Her campaign says she previously served as attorney general and as a U.S. senator, and that she lives in Nashua. She says her first term sped up housing construction, fully funded child-care scholarships, and produced a balanced budget with no new taxes. She says she got cell phones out of classrooms, raised per-student school funding, and put more weight on reading. She says she rewrote bail rules, strengthened laws on domestic violence and trafficking, and used her veto on bills she calls hidden sales taxes.

Navy veteran and small-business CFO running for Georgia's 8th District. His campaign says he served from 1999 to 2002 as a nuclear operator on the USS Henry M. Jackson, and that he was the first Black nuclear operator on that boat during his service. He earned a PhD in public policy from Walden University and is chief financial officer of BroTagz Embroidery. He says he served on the Hapeville zoning board, as a legislative aide to State Senator Donzella James, and on the effort that created the city of South Fulton. He says education is a public good and he would fund affordable learning beyond K-12, including job skills for the district's health-care, retail, and manufacturing workers. He says he would strengthen Medicaid, Medicare, and VA care and fund rural clinics and hospitals, in a district he ties to Robins Air Force Base. He says he would seek federal money for roads, broadband, and utility upgrades, including solar and wind where communities want them, and back labor standards for workers.

Educator and consultant running for lieutenant governor. His campaign says he is a lifelong Oklahoman raised in Skiatook and Broken Arrow, the first in his family to graduate from college, and the holder of a doctorate in administration and leadership. It says he has taught and administered schools, owns Kelly B's Consulting, and serves on the board of Oklahoma City's family justice center. He says he would invest in small business, CareerTech, workforce training, and partnerships with Native nations, and would work on affordable housing and food insecurity. He says he would put more funding into public schools, respect teachers, and keep public dollars in public schools. He says he would expand health-care access in underserved places, promote tourism, and lead the office with public integrity rather than as a career politician.

Longtime manager of teams and operations Kelly Grappe says she spent decades leading teams, managing complex systems, and serving customers and businesses, and that she is not running because she has had a career in politics. She says she is running for secretary of state to take politics out of the office and make it work for the public. She says she will show how votes are cast, protected, counted, and verified, and answer doubts with facts rather than dismiss them. She says she will defend Arkansas's authority to run its own elections and oppose efforts to nationalize that work. She says transparency is one of the ways to build confidence that elections are secure.

Former Sarasota mayor and Democratic nominee for Florida's 16th District His campaign says he is a third-generation Floridian and a single father who grew up working his family's citrus stand near the Sarasota-Bradenton airport. He earned bachelor's and master's degrees from Georgetown, then spent four years in the Peace Corps in northern Guatemala. He later served as a Sarasota commissioner and mayor, built a nonprofit that helped first-generation students reach college without debt, and was a vice president at Eckerd College. He says he would lower insurance, health-care, and prescription costs, restore Medicare and Medicaid funding, and let the government negotiate drug prices. He says he would expand affordable housing and stop Wall Street from buying single-family homes. He says he would protect Tampa Bay, Sarasota Bay, and the coast by prohibiting offshore drilling and enforcing the Clean Water Act.

U.S. representative and OB-GYN. Kelly Morrison's campaign says she is a sixth-generation Minnesotan who practiced as an OB-GYN for more than 20 years and is the first pro-choice OB-GYN elected to Congress. She says she grew up and raised three children in the west metro, and that her husband John is an Army combat veteran. She says she is fighting health-care cuts she says would push Minnesotans off insurance and force hospitals to close, and that no one should go bankrupt to get care. She says she is working to exempt small businesses from tariffs and get them refunds, and to lower the costs of housing and child care. She says she takes no corporate PAC, federal-lobbyist, or dark-money money, supports a constitutional amendment to overturn Citizens United, and backs a ban on stock ownership by presidents, vice presidents, and members of Congress.

Mother, concrete-business owner, and nonprofit founder running for Congress. She says she is a mother of six and grandmother of 12, married to her high school sweetheart, with a business degree from the University of Central Florida. She co-owns a concrete contracting company serving northern Indiana and founded a nonprofit for at-risk youth. She says she would lower costs for housing, health care, education, utilities, and energy, and fight for Medicare for All. She says she would fully fund education from child care to college by taxing Wall Street, and put Hoosiers ahead of corporations and foreign governments. She says she would end U.S. wars in the Middle East and bring troops home, ban stock trading by Congress and the president, and release the Epstein files.

U.S. representative running in a newly drawn district. Ken Calvert's campaign says he is a lifelong Corona resident and a former small-business owner who now chairs the Defense Appropriations Subcommittee. It says that after Proposition 50 he is running in the 40th District, where Corona is the largest city. He says he wrote the law that created E-Verify and wants employers required to use it. He says he has secured more than a billion dollars for transportation, water, and clean-air projects in Riverside County. He says his office has helped veterans and seniors get benefits they are owed.

Information technology entrepreneur and Libertarian candidate for governor Ken Krawchuk's campaign says he has been a registered Libertarian since 1993 and is running for governor with John Thomas for lieutenant governor. The site says he was born in Philadelphia's Feltonville section and has lived in Abington for decades. He says he would veto tax increases, use the line-item veto, phase out the personal income tax, and abolish property taxes. He says he would end the state's monopoly on schooling and privatize public schools because too many students are behind in reading and math. His listed program also says he would eliminate parole for violent criminals, pardon nonviolent drug offenders, and decriminalize marijuana.

Candidate for the U.S. Senate. His campaign calls him a former attorney general who fought federal policies in court and is now running for the Senate. He says he will carry the president's agenda in Washington. He says he will push tax cuts, border security, deportations, an end to what he calls the weaponization of government, and less federal spending. He says he will take on large drug and food companies, seek more transparency in food and health care, and side with a Make America Healthy Again effort. He says he will defend gun rights and laws against abortion, oppose transgender participation in girls' sports, and support a clear legal framework for crypto, including the CLARITY Act.

Independent candidate for governor Kenneth Block is running for governor as an independent. His site says he wants the state government held accountable for waste, failed projects, and rising taxes. He says the state budget is about $15 billion and that residents are not getting services that match what they pay. He points to the Washington Bridge and large technology projects as examples of agencies repeating mistakes. He says his focus is accountability, fixing broken processes, and results for residents.

Third-generation Wyomingite and Vietnam veteran running for governor. He told Wyoming Public Media he was born in Cheyenne in 1950, that his family has worked in Wyoming for three generations, and that he ran a small business in Elk Mountain for 28 years. He does not have a campaign website. He says his first issue is free and open elections: a person should be able to file and run without having to join a party. He says health care is the main reason young people leave, and he wants a statewide system that connects rural clinics. He says he wants small business to grow, and he wants property tax ended for people once they turn 65.

Mechanical engineer running for Utah's 3rd District. He was born in Lehi, worked with mining, petroleum, geothermal, and solar industries, and says much of his career was spent on water, environmental cleanup, and teaching engineers. He says he is running because Washington has grown more divisive and disconnected, and he wants a representative who honors the Constitution. He calls for a moratorium on new data centers and says his priorities include Utah's land and water, Social Security, and the cost of health care. He says he takes no corporate PAC money and has pledged to limit his own term.

Marine veteran running for Congress. Kevin Burge's campaign says he is a Marine veteran with more than 20 years of leadership and deployments to Iraq and Afghanistan, and that he grew up without wealth in Los Alamos. It says his wife immigrated from Honduras, serves in the Texas Army National Guard, and their son attends public school in Tarrant County. He says he would fast-track affordable housing, crack down on corporate landlords, raise the minimum wage, and expand Medicaid. He says he supports Medicare for All, restoring abortion rights, tuition-free public college, and rules so data centers recycle water and limit pollution.

Candidate for U.S. Senate who says he was born on an Air Force base. His campaign says he earned an architectural drafting certificate in high school, used it to pay for an engineering degree, and later earned an MBA. It says that in office he has backed the Trump administration's agenda. He says he has backed bills to recognize groups of veterans and a constitutional amendment aimed at a balanced budget. He says he has voted to fund a border wall and to cut off federal money for sanctuary campuses, and that he wants small businesses to get capital. He says he would protect religious liberty, restrict abortion funding, and protect gun rights, including concealed-carry reciprocity.

Independent U.S. representative running for another term. Kevin Kiley's campaign says he grew up in the communities of the new 6th District, taught high school English, and prosecuted cases as a deputy attorney general before serving in the Assembly and winning a House seat in 2022. It says he chairs the subcommittee covering K-12 education and child care. He says he has worked across parties on measures to lower the cost of gasoline, groceries, utilities, and insurance. He points to a federal grant to ease traffic near Highways 65 and 80 and to a Lake Tahoe restoration law he says funds wildfire mitigation. He says he helped restore Medicare funding for senior programs and is focused on prosecuting violent crime and protecting children from fentanyl.

Former Stockton mayor and Marine veteran running for Congress. Kevin Lincoln's campaign says he was born in Stockton, raised in a military family, and joined the Marines in 2001, later serving on Marine One. It says he then managed a private-security district in Silicon Valley, became a Stockton pastor, and was elected mayor in 2019. He says he would secure the border, enforce immigration laws, and treat fentanyl trafficking as a threat to Valley families. He says he would cut wasteful spending and lower taxes as grocery, gas, and rent costs climb, pointing to budgets he balanced as mayor without a tax increase. He says he would oppose early release and shorter sentences for repeat offenders, and he highlights police pay and budget increases he backed as mayor.

Corporate controller running for Congress in Georgia's 6th District. He says he has spent 30 years as a controller, the person who audits the books, and that he is a fifth-generation native of Cobb County who has lived in the district his whole life. He says voters should be in charge of the people they elect. On schools, he wants federal education money returned to Georgia without federal strings, and he wants student aid and career programs to cover shorter technical training. On the budget, he says Congress should pass a budget through regular order, fund core obligations first, and make every other program justify another appropriation. He also says law enforcement should be funded, federal law should focus on people who have done something, there should be no national gun registry, and defense spending should start from readiness and replenishment rather than the size of the check.

Green Party candidate for lieutenant governor. He says he is the Green Party candidate and that the campaign will depend on voters telling other people, because he expects little corporate-media coverage. He says the lieutenant governor should judge bills by whether they protect health and a decent life for every Texan. He says his first bills would expand city bus fleets, invest in rural family-farm greenhouses and hemp, and change elections to ranked-choice voting, one statewide primary, and a nonpartisan redistricting commission. He says he would appraise property by rent or lease value instead of comparable sales and drop exemptions he calls special-interest favors. He says he favors a moratorium on data centers with strict limits on their electricity and water, and legal THC with rules to protect the public.

U.S. representative running for another term. Kevin Mullin's campaign says he was raised in South San Francisco, has lived on the Peninsula his whole life, and has been a local business owner and a D.J. It says he has served in local, state, and federal office and sits on the Energy and Commerce Committee. He says he would lower housing costs, send federal money to local child-care programs, and update the federal poverty line. He says he is defending medical research and the innovation economy in his district. His campaign also lists health-care costs, climate action, reproductive rights, and a fairer tax policy among his priorities.

Arkansas state senator and pastor Kim Hammer of Benton was elected to the state Senate in 2018 after eight years in the House, and he chairs the Senate Efficiency Committee. He has been pastor of Saline Missionary Baptist Church in Tull since 1978 and chaired the start of Saline Memorial Hospice. His campaign biography says that in the 94th General Assembly he sponsored bills to protect election integrity, including limits on electioneering near voting sites and authority for the legislature to look into voting irregularities. It says his priorities include making motor-vehicle registration and driver's-license renewal simpler. It says he was the lead sponsor of Act 403 of 2021, which lets the legislature end an executive order for a statewide public-health emergency.

Pediatrician and U.S. representative for Washington's 8th District. She chairs the Democratic Doctors Caucus and says travel around the district keeps turning up families squeezed by higher prices. She wrote a bill to suspend the federal gas tax for temporary relief, and she says she is fighting corporate price gouging, grocery mergers, and tariffs that hit farmers and small businesses. She is pushing housing bills, including a permanent housing-affordability proposal and support for the bipartisan Road to Housing package. She wants ACA premium tax credits restored and Republican Medicaid cuts undone so rural hospitals and Apple Health coverage stay in place.

Former prosecutor running for attorney general Kimberly Ahern's campaign says she was a prosecutor, advised two governors and three attorneys general, and worked as a regulator. It says she lives in Providence. She says that as attorney general she would put the criminal unit first and prosecute violent offenders, including murder, sexual assault, domestic violence, and trafficking. She says she would expand diversion so people with mental illness or addiction can get treatment while communities stay safe.
District 7 · U.S. House · North Carolina · Democratic

Social worker and professor running for Congress in North Carolina's 7th District. Her campaign says she is a mother, social worker, and professor who was raised by a Marine and a federal agent. She says she is running because policymakers have ignored hard-working neighbors in southeastern North Carolina. She says she would raise the federal minimum wage, close the overtime salary loophole, and end taxes on tips. She says she would protect Medicare and Medicaid, lower drug costs, and restore cancer-research funding. She says she would fund Head Start, Title I, and career education, and protect drinking water and coastal towns from flooding.

Former Hillsborough County commissioner and Democratic nominee for Florida's 12th District Her campaign says she is a mother, grandmother, and small-business owner who put herself through college, became a certified financial planner, and built an advisory firm. She served as a Hillsborough County commissioner from 2018 to 2022, including during the COVID-19 pandemic. She says she grew up in a working-class family that faced housing insecurity. She says she would fight for affordable housing, infrastructure, and fair wages because she knows what it is like to juggle bills and worry about rent. She says health care is a right and she would expand access, lower prescription costs, and defend reproductive care and mental-health services. She says she would fully fund public schools, raise teacher pay, and make sure veterans get the benefits and care they earned.

Kansas attorney general running for re-election. Kris Kobach's campaign site presents him as the sitting attorney general who filed for another term and highlights work with sheriffs and other law enforcement. The site points to prosecutions involving fentanyl trafficking and to a partnership with federal immigration enforcement that detained people with serious criminal records. It describes a multistate settlement with Meta that requires new safety features for children on Instagram and Facebook. It also describes a push to cut off phone numbers used for scam robocalls.

Arizona attorney general Kris Mayes is Arizona's attorney general. Her campaign calls her a consumer advocate and says she is the second woman, and the first mother, to serve as the state's chief law-enforcement officer and chief attorney. Her campaign says she took on Saudi-owned mega-farms over Arizona's water and corporations she says gouged people on rent and groceries. She says she has gone after drug smugglers, elder abusers, and scammers, and that her priorities include protecting rural groundwater, prosecuting sexual predators, and cracking down on AI that targets kids. Her priorities page also lists overturning tariffs, protecting $2.3 billion in Arizona tax dollars, and protecting Arizonans' freedoms.

U.S. representative for Michigan's 8th District. Her campaign says she grew up in a working-class Michigan town and later led Michigan Head Start, served as chief of staff at the state Department of Education, and was a vice president at the Skillman Foundation. She says her work has centered on child care and education. She says she has introduced bipartisan bills to lower grocery, housing, and medicine costs and to invest in child care, and that she led an effort to let families on SNAP buy hot prepared chicken. She says she worked to keep Saginaw's Social Security office open and opposes cuts to Social Security benefits. She says she wants to ban members of Congress from trading stock on insider information and to reverse Citizens United.

Muralist running for Congress in Tennessee's 1st District. Her campaign says she is a muralist and neighbor, not a career politician, who decided to run because the district's seat was not representing local people. She says corporate interests have been put ahead of human dignity. She says health care should be a right and that workers should be empowered. She says people should have the freedom to live with integrity, and that the campaign relies on grassroots donations rather than corporate PAC money.

Scientist running for Congress. Kristin Hook's campaign says she taught middle-school science through Teach For America, earned a PhD in animal behavior from Cornell, and did postdoctoral research in reproductive biology. It says she later left the lab for federal science and technology work. She says she would lower costs, fight corruption, and stop AI data centers from taking local water and electricity. She says billionaires should pay more, health care and public schools should be expanded, abortion rights restored, and the border secured.

Air Force veteran and nurse practitioner running for Congress in Ohio's 10th District. Kristina Knickerbocker says she is an Air Force veteran, an oncology nurse practitioner, and a mother of two who served as a major and nurse at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base. She says she put herself through school and followed her grandmother into nursing. She says she would ban congressional stock trading, end corporate PAC influence, pass term limits, protect voting rights, and close the lobbying revolving door. She also says she would cut taxes for working families, repeal tariffs that raise prices, build more housing, cap child-care costs, and make data-center companies pay for their own infrastructure.

Former Montana budget director and revenue director. His campaign says he was born in Great Falls, graduated from high school in Miles City, and has worked as a prosecutor, nonprofit leader, revenue director, and budget director. He lives in Billings and is running for the Senate. He says that as revenue director he led the largest income-tax rate cut in state history and put money back with taxpayers. He says that as budget director he helped cut spending and balance the budget. He says he is running to make life more affordable, keep communities safe, and protect what he calls the Montana way of life.

Incumbent · seeking a third term · former state senator Unopposed in the Democratic primary. His office’s public docket has leaned on consumer protection, workers, civil rights, guns, and reproductive rights. Capitol News Illinois counted roughly 90 legal fights with the Trump administration in the last two years. The office says those cases kept Illinois from losing access to more than $8 billion in federal funds. If reelected, keep lawyers on staff and rebuild capacity after lawmakers cut the office budget by $10 million this year. Says corruption has been a priority for eight years, including cases the office cannot announce because the U.S. attorney takes the public lead. Will keep defending state laws on abortion, guns, and civil rights, and joining multistate cases when federal policy hits Illinois funding.

U.S. representative for Maryland's 7th District, seeking another term. His campaign says he was born and raised in Baltimore, graduated with honors from Morgan State, and earned a master's degree at Johns Hopkins. It says he served on the city council and in Congress, led the NAACP, and returned to the House in 2020. The campaign says he still argues for bipartisan work on economic, education, and health-care issues. It highlights his role on the Americans with Disabilities Act, a ban on assault weapons, and the Henrietta Lacks law on diversity in cancer research. It also points to legislation that codified and increased funding for the Minority Business Development Agency.

Pharmacist, pharmacy owner, and farmer. His campaign says he was born and raised on Montana's Hi-Line, worked his family's farm, earned a Doctor of Pharmacy, and founded an independent pharmacy. He is running for the Senate as a Libertarian. He says he still owns his grandfather's farm and wants policy that deals with the stress on farmers and ranchers. He says he is a gun owner and hunter and wants Americans to keep unrestricted access to firearms. He says his work as a pharmacist showed him corruption and other problems in health care.

Business owner running for Congress. Kyle Kirkland's campaign says he arrived in California 40 years ago with $700 and went on to build businesses that created more than 1,000 jobs. It says he owns Club One Casino in Fresno, leads the California Gaming Association, and previously chaired Steinway Musical Instruments. He says housing, food, gas, and health care are too expensive because of over-regulation, and he would restart domestic production to bring costs down. He says government should be audited so tax dollars are not lost to waste and fraud. He says law enforcement needs tools against fentanyl and trafficking, and farmers need more water storage and fewer regulatory barriers.

Army Reserve officer running for Congress. Kyle Rable's campaign says he commissioned through Army ROTC at the University of Toledo, earned a master's while working in restaurants, and is a Texas Tech doctoral student and Army Reserve captain in Lubbock. It says he is running for workers and family farmers he argues both parties have forgotten. He says he would pass fair-pricing rules, limit corporate purchases of single-family homes, and offer tax credits for first-time buyers. He says he would fund child-care training and facilities, curb presidential tariff power, and bring back manufacturing jobs. He says legal paths to citizenship should expand because immigrants are part of West Texas communities.
