District 14 · U.S. House · North Carolina · Democratic

Democratic nominee for Congress in North Carolina's 14th District. Her campaign says she is running to bring the experience of working families, entrepreneurs, and community leaders to Washington. She says her agenda comes from listening to families, workers, business owners, and faith leaders. She says health care is a necessity and that she would protect the Affordable Care Act, cap drug costs, and fund rural hospitals. She says she would raise the federal minimum wage, help small businesses get capital, and invest in affordable housing. She says she would put more federal money into public schools, apprenticeships, and student-debt relief, and demand oversight of federal spending.
District 10 · U.S. House · New Jersey · Democratic

U.S. representative for New Jersey's 10th District. Her campaign says she was born and raised in New Jersey, is a mother, and was the youngest woman elected to the Newark council, where she served as council president. It says she is the first Black woman to represent the 10th District and the youngest person New Jersey has elected to the House. She says she will not back down from attacks on women's rights or from a Justice Department prosecution she ties to her opposition to immigration enforcement. She says these are hard times and that she will keep protecting her community.

U.S. representative running for another term. Lance Gooden's campaign asks voters to send him back to Congress and says he has fought both the political swamp and calls for socialism. He says people are tired of Washington deal-making and of growing calls for socialism. He says another term would be used to protect what he calls God-given freedoms.

State's attorney for Fall River and Oglala Lakota counties Lance Russell's campaign says he is the longtime state's attorney for Fall River County and Oglala Lakota County and that he won the Republican nomination at the state party convention. The site describes him as a proponent of law and order. He says tough-on-crime policies work. He says his daily work is meant to protect the people of South Dakota.

Republican candidate for U.S. Senate. Larry Marker's campaign says that for nearly a decade, as a private citizen, he challenged political elites in New Mexico at personal cost. It says he is running to defend energy jobs, schools, and border security. He says he would defend oil and gas, including hydrogen and nuclear development, and oppose federal permitting delays that he says threaten school funding. He says the border is still a path for fentanyl and that he would back Border Patrol and local police. He says farmers and ranchers should not lose grazing, water, or working land to agency enforcement.

Governor of South Dakota Larry Rhoden's campaign says he is a fourth-generation South Dakotan and a rancher who served 16 years in the legislature and six years as lieutenant governor. It says he became governor and is running to stay in the office. He says his mission is to keep South Dakota strong, safe, and free, with less government and less red tape. He says his legislative record focused on low taxes, strong property rights, and personal freedom. He says he would stand up for law enforcement and for property rights, and keep the state open for business.

Businessman running for Congress in California's 32nd District. Larry Thompson's campaign describes him as a Catholic, a conservative, and an independent-minded Republican who has worked in business. He says he is running to bring together dissatisfied Democrats, conservatives, and no-party-preference voters. He says he will protect family values and wants people to use common sense and civility to find common ground. He says his goal is to get something done, and he asks for a vote in the November 3, 2026 general election.

Attorney and Democratic nominee for Florida's 4th District Her campaign says LaShonda "L.J." Holloway was named a Footsoldier for Justice by the Southern Christian Leadership Conference at 15, attended Howard University, and began a federal career at the Environmental Protection Agency. She graduated from Edward Waters University, earned a law degree at the University of Florida, worked on Capitol Hill for Representative Carrie Meek, and later led a mediation firm and community-lending work. She says she is a fourth-generation resident of the district. She says affordable health care should mean lower premiums and prescription costs, broader Medicare, and care that does not depend on a person's income. She says she would cut red tape and expand capital for small businesses, and make rent lower and homeownership more reachable for working families. She says Social Security should be protected and a full-time wage should cover food, housing, health care, and transportation.

U.S. representative running for another term. Lateefah Simon's campaign says she is a civil-rights advocate running for re-election in the 12th District, a vice chair of the Progressive and Equality caucuses, and the first Muslim woman elected to Congress from California. It says she was born blind, started organizing as a teenager, and lives in Oakland. Her campaign names public safety, affordable housing, homelessness, and job creation among her priorities. She also lists health care for all, reproductive freedom, immigration, disability rights, and LGBTQ rights. She highlights voting rights, climate, transportation, and what she calls a care economy.

U.S. representative running for another term. Laura Friedman's campaign says she served on the Glendale council and as mayor, then in the Assembly, before her election to Congress. It says her earlier work focused on climate, gun violence, reproductive freedom, LGBTQ rights, and housing. She says she is focused on affordable housing, universal health care and child care, and economic security for families. She says she has been a voice for public education, the environment, and safeguarding democracy. She says her legislative work expanded affordable housing and services for people with severe mental illness and people who are homeless.
District 4 · U.S. House · New York · Democratic

U.S. representative for New York's 4th District. Her campaign says she is a lawyer, a mother of four, and the former supervisor of the Town of Hempstead who grew up in Baldwin and is raising her family in Rockville Centre. It says she won the seat in 2024. She says she is committed to keeping families safe, growing the economy, and making Nassau County a place where people can afford a home or a business. She says her first term has focused on working across the aisle to lower the cost of living and bring federal investment back to the county.

Small-business owner running for Congress. Laura Jones's campaign says she is a lifelong Texan, an Army mom, a small-business owner, and a working-class candidate running in 2026. She says the minimum wage should rise and be tied to the cost of living so a full-time worker can cover housing, utilities, and food. She supports Medicare for All, including cutting out insurance middlemen and negotiating drug and medical prices. She says taxes should fall for most households and rise for billionaires and large corporations.

U.S. representative running for another term. Laurel Lee's campaign says she serves on the Judiciary, Energy and Commerce, and House Administration committees. It says she was an impeachment manager in the Mayorkas case and served on the task force on the attempt on President Trump's life and the House artificial-intelligence task force. The site says that under President Trump she is focused on turning conservative priorities into results for the 15th District. It quotes his endorsement of her on the border, innovation, the military and veterans, and the Second Amendment.

U.S. representative running for Colorado's 4th District. Lauren Boebert's campaign says she serves in the U.S. House and is running to represent the 4th District. It says she is the mother of four boys and, before Congress, volunteered with women in the Garfield County Jail and helped gather signatures against the National Popular Vote Compact. She says she believes in personal freedom, the rights of citizens, and the Constitution. She says she has passed House bills on energy production and water rights, and has pushed back on federal land rules she says hurt ranchers and farmers. She says a jobs bill she got signed in 2023 will create 1,000 jobs in southern Colorado.

Special-education teacher running for Congress in Louisiana's 1st District. She says she has spent 17 years beside Louisiana students, families, and educators and is a nationally board-certified special education teacher and union member. She says she is running because people who teach, care for neighbors, and build communities need someone who will fight as hard as they do. She says Louisiana families are squeezed by unaffordable insurance, health-care costs, underfunded schools, and an economy that leaves too many people behind. Her campaign says the district needs lower costs, strong schools and hospitals, safe communities, and a representative who fights for working people. She says she wants to advocate for environmental, constitutional, economic, and health protections in a region she calls overlooked.

Republican nominee who says she is a trafficking survivor and a mother of six. Her campaign says Lauren B. Peña grew up in Austin, survived human trafficking, and rebuilt her life through faith and family. It calls her a constitutional conservative and a longtime Austin resident running for the 37th District. She says she would audit agencies, expose fraud, cut federal spending she ties to inflation, and cut regulations she says are raising energy costs. She says she would defend parental rights and school choice, restore law-enforcement funding, and make veterans' care a priority. She says her first bill would be the SAFE NIGHTS Act to fight human trafficking, and that she would press to release the Epstein files.

Candidate for governor of Tennessee. She says she is a seventh-generation Tennessean who has started businesses with survivors of human trafficking, studied workforce gaps, led nonprofits, and advised organizations. She says she is running because she does not believe a person must be a political extremist to be represented. She says she would eliminate the grocery tax, cap property taxes, and make it possible to own a home. On schools, she says she would end vouchers, reduce testing, limit screens, and add 50,000 child-care slots. She says she would close health-care deserts, challenge middlemen who raise costs, and allow no new data centers until the state sets the rules.

Attorney and former Social Security Administration adviser running for Congress. Lauren Reinhold's site says she has been a Kansan for 32 years and an attorney for 28, including more than 25 years in public institutions as an attorney adviser at the Social Security Administration. She says she resigned after cuts at the agency and is running to defend working families and rural communities in the Big First. She says rural hospitals are the lifeblood of their communities and pledges to rebuild rural health care. She says farm policy should put producers, family operations, and main-street businesses ahead of corporate monopolies. She calls Social Security a hard-earned promise and says she will fight underfunding and political interference that delay benefits.

Libertarian nominee for Indiana secretary of state. Lauri Shillings's site says she is a creative director at the University of Indianapolis, has owned a small business since 2000, chairs the Hamilton County Libertarian Party, and holds a degree in community and nonprofit leadership. She says she is running to restore trust in elections and to keep the office from being used as a party tool. She wants simpler, reliable online services for business filings and records. She says government systems should be efficient and that voters should have clear guides for registration and voting.

Retired Army brigadier general and Democratic nominee for Florida's 13th District Her campaign says she is a retired Army brigadier general, a third-generation veteran, a lawyer, and a mother who put herself through college, including with Army ROTC at Elon. She says neighbors cannot keep up with the cost of housing, health care, insurance, food, and fuel, and that is why she is running. She says she would ban stock trading by officials in Washington, bar former members of Congress from corporate lobbying, and set term limits. She says she would protect the beaches and the coastal economy, and keep the promise of care for veterans and military families.

Republican nominee for New Hampshire's 2nd District. Her campaign says she was born to poor working-class parents in Sichuan and grew up during Mao's Cultural Revolution before coming to the United States. She says she has been married for 34 years, has three adult children, and manages rental properties while speaking about socialism and communism. She says she has signed a pledge to cosponsor and vote for a term-limits amendment of three House terms and two Senate terms. On prices she says special interests and the federal government should get out of managing the economy, energy should include nuclear, oil, solar, coal, and wind, and spending should come down so the debt can be paid down.

U.S. representative running for another term. Linda Sánchez's campaign says she was born in Orange County to Mexican immigrant parents, a mechanic and a teacher, and earned degrees from UC Berkeley and UCLA's law school. It says she is the first woman from the electrical workers' union elected to Congress and a co-founder of the Labor Caucus. She says she is fighting to lower costs for working families and to protect her community from the Trump administration and ICE. She says she wants safe, quality education for children and job growth through innovation and manufacturing. She says workers deserve safe jobs, good wages, and a dignified retirement.

Democratic candidate running for Louisiana's 6th District. She says she grew up stretching a dollar and waiting on doctors, and that she has worked in public schools, served in federal programs, stood with families in crisis, and studied the law. She says she is not a career politician. She says she would make daily life more affordable, protect Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid, lower prescription costs, and raise wages. She says she would bring federal money home for I-10 and I-12, bridges, drainage, flood protection, and affordable flood insurance. She says she would fight violent crime, trafficking, and fentanyl while supporting voting rights, civil rights, and due process.

Chaplain and Iowa state representative running for Congress. She says public service began as a chaplain beside people in their hardest hours, and that as a state representative she has argued government should serve people rather than the powerful. She is running to level the playing field for Iowans who are choosing between rent, food, medicine, and care for family. She says no one should go bankrupt or ration medicine because of a medical emergency, and that rural health care needs urgent changes as cancer rates rise. She says money in politics has fueled partisanship, and that getting money out of politics is necessary for a healthier system. She says Iowa farmers cannot wait another decade for a farm bill, and she opposes private-school vouchers she says benefit the most fortunate.

Speaker of the Minnesota House. Her campaign says she was elected to the Minnesota House in 2018, served on the ROCORI School Board, and ran a small business before that. In 2025 she became Speaker, and the site says she was the first Black lawmaker and the first Republican woman in that post. She says her first priority as governor would be helping families afford their lives, including lower income-tax brackets, lower car-tab fees, and an end to the state tax on Social Security benefits. She says she would create a nonpartisan inspector general to look for fraud in state programs before money leaves the door. She says she would back police, firefighters, and other first responders.

Former Wyoming state senator running for Congress. Her campaign says she was born and raised in Laramie, earned degrees from the University of Wyoming and the University of Oregon and a law degree from Wyoming, and served in the State Senate from Laramie for ten years, from 1985 to 1995, including as minority floor leader. She says she has directed the Albany County Library, practiced law, and worked more than twenty years as a financial advisor. She says public lands should stay public, and she would work with local communities to keep access open rather than sell or transfer the land. She says she would restore Affordable Care Act subsidies, keep the rural-hospital funding she says is set to end, and work toward health coverage for everyone. She says she would cut tariffs, raise taxes on the wealthy, lower taxes for people making under $100,000, and help first-time buyers and renters with housing.

U.S. representative and former financial-services executive. Her campaign says she grew up in Stockbridge, worked through high school and college, and earned a business degree from Northwood University. She says she spent 30 years in the private sector, including American Express and Hantz Financial, and lives in Romeo with her husband Mike and their four children. She says she would cut taxes and regulations on small business and support trade deals that help Michigan farmers and workers. She says she would build a border wall, enforce immigration law, and defend the Second Amendment for law-abiding owners. She says health coverage should be sold across state lines with wider use of health savings accounts, and she opposes taxpayer funding of abortion.

U.S. representative running for another term. Lizzie Fletcher's campaign says she is a Houston native who practiced business litigation at Vinson & Elkins and became the first woman partner at the firm AZA. It says she was first elected in 2018 and serves on Energy and Commerce, where she works on energy and health care. She says the district's values are inclusion, innovation, and collaboration, and that those should produce progress and opportunity. She says she looks for common-sense solutions for Houstonians rather than slogans, including on energy and health policy.

U.S. representative for Pennsylvania's 11th District. Lloyd Smucker owned the Smucker Company for 25 years, served in the state Senate as education committee chair, and was elected to Congress in 2016. His campaign highlights taxes, retirement, health care costs, energy, small business, and family farms. He says he wants to cut taxes, protect retirement, and spend taxpayer dollars more carefully. He also lists lower health care costs, American energy, and support for small businesses and family farms.

U.S. representative for Florida's 23rd District Her campaign says she has represented Palm Beach County in Congress since 2013, after 14 years in the Florida Legislature, including as the first Democratic woman to serve as minority leader, and eight years as mayor of West Palm Beach. She serves on the Appropriations Committee and is the lead Democrat on its national-security subcommittee. She founded the Democratic Women's Caucus and is the mother of a Marine veteran. She says she is fighting cuts to health care, Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid, and working to lower costs for families. She says she works to protect the environment and expand access to housing. She says she is an advocate for women's reproductive freedom.

Attorney running for attorney general. She says she never planned to run, and that she has practiced at a large New York firm, at Micron Technology, and for clients in Idaho. She says earlier attorneys general such as Jim Jones, Larry EchoHawk, and Lawrence Wasden kept the office on the law rather than on politics. She says she will give state agencies and the Land Board legal advice based on the law, and hire for ethics and skill rather than ideology. She says she will issue prompt opinions for legislators and state officials and follow the statute even when that is politically inconvenient. She says she will oppose selling federal public lands in Idaho or closing them to the public.

U.S. representative and working mother from Lowell. She says she was born and raised in a working-class family in Lowell, is the mother of two girls, and has about 25 years of experience in Congress and the private sector. She says she is an optimist who will work with both parties. She says health care is a right, that she would strengthen the Affordable Care Act, and that Medicare should be able to negotiate drug prices. She says she would invest in education from early childhood through apprenticeships and fight student debt. She says she supports a constitutional amendment to overturn Citizens United and a pathway to citizenship alongside updated border security.

U.S. representative and former state legislator running for another term. Lou Correa's campaign says he was raised by working-class parents and has focused since 1998 on helping Orange County families reach the middle class. It says he served in the Assembly, the state Senate, and as an Orange County supervisor before Congress. He says public service should be about people rather than partisan games. He says he wants practical results for a blue-collar district he describes as home to many veterans and Dreamers.

She supports the Equality Act to bar LGBTQ discrimination in work, housing, and credit, and she points to federal infrastructure spending for safe water, high-speed internet, and a cleaner environment.

Former mayor of Hartford running for Congress The campaign says Luke Bronin was mayor of Hartford from 2016 to 2024, where he worked to pull the city back from bankruptcy, add housing, and create the Hartford Youth Service Corps. He says he is running because families are struggling while billionaires get tax breaks. He says he will focus on bringing down costs for housing, health care, groceries, childcare, and elder care. He wants Medicare and Medicaid protected and a push toward universal health care. He says he would abolish ICE, build more housing, and safeguard reproductive freedom.

Engineer and U.S. representative running for another term. She says her Assembly priority was funding for infrastructure, education, and health care in the Valley, along with environmental justice. She says she worked to expand computer-science and climate education across California. Her campaign says that in her first House term she joined Democratic leadership and co-chairs a bipartisan STEM education caucus.

Libertarian candidate for the U.S. Senate. She says Michigan needs a senator who answers to residents rather than a political machine. She says she would protect the Great Lakes and push affordable health care, including Medicaid for all. She calls for fair wages, green jobs, and support for small businesses, and for social, racial, and LGBTQIA+ equity. She says she would defend voting rights and constitutional freedoms, and that she is not beholden to party bosses or corporate donors.

Former teacher running for governor. Her campaign says she is a lifelong Nebraskan, a former teacher, a mother, and a faith leader. She says she wants low taxes, strong schools, and an economy where people can get ahead. She says leaders should follow votes the public has already cast, including on medical marijuana, paid sick leave, the minimum wage, and school vouchers. She says she would push for a government that tells people what they need to know, not only what they want to hear.

U.S. representative for Florida's 27th District Her campaign says she was born in Miami's Little Havana to Cuban parents who fled after Fidel Castro took power. Attorney and former city council member running for Congress in Ohio's 14th District. She says she will defend the Constitution and the rule of law, and that she is looking for practical answers to a health system in which many people lack insurance or carry medical debt. She says she will stand up for workers and regular people and look for common ground instead of sorting the country into two extremes.

Louisville trauma nurse and small-business owner running for Congress. Born in Cuba, she says she arrived in the United States at 21 after an 11-year asylum process, became a citizen, built a small business, and later earned a nursing degree as a single mother of two. Doctor, Army veteran, and U.S. representative running for re-election. She says she is running for re-election because Iowans deserve someone who will keep fighting for them and for Iowa values. On her 2026 tour she says she is fighting for lower health-care costs, lower taxes, and common sense.

U.S. representative and auto-shop owner from southwest Washington. She says she will oppose a national abortion ban and protect the freedom to see a doctor. She wants local police and firefighters paid enough to stay, and she is pushing a right to repair so farmers and customers are not forced back to the manufacturer. She says the campaign takes no corporate PAC money and is working to lower housing, child care, and health-care costs.

U.S. representative working on family costs, health care, and military families. She says she has led bipartisan work on food insecurity and housing for military families in a district she describes as full of service members and veterans.

U.S. representative for Florida's 26th District His campaign says he was born and raised in Florida, spent 14 years in the Florida Legislature, and was the youngest person elected to the Florida Senate, at 31.
